records.text: Global Asset Allocation 19 February 2026 Citi Research 3 Goldilocks view tracking well. Our economists have made the case for decent global growth and benign inflation for 2026. This view is currently tracking well, with the US data momentum improving, and catching up with the rest of the world, at a time when inflation has been benign in most regions, including the US. Liquidity is also forecast to remain supportive, with Citi still seeing three Fed cuts this year, and strong liquidity. This continues to suggest a benign environment for risky assets. We stay long equities but broaden the exposure. We have been overweight equities, to varying degrees, since last April (Global Asset Allocation - House Views April 2025 – Shell shocked: Which eggs in which basket?). Given the strong macro environment, we remain overweight. However, the sector and geographic rotation has been extremely pronounced, partly driven by concerns on the AI side, both in terms of excess capex and AI disruption. While it is likely premature to call for the end of the AI led bubble, given plentiful liquidity, better diversification is essential. We therefore move half of our US overweight into small caps, and on an industry level we downgrade half our tech exposure (moving tech to neutral but keep the tech heavy communications sector as an overweight). records.text: -related investment boom in 2025 is expected to extend into 2026, even if its contribution to growth diminishes. At the same time, personal consumption saw a strong end to 2025, and fiscal impulse from OBBBA and record high tax refunds are in the pipeline for 1H26. These will likely make consumption an even bigger contributor to GDP growth in 2026, which we expect to accelerate to 2.8% (yoy avg). In addition, the fiscal deficit remains above 6% of GDP, without even considering a potential shock depending on the SCOTUS ruling on IEEPA, and the fact that incentives are lined up to juice up the economy in an electoral year. Put together, high investment and low savings (private and public) will sustain a wide current account deficit. So what would it take to close the US current account deficit? Absent any shock that sends the economy into a recession, the sound policy prescription would be to significantly reduce the fiscal deficit to put back public finances on a sustainable path.

Seasonally adjusted & core m/m run-rates expected to remain elevated Headline CPI in January will be muddied by volatile items & electricity subsidies expiring. Stripping out these items, we still see underlying inflation remaining elevated. Our estimate of CPI excluding volatiles, holiday, and electricity is still running at ~3.3% y/y; similar to the trimmed mean CPI. Meanwhile, UBS bottom-up models suggest prices rose 41bps m/m seasonally adjusted (after +20bps). The trimmed mean CPI (seasonally adjusted) on our calculation rose 31bps (after +23bps), which annualises to ~3¾%. We estimate trimmed mean CPI remained at 3.3% y/y, the same as the early consensus. This is also broadly tracking ~in line with UBS forecast for Q1-26 of 0.8% q/q and 3.4% y/y, but slightly below the RBA's implied profile. Meanwhile, housing (excluding utilities) and market services are also expected to pick up modestly in January. Overall, we see the January core measures are still 'too high', and remain inconsistent with inflation returning sustainably to the RBA's inflation target mid-point of 2.5% y/y. records.text: M Idea 2 Imports have likely retraced frontloading effects Volatility in trade was an important feature of the US economy in 2025, as "Liberation Day" increased trade policy uncertainty, contributed to a surge in imports early in the year, and a subsequent retracement in imports thereafter. Net trade subtracted 4.7pp from real GDP growth in 1Q 25, added 4.8pp in 2Q, and added another 1.6pp in 3Q. We estimate it added 0.1pp in 4Q based on our tracking estimate leading into the BEA's first estimate of 4Q 25 US GDP. A key question for the US economy in 2026 is whether trade flows will be a significant driver of volatility in real GDP estimates, or whether the shock to trade volumes following "Liberation Day" has run its course. If trade remains volatile, real GDP estimates will continue to be a noisy signal. If the shock from "Liberation Day" has largely faded, then the signal content from quarterly GDP releases should be stronger. Our view is the post "Liberation Day" volatility is largely behind us. The exception is pharmaceuticals, where there is room for further giveback after the frontloading of chemical imports early last year. records.text: Therapeutic Theme #1: Obesity goes oral...but consumerization remains the near-term market driver Relevant for LLY, PFE, AMGN The obesity drug market demonstrated fundamentally different dynamics compared to any other therapeutic markets in pharmaceutical industry. Although large-cap biopharmaceutical companies compete on the pipeline, consumer demand was shown to determine the winner in this sector. Global obesity/overweight population was estimated to expand to ~4B by 2035 (World Obesity Atlas 2023), representing the largest total addressable market (TAM) in pharmaceutical history, driven by scale, chronicity, and accelerating treatment adoption. A recent survey suggested that 38% users took GLIP-1 drugs solely to lose weight (LINK), showing behavioral patterns of consumer markets. By Dec 2025, GLP-1 drugs represented >7% of all U.S. prescriptions, with patient counts up ~6x since 2019. Notably, LLY's tirzepatide became the world’s best-selling drug in 2025 with revenue of $36.5B, exceeding Keytruda's $31.7B. The direct-to-consumer (DTC) platforms, integrated with telehealth providers and digital pharmacy partners, emerged as fundamental infrastructures to facilitate patient access and cross-sell, becoming the commercial moat for obesity commercialization amid gross-to-net margin compression. records.text: l uptake in 2L post TNFa setting In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), where patients often require long-term—if not lifelong— therapy for a chronic and potentially debilitating condition, our KOLs consistently emphasize that meaningful differentiation in efficacy and/or safety is far more important than formulation advantages alone. While route of administration and dosing convenience can influence initial prescribing, sustained uptake in IBD has historically been driven by therapies that either deliver superior disease control or offer a clearly differentiated long-term safety profile, given the cumulative exposure, infection risk, and malignancy concerns inherent to chronic immunomodulation. Entyvio provides a clear precedent for this dynamic: despite a relatively slower onset and the need for infusion (before September 2023), its gut-selective mechanism and favorable long- term safety profile enabled broad physician comfort and durable use, ultimately supporting blockbuster-level sales. 19 February 2026 226 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

Number of China Biotech Out-Licensing Deals 15 28 42 58 94 157 0 20 40 60 80 100 120 140 160 180 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Source: Company Reports and Barclays Research Large pharma buyers can access de-risked clinical assets directly at the source The efficiency advantages embedded in China’s biotech ecosystem — including streamlined clinical execution, deep R&D talent pools, and rapid patient enrollment driven by large and concentrated populations — have materially reshaped global BD dynamics. From a buyer’s perspective, China-based development enables assets to reach clinically meaningful inflection points earlier and at significantly lower costs. In many instances, Chinese biotech companies are able to generate first-in-human or early Phase I/II data while U.S. peers remain at the preclinical or animal model stage. This time-to-clinic advantage is particularly critical in BD decision-making, as access to early clinical data allows pharma companies to assess efficacy signals, safety margins, and differentiation with greater confidence before committing large amounts of capital. As a result, large-cap pharma has increasingly sourced innovation directly from China rather than waiting for US-based biotech intermediaries to advance assets through early clinical stages. Data source and sample size differences: Per Truflation, the "indexes are based on market price data collected from 30+ different data sources, comprising 15+ million data points. "3 As a result, our interpretation is that the Truflation indices are going to be highly dependent on web scraping for price collection, which is fundamentally different from the BLS/CPI, which relies on significant manual collection and collects a smaller sample of prices. Indeed, the BLS collects about 103,500 consumer prices from about 23,000 places of business each month, as well as approximately 8,400 rents. Only some 8-10% of these prices are collected online, and only about 11-12% of all prices come from secondary sources (Figure 8). Weighting methodology differences: The CPI basket weights are updated annually using the BLS's Consumer Expenditure Survey from two years prior to determine consumer spending patterns. While the CPI allows for some substitution effects through geometric mean formulas in certain categories, the weights are largely lagging and reflective of historical spending patterns. In contrast, Truflation adjusts its component weights annually in February, updating them with daily high-frequency consumption data, enabling it to capture substitution effects more quickly. However, now we're in an environment where specs may be getting retained by portfolios instead of sold, and rolls are financing specials, making it much harder to carry your way to profitability for spec holders. Of course, refi incentive is picking up with effectively 75% new recent production having at least 25bp of incentive to refi (MBSTRIN on Bloomberg). This is more of a ~2019 experience where rolls traded better, rates started to rally, and specs traded rich as investors looked for call protection when rates rallied. The lack of supply in higher coupons is likely to cause higher coupons to trade a bit tight relative to other stories, whereas the special financing on lower coupons is likely to make production coupons occasionally look cheap to the TBA, though right now that isn't happening as much. This leaves us thinking that the higher coupon specs are still reasonable to own on basis, though investors have to recognize that owning premium specs which are already in the money result in being short something like low strike receivers as those higher coupons specs will actually start to refi. Owning production specs vs TBA is actually long those low strike receivers (since the TBA will pay before the specs), so in a way, if someone wanted to be long specs, they could go long par coupon specs vs TBA and long higher coupon specs; we're currently more neutral the sector. records.text: M Update 2 January FOMC minutes: Awaiting clear evidence of disinflation Economic activity: "Expanding at a solid pace" Participants judged that economic activity was “expanding at a solid pace” and generally anticipated that growth would “remain solid in 2026,” while emphasizing that uncertainty around the outlook remained high. Most participants expected growth to be supported by continued favorable financial conditions, fiscal policy, and possibly changes in regulatory policy. Several pointed to the resilience of consumer spending, supported by gains in household wealth, as providing momentum. However, concerns about a "K-shaped" economy remain. The Fed cited information from business contacts and analysis suggesting a distributional split in demand, noting a “disparity between strong sales to higher-income consumers and soft sales to lower- income consumers.” Participants also observed that business fixed investment remained robust, “particularly in the technology sector,” and several participants explicitly tied the growth outlook to the “strong pace of AI-related investment” and “higher productivity growth of recent years,” judging that ongoing productivity gains would be supportive of economic growth. Labor market: "May be stabilizing" after a gradual cool The committee characterized the labor market as in a low-hire/low-fire regime. records.text: Imdelltra in ES-SCLC: We see potential in Front line ES-SCLC While Amgen’s Imdelltra has clearly validated DLL3 as a clinically relevant target in SCLC and demonstrates potential utility even in earlier-line settings, competitive intensity in the DLL3 space is rising rapidly. Earlier DLL3 approaches (including BiTEs) were constrained by tolerability issues such as CRS, but the field has since pivoted toward ADC-based modalities, which appear to offer a more favorable safety profile alongside improving efficacy. As a result, multiple DLL3 ADC programs are now advancing in parallel, including assets from Zai Lab and other global players, compressing the window of differentiation for first movers. In this context, we view Amgen’s current advantage as primarily time-based rather than structurally defensible, with longer-term positioning likely to depend on durability of benefit, safety in broader populations, and head-to-head differentiation versus a growing wave of next-generation DLL3 ADCs. Quite clearly, the accumulation of government debt cannot account for cyclical movements in spreads. However, it does appear to be a quantitatively significant driver of longer-term movements, particularly since the GFC. During the 1990s, spreads generally tightened while debt-to-GDP was increas- ing and widened while it was decreasing, though debt does not appear to explain much of the observed change. Debt-to- GDP was reasonably stable in the pre-GFC 2000s, and thus cannot explain the period of tighter spreads in 2003-2007. Through the lens of the model, this appears to reflect corpo- rate deleveraging and economic recovery after the Dotcom recession. However, fiscal debt does appear to be a quantita- tively important driver of the steady decline in spreads post- GFC. In fact, the magnitude of debt-implied narrowing of high-grade corporate spreads matches quite closely the appar- ent trend decline seen over this time. This suggests further that presently tight credit spreads may not simply be an indi- cator of assessments of the underlying credit quality of issu- ers, but also of a structural deterioration in US fiscal condi- tions. This is because much of the data collection remains manual, relying on BLS staffers making either in- person visits or telephone calls to collect price quotes. Indeed, only 8-10% of all BLS prices are collected online. This seems inefficient in a world where the US consumer's online footprint is rapidly growing. This is not to say there is an unwillingness to modernize the BLS. In 2022, the National Academies of Sciences published a report, "Modernizing the Consumer Price Index for the 21st Century, " that offers guidelines for the BLS to transition CPI measurement away from exclusively in-person data collection and toward large-scale digital data sources. The report emphasizes expanding the use of scanner data, online prices, corporate data feeds and automated collection technologies to improve coverage, accuracy and timeliness, framing these shifts as essential to keeping the CPI representative of modern consumer transactions, which have migrated heavily to online and digitally intermediated markets. That said, this report is already four years old, and there have been few notable changes to price collection methodologies. records.text: alcitonin receptor agonists (e.g., cagrilintide in CagriSema) is selectivity for amylin vs. calcitonin receptors, which theoretically improves tolerability by avoiding aversive nausea/ vomiting pathways driven by calcitonin receptor activation. Phase 1 data has been encouraging with weight loss up to 11.3% at 12 weeks, GI AEs <10% overall, no nausea or vomiting at the most effective dose (Dose 2, ~9% weight loss) and no dose titration was employed in Phase 1. Half-life of 14–16 days also enables weekly dosing. Eloralintide is now in Phase 3 (ENLIGHTEN program) with the Phase 3 ENLIGHTEN-2 targeting primary completion January 2028. Combination studies with tirzepatide are in progress. Bimagrumab (activin type II receptor blocker): A monoclonal antibody with a fundamentally different mechanism — it blocks activin E/GDF3 in adipose (↓fat storage) and activin A/ myostatin in muscle (↑muscle mass). Gimeno emphasized this is "probably energy expenditure" driven, not food-intake driven, making it orthogonal to incretins. The BELIEVE Phase 2B study evaluated IV bimagrumab + semaglutide; additional Phase 2 trials evaluating SC bimagrumab + tirzepatide are underway. A Phase 1 study of a new SC formulation (LY3985863) is ongoing with primary completion April 2026. Brenipatide (next-generation GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist): Now in Phase 3 for alcohol use disorder (RENEW-ALC-1 and RENEW-ALC- 2, n=1,100 each), and Phase 2 for tobacco use disorder, bipolar disorder, and asthma. We have partially accounted for that in our 0.8% trend growth estimate by assuming that reduced Brexit uncertainty leads to faster capital accumulation. That said, we have assumed that the headwind to so-called total factor productivity (TFP) growth (the part of output growth not explained by changes in labour and capital) takes longer to dissipate. But even if the headwind to TFP growth has faded more quickly than our estimates, that is still unlikely to fully explain the recent pickup in productivity growth. This is because even if one assumes a significant productivity level hit from Brexit and supposes that this has largely played out already, the underlying trend excluding the Brexit headwind is still slightly weaker than the latest productivity growth outturns. On February 3, 2026, Pfizer disclosed new data from the Phase 2b VESPER-3 trial of MET-097 (this study includes monthly dosing following weekly titration). The data showed continued weight loss following switch to monthly maintenance dosing as well as dose-dependent reduction in weight loss (3.2mg to 9.6mg monthly). Safety/tolerability profile looks consistent as well with a 5% discontinuation rate during the weekly phase and a 5% discontinuation rate during the monthly phase. Most GI adverse events were mild or moderate. There was one case of severe nausea and one case of severe vomiting across 100+ patients treated. The next key data update will be at the ADA conference June 5-8 where Pfizer will disclose more fulsome VESPER-3 data as well as initial monotherapy and combination data with MET-233 (amylin analog). C. mRNA-4157 (V940) — Personalized Cancer Vaccine mRNA-4157 is a personalized neoantigen cancer vaccine in Phase 3 development, being evaluated in combination with Keytruda in high-risk melanoma. While technically categorized as a vaccine, mRNA-4157 sits at the intersection of oncology and immunization, representing a strategic shift toward higher-value, lower-volume assets within the broader vaccine franchise. ertainty remains concerning other aspects of regional relations with Washington. This is particularly evident in Mexico, which has the closest ties to the US economy and a left-wing president. The recent US intervention in Venezuela and capture of President Nicolás Maduro added another layer of complexity for some political leaders in the region, particularly in Brazil and Colombia. Economic exposure to China – a significant trade and investment partner for many Latam countries – might also become a growing topic of difficult conversations, as Brasilia and other capitals try to strike a neutral balance between the world’s two biggest economies. … with plenty of domestic political drivers: Some key domestic political events are on the agenda as well, and we single out the ones that might have more impact on economic perspectives. We see a split between those countries that will hold – possibly very tight – presidential elections (Brazil, Colombia) and others that experienced leadership change in recent years and are now focused on reform agendas (Argentina, Chile, Mexico). The prospect of installing more fiscally conservative governments is a positive trigger for the two countries facing elections, as both Brazil and Colombia have rising debt/GDP ratios and challenging fiscal conditions that will require action soon. But the political noise associated with elections can result in market volatility, with fiscal issues certainly not a prominent topic so far during the campaigns.

records.text: 18 Global Economic Weekly | 20 February 2026 Why did remittances to other countries in LatAm rise? CEMLA points to migration dynamics: between 2015–2024, the Mexican immigrant population in the US fell by ~500k, while other Latin American groups grew by more than 4mn total (notably Guatemala, Honduras, Cuba, Colombia, and Venezuela). That shift likely boosted non‑Mexican remittance inflows, even as Mexico’s slowed. We think that another relevant factor is that most remittances to Mexico originate in the US, whereas other LatAm countries receive a larger share from outside the US. For example, Spain is an important source of remittances for Colombia. We expect remittances to stabilize, but risks remain to the downside Mexico’s remittance flows in USD appear to be stabilizing (Exhibit 34, Exhibit 35), and we maintain a constructive view on the US outlook (our US economists forecast 2.8% growth in 2026, see report ). As a result, our baseline assumes remittances hold near US$61bn this year. However, risks remain skewed to the downside if US migration enforcement stays tight or intensifies, potentially ahead of the November midterm elections, or if US labor‑market conditions deteriorate (Exhibit 36, Exhibit 37), particularly for Mexican migrants. records.text: Ozurdex (Dexamethasone Intravitreal Implant): Ozurdex is a sustained-release corticosteroid implant indicated for diabetic macular edema, retinal vein occlusion, and non-infectious uveitis, offering differentiated durability versus topical or short-acting injectable steroids. The asset benefits from physician preference for longer dosing intervals in appropriate patients, though uptake is naturally constrained by steroid-related safety considerations. Ozurdex represents a defensible niche product within retinal disease rather than a broad-based growth driver. Vuity (Pilocarpine): Vuity launched as the first FDA-approved eye drop for presbyopia, aiming to replace reading glasses for millions of adults. It works by contracting the iris sphincter muscle (miosis), increasing the depth of focus (pinhole effect). Durysta (Bimatoprost Implant): Durysta is an intracameral implant that slowly releases bimatoprost, lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) for several months. It addresses the critical issue of patient non-compliance with daily eye drops. ABBV-RGX-314 (Surabgene Lomparvovec): ABBV-314 is an AAV8 vector gene therapy that encodes a monoclonal antibody fragment similar to ranibizumab. Once transduced, the retinal cells become "bio-factories, " continuously producing anti-VEGF protein. records.text: 2 Alexander Wise AC (1-212) 622-6205 alexander.c.wise@jpmchase.com Markets Strategy 20 February 2026 J P M O R G A N As the finances of the US government have deteriorated over the past two decades, the government share of the aggregate US bond market has grown markedly. Figure 1 shows the Treasury share of US Aggregate Bond Index outstandings, and the investment-grade corporate spread (right, inverted). As the US federal budget moved into a surplus in the late- 1990s and early-2000s, the Treasury share of the bond market shrank rapidly. In the two decades since then, Treasury out- standings grew rapidly as budget deficits burgeoned, raising the Treasury share of outstandings to ~46% as of the end of 2025. At a low frequency, this shift in the relative supply of Treasuries appears inversely related to the evolution of corpo- rate spreads. This suggests that the growing supply glut of government debt in the last two decades may have steadily diminished the so-called ‘convenience yield’ of US Treasuries – the premium investors are prepared to pay for their per- ceived unique safety and liquidity. In this note, we examine how important this exceptional growth in government indebt- edness has been for the long-run dynamics of credit spreads, and the implications for the asset allocator. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 19 February 2026 Citi Research 3 Global resilience remains the key theme framing our outlook. The available data now point to global growth last year of 3%, which matches our estimate of trend and is a tenth stronger than our January projection. We see this solid growth continuing over the next two years, with the global economy expanding 2.9% this year and 2.8% in 2027 . If our forecast materializes, it will mark six consecutive years of stable, near-trend global performance (Figure 1). Importantly, this stability does not reflect an absence of shocks—the reality has been quite the opposite. Through these years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable series of challenges, including disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war, a sharp tightening of global monetary policy, President Trump’s tariffs, and a range of other pressures and stresses. This broad assessment is echoed by the global purchasing managers indexes, which offer an alternative picture of global performance (Figure 2). Since 2023, these PMIs have told a broadly consistent story. Despite some volatility, the services PMI has pointed to ongoing growth, as readings have cycled comfortably above the 50 breakpoint between expansion and contraction. The global manufacturing sector has been softer, with the PMI hovering near 50, but it has avoided a sustained downturn. In Exhibit 3 , we plot imports of computers and electronic products, an important input into AI-related equipment spending, and pharmaceuticals. It is clear that imports of computers and electronic parts continues to move higher, reflective of the ever-increasing hyperscaler capex spending plans and construction of data centers. We do not see restrictive trade policies as hindering this demand; expected returns to AI spending are likely to outweigh concerns about US trade policy. Pharmaceutical imports rose sharply in early 2025, likely on account of concerns over threatened tariffs on such imports. Pharma manufacturing output was also solid in 2025, on account of persistent tariff threats coming from the Trump administration. We see room for some further give-back in pharmaceutical imports in 2026 should production slow off of last year's robust increase. That said, downside to total imports should be relatively limited given the small weight of these imports in overall goods imports. While capital efficiency and return discipline remain heterogeneous, this policy-driven funding ecosystem has meaningfully lowered the barrier to entry for domestic innovators and enabled China’s biotech sector to transition from generics-focused manufacturing toward an innovation- led model. Capital intensity gives rise to China’s “externalized R&D” (license-out) model The capital-intensive nature of innovative drug development has given rise to a business development model that is distinctive to China’s biotech ecosystem: we now see large-scale licensing-out of pipeline assets to global pharmaceutical partners, which effectively externalizes late-stage R&D and commercialization. Under this model, Chinese biotech companies grant ex- China (or global) rights for promising drug candidates to multinational pharma partners in exchange for upfront payments, development and regulatory milestones, and downstream sales royalties. In practice, the size of a licensing transaction serves as both a financing mechanism and a third- party validation of R&D quality. Larger upfront payments and milestone packages not only provide meaningful non-dilutive capital to fund internal pipelines, but also signal increasing confidence from global buyers in the scientific robustness, clinical differentiation, and execution capabilities of Chinese developers, in our view. Inluriyo has a solid and differentiated safety/tolerability profile which we believe will be highly beneficial in combination with other therapies in breast cancer. Secondly, Eli Lilly acquired Scorpion Therapeutics' mutant selective PI3Kalpha inhibitor (STX-478) in January 2025. We believe this asset could help offset Verzenio sales (post LOE) in the 1L metastatic HR+/HER2- breast cancer setting. Adjuvant HR+/HER2- breast cancer represents a significant market opportunity given the size of the patient population is ~3x higher compared to the 1L metastatic disease setting (~270k patients in U.S. + Major 5 EU countries in adjuvant setting compared to ~90k patients in 1L metastatic setting). Eli Lilly already has a presence in this setting with abemaciclib (CDK4/6 inhibitor) approved in October 2021 based on the monarchE trial conducted in high-risk patients (~20% of adjuvant patient population) and we note the EMBER-4 trial is being conducted in a very similar (high-risk) patient population compared to monarchE. We note the recent positive results from Roche's oral SERD trial in the adjuvant setting (lidERA) provides important de-risking for the oral SERD class in the adjuvant setting, with the caveat being the control arm used. We have been positioned for a return of the AI trade via our long US and China equities, and reflation via our long Japan equities. Given the relatively higher concentration of defensive stocks in the UK equity index, relative to most other major country-level indices, we’ve been underweight the UK market. AI worries instead have caused a rotation into cyclical and defensives. Given the light positioning in defensives, the rotation has caused outsized moves in the sector and has supported the UK market. Besides that, mining stocks Q4 through Q1 have also outperformed on the commodities bull run and supported the UK market. Lastly, in Debating the rotation (13-Feb-26) we turned bearish GBP medium-term on political risks. While we think these risks are overblown near-term, we do think they will resurface in late Q2 / early Q3 and remain a drag on GBP . Given ~80% of FTSE100 revenues are coming from abroad, GBP weakness can become a tailwind for UK equities. Given we are cutting our China long and the UK is enjoying some tailwinds, we also cut our UK underweight by half, so to keep our total equity position stable to +1. We still expect Spain to conduct its 2nd syndication (long-end of the curve) of the year in February (next week), as it has been doing consistently over the past few years. The lack of syndications coincided with a notable drop in term premia, with our 5s10s TP proxy down 4bp from its peak earlier in February. The combined front-end rally and lower term premia drove the Bund yield lower, by almost 15bp from its February peak. Nonetheless, this move wasn’t EUR rates specific as both 10y UST & UKT outperformed vs the Bund within this timeframe. Despite the Bund rally and some broader risk-off sentiment, the average 10yr EGB spread vs Bund has stayed within a tight trading range (2bp) in February and has exhibited a lower beta to other risky assets. Versus iTraxx Main, EGB spreads have continued outperforming year-to-date and especially in February. When it comes to individual countries, OATs, OLOs & Irish bonds remain the best YTD performers in beta-adjusted terms. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 20 February 2026 Citi Research 3 Momentum dominates Interest rates continued to decline this week, with trend following evident. We think the 50-day moving averages have become key levels for futures and for the 10y swap in particular, while volatility has risen once these levels have been broken. However, the market has been somewhat stagnant in this area, which is clearly different from the moves in the super-long sector. In the money market caution regarding an early rate hike has receded. Pricing for the March meeting has declined to around 10% and we think the market is conscious of underperformance by GDP and a slowdown in inflation. However, the weak yen environment continues, with the USDJPY having rebounded to around ¥155/$. US rates continue to be impacted by USD performance, but it will be difficult to reduce the pricing of a big rate hike. In fact, the market continues to fully price in two rate hikes by year-end. Both ends of the curve have relatively firm support and the pricing in of risk, including fiscal risk, is evident around 10y to maturity. There are insufficient catalysts to force the 10y bond yield below 2%, and upside will tend to be limited. Once this pattern collapses, we think there may be position adjustment unrelated to fundamentals, as there was this week. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 20 February 2026 Citi Research 7 At the last Z5-H6 change in the current contract month, calendar remained in a narrow zone close to the top of the expected range. Trading volume was larger by around 70,000 contracts on the ask side than the bid side. This is consistent with the active construction of short positions on concern about fiscal policy and rate hike pricing. However, the peak in the short roll was concentrated sooner than has been the past pattern (December 5 or six trading days before the final day of trading). Once the long roll started in full, flows were easily digested and daily trading volume on the bid side did not rise above that on the ask side. As a result, calendar started to trend upward again before the last day of trading, which is a pattern not seen before. Another reason calendar remained high was that the H6 IRR remained low. Even once it became largely certain that the BoJ would hike, the IRR remained mostly within the 40bp–50bp range. This is roughly 25bp lower relative to the OIS. We think this was impacted by the view that the repo rate would remain low directly after a rate hike and at the turn-of-the-year, as well by big shorts in the H6. Figure 10. Heme Oncology - hematology portfolio moving past Revlimid CELMODs in Multiple Myeloma We are positive on Bristol Myers' portfolio of CELMoDs (Cereblon E3 ligase modulators; iberdomide and mezigdomide). We see significant potential for these agents to replace standard of care immunomodulatory drugs (lenalidomide and pomalidomide); both of which hold ~40% market share in multiple myeloma. We note CELMoDs from BMS have enhanced binding affinity between cereblon and its substrates, driving more potent and faster degradation of disease related proteins. On Sept. 23, 2025, Bristol Myers announced that the Phase 3 (EXCALIBER-RRMM) trial of iberdomide (CELMoD) combined with daratumumab and dexamethasone in 2L+ setting achieved a statistically significant improvement in minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity rates compared with control arm; an important positive data point in our view that meaningfully de-risks the program. Based on this data, Bristol Myers submitted an NDA. The trial is ongoing to evaluate the other dual-primary endpoint of progression-free survival (PFS) expected to read out in 2026. Also, on 2/17/26, Bristol Myers announced FDA acceptance of the NDA with a PDUFA date of August, 17, 2026 (under priority review). Iberdomide has breakthrough therapy designation, and the review is being conducted under Project Orbis (enabling concurrent review by health authorities in several other countries). records.text: M Idea 2 Rising Capex Risks Are Underappreciated We ran an AI query for both capex and M&A risks by hospital system. Unsurprisingly, AI found more capex risk than M&A risk. This makes sense, because capex is well- telegraphed ahead of time, whereas M&A is by nature kept confidential. Even so, a few things stood out to us: • M&A scores were significantly lower than capex scores, reflecting the fact that many systems are still integrating earlier acquisitions. • Every system we looked at had some exposure to M&A risk. If you don't want M&A exposure, don't buy hospital bonds. On the capex front, we were surprised by how many systems had some kind of published facilities plan: • Our analysis identifies about $35 billion of capital plans among the roughly 75 largest not-for-profit hospital systems. For the following 100 smaller systems, AI tallied another $35 billion. These plans generally highlight new or special capital projects, not run-of-the-mill capex. • Even if a good share of this capex is already in process, the number is large enough to expect a meaningful uptick in new money supply. • This number strikes us as conceivable, considering that annual hospital capital expenditures across a dataset of ~1500 hospitals total about $100 billion. All in, we have relatively higher conviction in the pace of NFP hospital capex over the next 3-5 years compared to our views before our analysis. Completing a capital plan drives upgrades – starting one does not We utilized AI to review recent upgrade and downgrade actions. Our conclusion: with many systems pondering capital plans, it seems plausible that upgrade momentum may slow from here.

From a safety perspective, all four agents exhibited generally favorable and manageable profiles in Phase 2, with no signals of hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity, or thrombotic risk. Injection-site reactions were observed with RNA-based therapies but were largely mild and infrequent, while the oral agent avoided injection-related adverse events entirely. Overall discontinuation rates were low across programs, supporting advancement into Phase 3 outcome studies, although selected safety observations (e.g., glycemic signals) likely warrant continued monitoring in larger trials. Olpasiran (siRNA) Delivered among the deepest Lp(a) reductions reported to date (≈94–97%), with effects sustained for over 12 months following dosing. The combination of high efficacy and extended durability underpins a low-frequency dosing paradigm. Safety was generally favorable, with mostly mild injection-site reactions; a modest hyperglycemia imbalance versus placebo was observed and remains an area for ongoing Phase 3 surveillance. Modeling CPI components with Truflation We next look to model CPI components using only Truflation inputs. At a high level, rather than presume a priori the best corresponding Truflation index for the CPI component in question (eg, CPI apparel ~ Truflation clothing & footwear), we take a more agnostic approach and allow for informational content to potentially show up in other categories as well. To avoid over-fitting the model, we penalize incorporation of useless explanatory variables, allowing the regression structure to determine what actually has valuable informational content. To do this, we deploy a technique called an elastic net (for more details, see the technical appendix, including a discussion on why we chose an elastic net over LASSO). As a smell test, we will check the resulting identified explanatory variables to ensure that they should be intuitively related, and that the model is not just picking up statistical nonsense. records.text: 9. Limited spillovers to EM from global vol for now. Amid the ‘software sell-off’ and ‘momentum’ unwind in crowded positions, the spillovers to EM assets have remained relatively contained. EM equities have been at the forefront again, with double-digit returns YTD, spread across the chip-heavy markets in North Asia and commodity-heavy markets outside Asia. In contrast to last year, when valuation expansion contributed nearly half of the 30% EM equity index gains, this year’s gains are almost entirely driven by earnings upgrades at an EM index level, with revisions concentrated in those tech and commodity markets. There have also been fundamentally driven gains in EM fixed income as the steady EM disinflation trend is now encompassing the last hawkish laggards from last year (Hungary and Brazil), where policymakers are gearing up to cut rates in coming months. As inflows into EM have picked up on the back of strong performance, there is increasing concern about whether EM assets could be vulnerable to global market volatility, even if domestic macro fundamentals are sound. That is a reasonable concern but investor perception of the riskiness of EM assets now lags reality. EM assets broadly are demonstrating more resilience over time, and over the past five years—a period rich in global shocks—that resilience is especially striking in the case of EM local rates, which now act to ease local financial conditions in response to global shocks, similar to DM rates. The sharp contraction of Gardasil revenue in China—down 55% in Q2 2025 and continuing to drag in 24% Q3—is in our view not merely a cyclical inventory adjustment but a structural reset of the market. We see multiple factors that contributed into this dynamic: • The Inventory Built: Between 2021 and 2023, Merck aggressively shipped supply to Zhifei. As China’s economy slowed and consumer discretionary spending on healthcare contracted, end-user demand decoupled from shipment volume. This resulted in a massive inventory build at the distributor level. Merck consequently paused shipments through the end of 2025 to allow the channel to clear. • Competitive Commoditization: The most significant long-term threat is the rise of domestic competition. Such an outcome will lead to an adverse reaction at the long end as markets would start to put weight on IEEPA tariffs not being replaced which will hurt the fiscal profile. We estimate that a persistent increase in annual budget deficits of 1pp GDP would tighten 30y swap spreads by 15bp and push 30y Treasury yields higher by 40bp ( Figures 13 and 14). IEEPA tariffs account for about 0.5-0.7% GDP in revenues. Hence, if the market increases the probability of the IEEPA tariffs not being replaced by 50%, long-term yields would go up by about 10-15bp (=50%*60%*40bp) and 30y swap spreads will tighten by 5bp (=50%*60%*15bp). While it hard to know in this scenario what probability the market would assign to the tariffs being replaced, the longer a replacement is delayed, the probability would rise. A third scenario is that the Supreme Court rules in favor of the the administration and IEEPA tariffs are deemed legal. There is likely to be a knee-jerk rally at the long end, given the focus on this risk and this scenario currently priced in the prediction markets with just a 25% probability. However, we think that the market reaction should be limited as it does not appear to be pricing in a worsening of the fiscal profile. 19 February 2026 8

records.text: M Idea 26 A note on methodology We use changes in month-to-month holdings to analyze overseas demand. To account for changes in market value each month, we adjust holdings changes by the Treasury's published monthly valuation changes for data from February 2023 to the present. For historical data without valuation change reporting, we approximate valuation changes using the MoM change in the Bloomberg Agency MBS index price. We subtract this change in portfolio value from the recorded month-on-month difference in portfolio value to determine if there was real buying or selling of mortgages that month. We note that the Treasury also publishes net transactions data, not adjusted for market value. There exists a substantial difference between our calculation of net flows from holdings data compared to the published net transactions data. Adjusting our calculations with the new monthly valuation change data seems to improve the correlation for recent data. The inconsistency between holdings data and transactions data has been previously acknowledged in a federal register, which also includes data improvement strategies. The Federal Reserve has similarly highlighted reconciliation challenges between the holdings data and the transactions data. Merck, Bristol Myers and Pfizer have the largest oncology businesses among our coverage universe with significant contribution to total company revenue (~55%, ~50%, ~27%, respectively) as shown below. We are starting to see novel modalities emerging and racing to define potential novel treatment paradigms across solid tumors in the post-Keytruda era. Our thesis for solid tumors is that we are unlikely to see a Keytruda 2.0 with its breadth and depth

AI’s labor market impact is becoming more visible but remains narrow. n Employment in specific industries like marketing, graphic design, customer service, and especially tech where AI-use cases have been established is contracting by 5-10k/month, and the economy-wide correlation between industry-level AI adoption and job growth is beginning to point towards a small (although still statistically insignificant) employment headwind. That said, there is no meaningful correlation between AI adoption and other labor market slack measures, and only 8k employees were affected by corporate layoffs attributed to AI in January. Furthermore, construction jobs exposed to the data center build-out have increased by 216k since 2022 (vs. broader construction employment trends), and the share of AI-related job postings continues to rise in the US and other major DMs. We continue to observe large impacts on labor productivity in the limited areas n where generative AI has been deployed. Metsera platform differentiation A key differentiation for Metsera revolves around its half-life extension technology. Metsera highlights its HALO platform (Half-life Augmentation by Lipid Optimization) to enable extended half-life. This is achieved by covalently attaching a fatty molecule ("lipidation") to NuSH (nutrient stimulated hormone) peptides. This lipidation is traditionally done in the middle of a peptide, creating strong binding to albumin and requiring dissociation from albumin in order to bind to GLP1 (left diagram, figure below). In contrast, HALO uses lipidation at the end of the peptide (C or N terminal). As a result, there is no dissociation required from albumin for binding to GLP1 and the peptide binds simultaneously to serum albumin and GLP1, reducing clearance and enzymatic degradation (right diagram, see Figure below). 19 February 2026 250 Barclays | U.S

records.text: 6 Europe Economic Weekly | 20 February 2026 The other cliff ahead While the backdrop for Spain remains constructive, we want to focus in this report on a non-immediate but not too distant cliff – the demographic one. Employment (and population growth) should still help in the very short term and is part of the reason we expect above-average growth. But demographics will act as a constraint in the not-too- distant future, both in terms of long-term growth and public finances. Potential output at risk Exhibit 8 shows Bank of Spain´s estimates of potential growth both in the near term (2025-2028) and immediately after (2029-2035). In the next 2-3 years, as long as recent immigration flows show some persistence, Spain’s potential growth would not be far from 2%, almost twice that of the Euro area. But that is unlikely to last. Under realistic assumptions for population growth (Eurostat), potential growth is likely to drop to 1.3% in 2029-2035. And even under more optimistic scenarios for population growth (based on the projections of the Spanish statistical institute INE), the deceleration in potential growth would be sizeable. records.text: AI-driven disruption: Dispersion is rising. After initially reshaping software, AI-driven disruption is increasingly spreading into insurance, brokers, and other industries where workflows are susceptible to automation. In credit markets, the read-through has been wider secondary spreads in the most exposed industries and tepid issuance in the primary market, often with sizable new issue concessions, for affected sectors. Using our Economics and Portfolio Strategy colleagues’ automation-exposure estimates, we find that year-to-date spread changes across IG and HY industries have been correlated with automation exposure, with the most pronounced underperformance at the high-exposure end of the spectrum (Exhibit 8 and 9). We expect this dynamic to persist for two reasons. First, AI-native entrants are still in the early stages, suggesting more industries will contend with disruption risk over time. Second, dispersion within industries should rise as firms’ outcomes diverge based on execution of AI adoption strategies, making issuer-specific risk more salient. For investors, calibrating fair-value for exposed sectors will get harder, but the alpha generating opportunity set for active managers should expand as security selection among firms that can defensively adapt (or benefit) becomes more important. records.text: Today’s market pressures have some parallels to those in 2013. PM Takaichi’s Abenomics-like policy proposals have resulted in significant Yen weakness, and CHF has seen strong appreciation pressures from rising geopolitical risks and broader European FX outperformance. These dynamics have been overwhelmingly CHF/JPY positive in recent months. However, the market’s more recent reassessment of what the Japanese administration’s policies will mean for Japan has shifted the market response in CHF/JPY over the past few weeks. In direct contrast to 2013, the market has now repriced inflation lower, real rates higher, and a stronger JPY. There are some clear differences in Japan’s economic backdrop that could explain some of the difference in reaction, though. The Yen is much weaker, and Japan is further along in its process of raising inflation and normalizing monetary policy, so a more muted version of those 2013 pressures may be likely. However, we argue that until the BoJ moves towards more expeditious hikes or fiscal policy becomes more restrained, Yen depreciation pressures are likely to persist. The burden is now on the BoJ to deliver the degree of tightening priced into real rates. If they do not, markets may rebuild inflation risks and fiscal risk premia into the long end of the JGB curve and CHF/JPY. records.text: 10 Todd E. Clark, Kenneth D. West. 2007. Approximately normal tests for equal predictive accuracy in nested models. Journal of Econometrics, Volume 138, Issue 1. Technical Appendix: Elastic net with expanding- window cross-validation This appendix describes the empirical framework used to model and forecast monthly percentage changes in CPI NSA components using high-frequency Truflation data. The methodology combines elastic net regularization, expanding-window out-of-sample forecasting, seasonality controls, and a Clark & West (2007)10 forecast-comparison test. The goal is to evaluate whether Truflation-based signals provide statistically significant incremental information beyond seasonal patterns alone. Model specification The analysis is run separately for each major CPI category. For each series, the predictor matrix X includes: • Monthly changes in Truflation category-level indices • One-month lags of those same changes • A full set of month-fixed-effect dummies to capture seasonality The dependent variable is the m/m percentage change in each CPI NSA subcomponent. This structure allows the model to capture contemporaneous alternative-data price signals, delayed passthrough from Truflation to CPI, and stable seasonal patterns in CPI NSA. Elastic net regularization Elastic net structures use both variable selection and coefficient stabilization, allowing the model to identify a small set of meaningful predictors while handling strong collinearity across inputs. Those are annual numbers and lagged estimates. Real time data, on the other hand, is scarce. We know from the national accounts that EA total investment rebounded mid-2024 and is running at 2.6%Y in 3Q25, on the back of solid spending in intellectual property, non-housing construction and machinery and equipment. How much of that might be AI-related? We can only give a rough guess from indirect observations. One avenue is to look at EA imports of "AI-related goods" (such as processors or memory chips). They show solid growth rates (ca 10%Y), but that is from a low base and nothing close to the uptick observed in the US. Another angle is to look at activity in sectors likely to benefit from AI-investment such as computer programming or information services. Here too, we see relatively healthy growth rates (ca 7%Y) – a touch higher than in previous years, but certainly not looking exponential. If we assume "AI-related" investment grows at this kind of pace ie 7- 10%Y, it would contribute ca 70bp to total investment and 15bp to GDP (but we would also need to deduct the high import content). Following drone attacks, companies redirected capex toward refinery repairs, with drilling activity easing from the summer as infrastructure disruptions intensified. Budgets were also trimmed due to wider discounts, a stronger rouble, and tighter domestic financing. In parallel, firms have shifted toward efficiency: most drilling now offsets natural declines rather than materially expanding well counts, and overall activity remains at historically high levels (Figure 7). While investment conditions have tightened, we do not expect a material impact on near‑term production. Concerns about a narrowing buyer base—especially in India—are understandable but overdone, in our view. Russian crude remains among the cheapest grades available locally, which benefits both India and China (Figure 9). Our base case assumes India maintains imports around 1 mbd (roughly 600 kbd below 2025 levels), while China takes about 1.6 mbd (Figures 10 & 11) ( Russian oil re-rerouted again—India steps back, China steps in , 4 February 2026). Year-to-date, China has imported around 2.0 mbd from Russia, well above its informal 20% cap on any single supplier’s share—a development worth monitoring (Figure 8). Catalyst.Metric: Working week reduction from 48 to 40 hours

records.text: Reducing working hours over a four-year period: The labor reform would cut the legal working week to 40 hours from 48 over a four-year period (2027-2030). Additionally, permitted overtime at double pay would rise to 12 hours/week from 9, with a ceiling at 4 hours daily for a maximum of 4 days/week. Any overtime beyond this would be at triple pay. Finally, the Ministry of Labor and Social Welfare will seek to keep an electronic record of employed persons. The Ministry of Economy estimates that the reform will affect 13.4 million people in total. Shorter working day implies higher unit labor costs: In other countries, reduced working hours and minimum wages rising faster than inflation (as is now the case in Mexico) have resulted in declines in formal employment and elevated labor costs. The increased Mexican minimum wage has led to higher labor expenses – for example, remuneration of wage-earners (salaries, wages and benefits) rose from 10.5% of GDP in 2018 to 13.6% in 2024. The reform implies a new round of increases in labor costs. Formal sector will be affected, greatest impact is in 2027: Economic figures indicate that the reform will affect only the formal labor sector in Mexico. We estimate that over 14.2 million Mexicans work more than 40 hours/week. Of this group, 11 million work more than 46 hours/week, and they are the ones who will feel the effect next year. records.text: Investor Expectations for Policy in 2026 Similar to the surveys of investors we conducted just before and after the start of the second Trump administration, we recently surveyed over 200 investors in collaboration with our Marquee team regarding their expectations for policy over the coming year. Most Investors Expect Benign Tariff Policy for 2026 Most respondents expect the Supreme Court to block the “reciprocal” tariffs the Trump administration imposed in 2025, but slightly less than half expect the court to block country-specific tariffs on Canada, China, and Mexico that President Trump declared under separate emergencies. Our own view is that the court is likely to block the reciprocal and the country-specific tariffs, but that the court’s decision on the latter set of tariffs is a closer call as they deal more directly with foreign policy issues, on which the court has typically shown greater deference to the President. Despite the broad expectation among respondents that the Supreme Court will block at least some of the tariffs, only 30% expect the ruling to lead to tariff refunds. It would not be unprecedented for the Supreme Court to apply relief only prospectively, and we do not expect the Supreme Court decision to explicitly allow for refunds of tariffs other than those paid by the small businesses that brought the case. Meanwhile, the fiscal deficit – the key theme for markets — is almost a nonexistent concern for voters. But the fiscal stance adopted by the next administration will do much to shape Brazil’s macroeconomic regime from 2027 onward, as we laid out in Brazil: Dual election-driven scenarios for 2026, dated January 20). A reform-driven path would aim to restrain spending growth, de-link minimum-wage adjustments from past real GDP growth, keep education and health expenditures within the fiscal framework, and revise tax subsidies and social-benefit programs. This would probably lead to lower risk premia, a stronger BRL and anchored inflation expectations, possibly allowing the BCB to reach neutral rates in 2027. By contrast, a status quo approach would rely on revenue-side measures and ad-hoc rules for judicial claims and spending on education and health. This would likely keep risk premia elevated and increase FX volatility, potentially forcing the BCB to halt easing sooner than anticipated and possibly even resume tightening. Our base case sees a middle ground: modestly lower growth in government spending coupled with stronger consumption-driven tax receipts and fewer low-value judicial claims. This balanced trajectory preserves the favorable economic momentum that could aid Lula but does not address the debt-sustainability concerns that have long overshadowed Brazil’s economic outlook. records.text: Another reason for the strength in TFP growth over the last two years could simply be a cyclical recovery. As we have previously argued, recent fluctuations in TFP could simply have resulted from changes in how intensively businesses use labour and capital rather than changes in potential output. The fact that TFP dropped notably relative to trend in 2022 and 2023 and then rebounded sharply suggests that much of the growth in 2024 could have resulted from these cyclical factors. While this story might appear to conflict with continued declines in capacity utilisation over the last two years, it would be consistent with reports that labour hoarding was widespread in 2022 and 2023 but then became less prevalent. That would also reconcile with survey data suggesting that employment growth was unusually firm in the face of declining output growth in 2022 and 2023 before reversing the following year. As such, we agree with the Bank’s assessment in the February MPR that cyclical factors could explain part of the recent strength in productivity. records.text: Coordination between monetary and fiscal authorities is less common outside of crises in G10 economies. In the case of Japan though, in 2013, the BoJ took a series of steps to address Japan’s economic stagnation in explicit coordination with the administration’s “Abenomics” policy, which has strongly informed PM Takaichi’s current policy platform. The first arrow of Abenomics was “aggressive monetary policy.” As part of this arrow, the government and BoJ jointly introduced aggressive easing measures designed to support higher growth and inflation through a weaker currency. At the outset of Abenomics, markets saw a significant shift higher in inflation expectations alongside a large drop in real interest rates and material JPY weakness, which we argued at the time was a reaction consistent with an exit from a liquidity trap. JPY depreciated by over 50% versus USD from late-2012 through end-2014. At the same time, CHF was seeing strong appreciation pressure in the aftermath of the GFC. SNB officials imposed a floor in EUR/CHF at 1.20 as a response, arguing that the overvaluation of the Franc—which reached over 20% at its peak—posed a threat to the Swiss economy (Exhibit 5). This floor held until 2015, and while JPY weakness pushed CHF/JPY higher, it dampened the extent of the move stronger in CHF. All eyes will be on the Supreme Court ruling on the legality of the IEEPA tariffs, which may be issued as early as this Friday. We believe the rates market's baseline is that the projected tariff revenue stream will not be affected regardless of the Supreme court ruling. Hence, the response of the administration to a ruling will be key to watch. • If the Supreme Court rules against the administration, which in turn immediately puts in• place other legal authorities to revert to the status quo outcome, there would likely to be little effect on the rates market, as that is the baseline anyway. • However, if the administration remains silent on the replacement, there would likely be an• adverse reaction at the long end (both in yields and swap spreads), as markets would start to put some weight on IEEPA tariffs not being replaced eventually, which would hurt the fiscal profile. • On the other hand, if the Supreme Court rules in favor of the the administration, it would be a• surprising development, but any knee-jerk rally would likely be limited, as markets do not appear to be pricing in a worsening of the fiscal profile in the first place. records.text: Key marketed products face LOE risk, but we see early signs of mitigation We see near-term LOE risk and competitive pressure across multiple key immunology assets. The Prolia and Xgeva franchises lost exclusivity in 2025; Enbrel will be included in the IRA in 2026 and face biosimilar competition in 2028. Otezla is expected to face competition from newer agents and lose exclusivity in 2028. However, as the largest biosimilars player with a strong track record of managing LOE risk, we see potential for the company to mitigate upcoming LOEs, with the initial post-LOE momentum of the denosumab franchise signaling manageable erosion rather than a cliff. Prolia and Xgeva LOE in 2025: Prolia and Xgeva are both based on densosumab, an anti- EANKL mAb to inhibit osteoclast formation and bone resorption. Prolia is primarily used to treat osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men at high risk of fracture, while Xgeva is approved to prevent skeletal-related events in patients with bone metastases and to treat giant cell tumors of the bone.Prolia reported a 10% Y/Y decline in 4Q25, suggesting manageable erosion in the early post-LOE period. records.text: 20 February 2026 Fixed Income Blog Page 16 Deutsche Bank AG Seasonality Framework: In this section, we examine the seasonality patterns across a range of rates products with a focus on EUR rates. We split the calendar year to 24 half- month periods for which we estimate a seasonal signal. The data we analyze are demeaned (to neutralize for periods of persistently rising or falling rates or spreads), while we also exclude extreme data points by looking at the trimmed mean (20%) adjusted for standard deviation (stronger signal for variables with smaller standard deviation). Among other things, we look at the median change and the hit ratio. The combination of all these metrics leads to a seasonality score that is reflected in the colour-coded heatmap in our table. To determine the strength of the signal, we also look at the success rate of the seasonal signal achieved over the five most recent years. For more details regarding our framework, please see the relevant publication. records.text: Software selloff in loans: Early signs of rotation. Following the first leg of the selloff in software-related loans, attention has shifted to the industry’s long tail, with investors flagging software-reliant issuers across Financial Services, Healthcare and Media/Communications. At the same time, the market’s broader rotation toward cyclical, “real asset” exposures has produced a narrow set of winners year to date. Basic Industrials stands out as the only loan sector showing meaningful price appreciation while the broader market has largely traded softer to sideways (Exhibit 10). In our view, part of the challenge is underwriting: with limited upside convexity in their mandate, many CLO managers are reluctant to add exposure to software and technology business models that could be in the midst of structural change. Recent trading data suggest CLO managers have been net sellers of Technology and Business Services loans, at the lowest average sale prices seen over the past year (Exhibit 11). While it is still early, the relative resilience in Energy and the nascent improvement in Chemicals (Exhibit 12) suggest risk-averse CLO managers are more comfortable selecting from already stressed capital structures where the outlook is improving vs. sectors facing a potential paradigm shift. records.text: Myqorzo with a differentiated drug profile was approved at YE25 with a favorable label Myqorzo (aficamten) preclinical data showed a differentiated drug profile compared to Camzyos, with ~2.5x wider therapeutic window, shorter life-time (3.4 vs 7-9 days), and minimal drug-drug interaction (DDI). Aficamten Phase 3 SEQUOIA trial showed modestly better efficacy vs. Camzyos. Cross trial comparison (Figure below) showed that Aficamten was numerically better to Camzyos in pVO2 improvement (1.74 vs 1.4 mL/kg/min), Valsalva LVOT-G reduction (-50.0 vs -36.4 mm Hg), resting LVOT-G reduction (-40.0 vs -32.4 mm Hg), on par with ≥1 NYHA class improvement (34.2% vs 34%) and NT-proBNP reduction (80.9% vs 79.0%), but modestly less KCCQ-CSS change (7 vs 9.1). Across all measurements, Valsalva LVOT-G, was noted as most important clinical measurement per our KOL feedback. 19 February 2026 265 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

records.text: Ohtuvayre is set to reach ~$3.5Bn peak sales in COPD Merck acquired Ohtuvayre in July through the Verona acquisition. We are bullish on this deal, with Ohtuvayre's broader market access, strong uptake momentum, and favorable reimbursement structure. Recall, Ohtuvayre (ensifentrine) is a PDE3/4 inhibitor as a maintenance therapy for COPD, which gives it a broader label that covers most symptomatic COPD patients, especially those who failed dual and triple therapy, which represents over 1.2 million COPD patients in the U.S. Ohtuvayre had the best COPD launch in history. Ohtuvayre was launched in August 2024 and was added to the GOLD guidelines for COPD treatment paradigm in November 2024. It showed solid uptake momentum since launch and is often considered the best COPD launch in history, driven by favorable formulation (BID), broader label (applicable to all symptomatic patients), and favorable benefit/risk profile. It is widely accepted by the medical community and welcomed by patients. Verona Pharma reported $102M revenue by 2Q25, the 5th quarter since initial product launch. FIGURE 278. Tezspire is currently under Ph.3 study in COPD with PCD of Q1 2029. Tezspire's Ph2a COURSE study in moderate to very severe COPD patients missed the primary endpoint, but leaves open the opportunity for further exploration in a Ph 3 trial. In the study, Tezspire was able to achieve a 17% reduction in COPD exacerbations vs. placebo; these results were not statistically significant (p=0.1042). Although Tezspire missed on its primary endpoint, a 37% reduction in exacerbations was observed in patients with baseline eosinophil counts (BECs) > 150 cells/uL. Additionally, this trend of increased exacerbation reductions was greater in patients with BEC > 300 cells/uL. Trends of improved exacerbation rates in higher BEC patient populations still leave hope for Tezspire COPD success in patients with higher BEC levels. As a reminder, Regeneron / Sanofi's Dupixent was able to demonstrate a 30% reduction in COPD exacerbations in its Ph 3 BOREAS and NOTUS study. With the UK having already committed to hitting defence spending worth 2.5% of GDP now, news reports suggest that the Government could be looking to lift its defence spending to nearly 3% of GDP by the end of the current parliament (2029). How much will this cost? Just under GBP 20bn/annum. Is this a surprise? This shouldn’t be a big surprise. It was always likely that the UK would have to make some concessions on its defence spending to a) get access to the EU's SAFE program - something it has wanted to get for some time and b) broker a better trade deal (particularly with non- tariff barriers) with the EU as part of its upcoming TCA negotiations. How could the UK deliver this? We explore how the government can strategically increase defense spending while optimizing its efficiency and productivity. Carving out some of the existing capital Budget. " For those looking to nowcast the upcoming CPI release—ie, economists or those trading front-end inflation—we see this as an apt analogy in an increasingly competitive and rapidly changing data environment. The inflation market should take note. As such, we hypothesize a market evolution in the coming months, quarters and years: • Nowcasting CPI components that are scrapable will become increasingly commoditized. records.text: Immunology pipeline: Blockbuster combinations position pipeline assets for accelerated growth. Capitalizing on the cash flow generated by the commercial dominance of Skyrizi and Rinvoq, AbbVie adopts a ‘leave-no-stone-unturned’ strategy for its immunology pipeline, simultaneously pursuing validated, high-conviction blockbuster targets while aggressively investing in revolutionary modalities. AbbVie has also implemented a combination strategy in which pipeline assets such as Lukikizumab, α4β7 and TL1A are studied in combination with Skyrizi—an approach that could significantly accelerate their path to launch by leveraging Skyrizi’s broad adoption. Lutikizumab is a dual-variable-domain (DVD) immunoglobulin targeting both IL-1a and IL-1b, addressing the high unmet need in moderate-to-severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS). Following positive Phase 2 data which demonstrated superior response rates in patients who had failed anti-TNF therapies, AbbVie has advanced the asset into the Phase 3 INTREPID program; we see Lutikizumab as a critical successor in the HS market, potentially offering a more potent anti-inflammatory profile than Humira or current IL-17 inhibitors. While the product is in a managed decline phase due to competition from next-generation BTK inhibitors, it continues to generate meaningful cash flow. We view Imbruvica primarily as a funding asset that supports oncology R&D rather than a growth driver. Venclexta (venetoclax) – BCL-2 inhibitor | Hematologic malignancies: Venclexta plays a central role in fixed-duration combination regimens in CLL and AML, supported by strong clinical validation and guideline inclusion. The product provides durability to AbbVie’s hematology revenues and partially offsets Imbruvica erosion. Its established positioning in combination therapy limits volatility and supports stable mid-term contributions. After the BoJ adopted Yield Curve Control (YCC) in September 2016, “stealth tapering” began as the policy focus shifted from “quantity” to “rates” . • Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are index-linked trust funds listed in Japan. The BoJ originally started buying ETFs in December 2010, and doubled its pace to JPY6.0trn per year in July 2016. The BoJ allots JPY300bn to support firms proactively investing in physical and human capital with daily purchases of JPY1.2bn/daily. The rest of the purchasing is conducted on an ad hoc basis, with a tendency to buy when stocks drop in the morning session. In July 2018, the BoJ explicitly recognized flexibility around its pace of purchases. • Japanese real estate investment trusts (J-REITs) are mutual funds listed in Japan. A key reason is that the catalysts we were watching for to stimulate bank demand didn't end up arriving in 2025 – most notably, clarity on Basel III endgame and the easing effect we believe a re-proposal would have on bank capital requirements. However, recent color from Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman suggests that the Basel reproposal "is on track to be released by the end of the first quarter." At the risk of sounding like a broken record, we think this time the reproposal will happen, and we’re starting to see early signals of a more accommodative direction more broadly as well. In a speech this week, Bowman flagged two potential mortgage-related capital changes intended to “increase bank incentives to engage in mortgage origination and servicing”: (1) removing the deduction for mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) from regulatory capital, and (2) moving toward a more risk-sensitive framework for mortgage capital requirements that varies by L TV. While we don’t have a precise L TV distribution for bank-originated/held mortgages, a more granular calibration based on L TV would likely lower the average risk weight versus today’s one-size-fits-all approach. All in all, we think this latest development bodes positively for direction of travel towards easier regulation as we await Basel III endgame, and generally is positive for the MBS basis.

records.text: 2024, Lilly did something unprecedented in branded biopharma: it launched single-dose vials of Zepbound at $399 (2.5mg) and $549 (5mg) per month exclusively through LillyDirect, its direct-to-consumer platform—bypassing PBMs, insurance, and the traditional pharmacy supply chain entirely. Novo did not launch a comparable self-pay channel until November 17, 2025,15 months after Lilly's initial vial launch. NovoCare, Novo's self-pay platform, was launched in March 2025, but it operated through 70,000 retail pharmacies rather than as a direct-to-patient fulfillment model, meaning distributor and retail margins of 15–20% applied, structurally disadvantaging Novo's per-script economics relative to LillyDirect's direct fulfillment. Second, Novo lacks a vial form factor—all Wegovy self-pay goes through pens distributed via retail pharmacies. There is no Novo equivalent to the LillyDirect vial. The vial trajectory is striking. In 2Q25, the first full quarter of meaningful vial volum, vials represented just 3.1% of branded obesity TRx. By 4Q25, that figure was 19.8%, and vials comprised roughly one-third of all Zepbound prescriptions and nearly 50% of new Zepbound prescriptions, per LLY's Q4 2025 earnings call. Eli Lilly noted at the Q4 call that LillyDirect surpassed 1 million users in 2025. Zepbound self-pay vials accounted for approximately one- third of new patient starts across all branded obesity medicines; not just Zepbound. 19 February 2026 170 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceutical

records.text: st proposal focuses on mortgage servicing rights (MSRs). Under Basel III, MSRs are assigned a 250% risk weight and are capped at 10% of a bank’s CET1 capital, with any excess deducted from CET1. Governor Bowman proposed removing the deduction of MSRs from regulatory capital while retaining the 250% RW. In our view, eliminating the deduction alone is unlikely to significantly increase banks’ participation in the MSR market, as the largest banks are not constrained by the cap. While this change may be more relevant for smaller banks, limited scale could remain a barrier. The risk weight itself needs to be reduced for banks to meaningfully re-engage with MSRs. records.text: CHF and JPY share similar risk correlations but differ enough on a few measures that make them ideal safe havens for different environments. The Yen tends to be most sensitive to US rates and strengthens the most in a negative US growth shock when yields and equities are falling at the same time. The Swiss Franc strengthens the most against rising European sovereign risk and global inflation pressures owing to its regional banking ties and strict inflation targeting, as well as regional geopolitical risks. Recently the Franc has also begun to appreciate alongside the Euro and European satellites. We think this at least partly reflects flow dynamics as Europe has been the main source of repatriation flows out of US assets. Typically, CHF/JPY is positively correlated with rising equity prices, higher yields, and commodities, and negatively correlated with the VIX (Exhibit 2). This reflects JPY’s tendency to outperform when growth expectations are falling, while CHF tends to strengthen when inflation expectations are rising. This makes Yen a better safe haven for negative growth environments and CHF a better hedge against rising inflation risks. That said, CHF/JPY’s more fundamental, long-run driver has been relative inflation (Exhibit 3). Japan and Switzerland are both low inflation economies, though for different reasons. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 January Inflation: Mishmash Wednesday Bruna Skarica What happened: Our initial take on the January inflation print is here. Looking at the details of the print, we can't help but be reminded of the summer period, where what turned out to have been artificially elevated cultural services readings kept underlying headline and underlying services inflation propped up. There are questions to be asked around how high inflation in insurance fees could go this year, and on catering inflation. Very gradually, the latter has climbed to 4.8%Y as of January, where we had expected it to plateau at ~4.5%Y. This delta might just be down to the pass-through of elevated wholesale food costs in 2H25 - keeping the disinflation story over 2026 still broadly intact. But if this is the case, catering inflation would need to start subsiding from February, we think. The decline in headline inflation to 2%Y in April is not just down to energy and volatile components - underlying inflation, and core inflation more broadly, needs to cool a bit more notably over March and April for us to be reassured that the (dis)inflationary process is ticking along as expected. On the whole, however, there is a lot to like in this print - core goods and food price pressures are looking manageable, and fuel prices are likely to be a drag on headline come February too. records.text: The likely succession doesn’t change the policy outlook for this year, with a high bar for a move in either direction. Longer-term, a candidate more sensitive to European growth that positions the ECB to support investment could be a twist- steepener. However, the more likely scenarios are perhaps for a successor that reinforces and extends the apparent hawkish bias of the ECB and makes the market more willing to add hike premium. Front-end steepeners: We already hold a long-term hawkish trade via via Euribor U6/U8 steepeners (34.5bp as of 16:30 GMT 19Feb26. NB: Futures trading involves substantial risk of loss). The trade has not been performing, and the decision over the next ECB president may take too long to be relevant – Figure 1. Still, we find it hard to fully explain the extent of the recent flattening other than via global spillovers acting as a constraint and growing concern of a risk-off episode or AI- induced weakness in global labour markets - Figure 2.
