The asset functions largely as a defensive product, ensuring Merck maintains relevance in pediatric vaccination and enabling bundling with the company’s broader childhood vaccine portfolio. While V114 is not expected to be a material growth driver given entrenched competition and pricing pressure, it provides continuity and limits further share erosion in the pediatric segment. • Pneumovax 23 – Pneumovax 23 remains in structural decline as clinical practice has shifted decisively toward conjugate vaccines that generate T-cell–dependent immune memory and longer-lasting protection. Historically, AFPs’ hedging activity tracked the size of their foreign-asset holdings, but that relationship broke down at the end of 2023: foreign assets surged while the corresponding hedge volumes lagged behind (see Figure 1). Given the mismatch between AFPs’ foreign-asset holdings and their hedges—and the persistent weakness of the US dollar, which encourages AFPs to shore up currency-risk protection—we anticipate the funds will step up their USDCLP NDF sales, narrowing the gap between foreign holdings and AFPs FX hedging. Since AFPs hold a large share of foreign assets, their hedging decisions move not only impact the CLP but also the cross-currency basis (see CLP: Further underperformance likely in medium term). An uptick in the AFP hedging ratio would push FX points and the CLP basis lower (see Chile: Pension fund hedging shift to stabilize CLP basis) Basis reconnects with CLP derivative positions: The CLP basis spiked after Dec 2025 as offshore investors added short CLP exposure. However, such shorts have reverted to prior levels, leaving the basis mis-aligned with CLP’s positioning and implying a likely downward correction bias. Market consensus appears tilted toward an opposition victory, supported by still-high disapproval of the current left-wing government and an agenda increasingly dominated by security-related issues, where the right wing holds a comparative advantage. That said, high dispersion across polls, the strong likelihood of a runoff vote, and the recent improvement in President Petro’s approval ratings suggest that the race remains open and could prove more competitive than currently expected. Regardless of the outcome, the next administration will face significant political constraints when addressing the fiscal adjustment the economy requires. Hard-to-read primaries: Colombia will hold legislative elections on 8 March to renew both the House of Representatives and the Senate, alongside inter-party consultations to select presidential candidates. These consultations operate as a candidate-selection mechanism within a political bloc or coalition, allowing multiple parties to nominate a single candidate for the presidential election’s first round. records.text: 4 https://www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/2025-federal-government-shutdown-impact-cpi.htm#12 BLS: 2025 federal government shutdown impact on the Consumer Price Index4 How were the missing October 2025 data handled in the seasonal adjustment process? BLS computes seasonally adjusted data using seasonal factors derived by the X-13ARIMA- SEATS Seasonal Adjustment Method. These factors are updated with the release of January data in February and reflect price movements from the previous calendar year. This process typically requires that 60 consecutive recent observations for both CPI-U and CPI-W be available at a minimum. When a month of data for a directly adjusted series (CPI-U or CPI-W) is not available due to inadequacy for publication, BLS no longer seasonally adjusts either series until sufficient data is available again. Due to the 2025 lapse in funding, BLS could not publish October 2025 indexes for most CPI series. This resulted in BLS using atypical methods in order to maintain a continuous time series on which to calculate revised seasonal factors, including a seasonal factor for October 2025. For the seasonal adjustment process, BLS approximated the missing October data by taking the geometric mean of the September and November index values. There were two series also missing November data, which was inadequate for publication after BLS attempted to collect data from all scheduled establishments and respondents. In our view, the ECB continues to err on the hawkish side of policy choices – the Bundesbank is ideologically at the forefront of this bias. The “good place” the ECB says it is in, is one where inflation will be at best at target, or more likely (actually our base case) below. Or put differently, the ECB still seems to prefer an inflation undershoot over an overshoot. We still think the ECB will ultimately have to cut rates again next year, as it becomes obvious the inflation undershoot is here to stay. This may be a dovish call vs consensus or markets, but not vs our view of the economy. A more proactive ECB would cut policy rates earlier (it wouldn’t have hiked as far, or cut deeper already) and make sure the risk of endogenous weakness is minimised. Of course, that cannot be enough to deliver strong Euro area growth itself. But it can help at the margin, not least in the context of an unspectacular credit cycle where lending rates seem to transmit the past policy cuts only partly to the economy. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 19 February 2026 Citi Research 9 Assessing the Global Risks The overall tone of our global forecast may seem surprisingly sanguine, given the litany of risks and challenges that permeate the global outlook. However, as we’ve emphasized above, the core of our resilience hypothesis is not that the global economy will somehow avoid shocks. Meaningful shocks will inevitably come—just as they have in recent years. Rather, our view is that even as shocks occur, the global economy will have the capacity to adjust, and growth will continue at a solid pace. An important corollary is that the global economy has not endured a downturn driven by economic, financial, or even geopolitical factors since the onset of the Global Financial Crisis nearly two decades ago. The one full-blown recession during this two-decade period was triggered by a global pandemic, which was an entirely exogenous shock. The upshot is that it may be time for economists to reconsider the mechanisms through which downturns occur and the size (and type) of shocks necessary to trigger such outcomes. Of course, we don’t want to overstate this point. There no doubt are shocks that are sufficiently large—or combination of shocks that are sufficiently severe—that could push the economy into recession or, at least, toward significantly softer performance. Source: Citi Research The key observation that drives our outlook is that global growth has remained solid and stable despite the ongoing stresses. Stated differently, the global economy has shown a capacity to adapt flexibly to a wide array of shocks and challenges. We judge that the roots of this resilience reflect technological advances, which have transformed the supply side of the economy. Firms today have immediate access to information about alternative inputs, new suppliers, and the stance of competitors. They also have extensive capacity to communicate worldwide in real time. T o be clear, we see little evidence to link these gains to any productivity benefits associated with AI, which we judge are still largely in the pipeline. But the handiwork of technology is very much in play. A complementary hypothesis is that the series of challenges encountered in recent years has trained and stress tested firms, so they are optimized and well positioned to respond to further pressures. Rather than leaving firms fatigued, depleted, and brittle, these challenges have helped the production-side of the economy achieve peak fitness and conditioning. A recent Axios (18-Feb-2026) report suggested that the US was not pleased with latest talks in Geneva, quoting Vice President Vance that whilst President Trump wants a deal, diplomacy may have “reached its natural end” . This has triggered concern that we may be closer to a military escalation. We would note that this could be a negotiation tactic to bring us closer to a deal, and that even in a slightly stronger escalation, ample OPEC+ supply will likely act as a buffer against more local (i.e. domestic Iranian supply) disruptions (Figure 42). However, an escalation that leads to closure of the Strait of Hormuz would be an extremely bullish price scenario, likely triggering a flat price response closer to the aggressive options market pricing. That said, even in the event of a strong U.S. military escalation, it is very difficult to assign a fair probability of Iran following up by closing or disrupting the Strait given that it has not been done before, and the general lack of clarity surrounding what the specific incentives of the Iranian leadership might be at this point. It is administered at a once monthly dosing interval, which many believe to be a differentiation factor. Amgen announced 52-week Ph.2 topline data late last year, then full ph.2 data at ADA 2025. The bar for the Street was a weight loss profile in non-T2D patients of =>25%, which was not met. In addition, MariTide did not show dose response in the Ph.2 study. In the non-diabetic patient group, MariTide’s monthly 280mg dose had a better weight loss trajectory vs the 420mg cohort. In the T2D patient group, the 140/280mg dose group showed indifferent weight loss profile, but the 420mg dose performed significantly better. We await additional color on how GI toxicity impacted the efficacy among different patient groups. APOC3 for TG lowering: APOC3 (apolipoprotein C-III) is a potent inhibitor of the activation of LPL majorly synthesized in the liver that is mediated by apolipoprotein C-II, resulting in the inhibition of lipolysis of triglyceride-rich-lipoproteins. Knockdown of APOC3 has emerged as the most efficient way to decrease TG with major therapeutic approaches developed with RNA and genetic approaches. Inventories have declined year to date, spare capacity is low and shrinking, and the cyclical demand vector is strong. Therefore, risks from elevated geopolitical tensions remain skewed to the upside. • Oil price action year to date affirms our core views that the expected surplus was comfortably priced in at the end of last year and geopolitical tensions pose asymmetric upside risks to prices. Despite the 15% move higher year to date, we think geopolitical tensions still pose asymmetric upside risks to oil prices. • Unlike most of the period since late 2023 when Middle East tensions came to the fore, spare capacity is low and shrinking and the cyclical demand vector is strong. The inflation rate is expected to trend below 2%, owing to a slowdown in food inflation and government measures to counter high energy prices. French budget This week, the Constitutional Council validated the 2026 budget, only removing seven minor articles (parts) from the budget. Overall, the deficit for 2026 is unlikely to be affected by the removal of these articles. In a somewhat unusual move, the Prime Minster himself referred parts of the budget on taxing capital to the Constitutional Council. records.text: Second part of report title Dav id Wilson, Director – Commodities Desk Strategist | BNP Paribas Singapore Branch 12 China imported 2.55Mt of primary in 2025, up 20% y/y: China’s full-year 2025 primary aluminium demand growth was 2.8% (about 1.2Mt),down from 3.7% (1.4Mt) in 2024, as the slowdown in construction was offset by strong demand for transport, consumer goods and renewable energy. In 2026, we expect a slowing in demand growth to 2.0% (900Kt), on a likely slowing in solar demand, plus the domestic impact of fewer aluminium semi-fabricated product exports. However, we also forecast almost no Chinese domestic supply growth in 2026, which will lead to a tightening of the Chinese market.Indeed, we expect China’s import demand to grow again this year. Chinese import demand a key tightening factor : We expect China’s ongoing demand for imports to help tighten the ex-China market, and to drive continued draw-downs from LME inventory. Currently cash-to-3m spreads have slipped back into contango of c.USD33/t as of 18 February 2026, but we expect this to tighten through H1-26. Longer- dated 3-to-15-month spreads are in a backwardation of around USD17/t. Dual risk: We see two main risks to a positive price outlook: 1) Chinese authorities relax the mandated 45Mt/t operational smelter capacity cap (although we see a relaxation as extremely unlikely given regional power consumption targets); and 2) tariff policy uncertainty driving a more severe impact on global demand growth. 19/02

records.text: José Antonio Kast will take office as Chile’s president in March amid high public expectations centered on three objectives: improving security, reviving economic growth and restoring fiscal discipline. Recent polling shows that security dominates popular concerns, while expectations around economic management and growth have also improved as the new administration nears. Early signals from Kast’s economic team point to a pro-growth orientation. The appointment of Jorge Quiroz as finance minister, together with an emphasis on deregulation, tax cuts and fiscal probity, suggests an attempt to combine fiscal consolidation with policies aimed at lifting investment and productivity. At the same time, the new administration faces constraints in Congress that will shape both the pace and the scope of reforms. Political constraints – the role of Congress: The government will enter office with minorities in the Chamber of Deputies and a closely divided Senate. In the upper house, the administration is near a majority but still a few seats short, meaning that passing legislation will require support from outside its core coalition. Those votes could come from moderate center-left lawmakers associated with the former Concertación, a bloc that controls a material share of Senate seats and has historically supported pro-growth and fiscally pragmatic initiatives. records.text: The Pneumococcal Franchise: Strategic Bifurcation Merck has executed a strategic bifurcation of the pneumococcal market, effectively conceding the competitive pediatric segment to Pfizer to focus on dominating the high-margin adult segment. • Capvaxive (V116) – Capvaxive is positioned as Merck’s primary growth driver within pneumococcal vaccines, reflecting a strategic pivot toward the higher-margin adult segment. Unlike prior pneumococcal vaccines that were pediatric platforms adapted for adult use, V116 is the first conjugate vaccine designed specifically for adults, targeting 21 serotypes including eight not covered by Pfizer’s Prevnar 20 and estimated to account for ~30% of invasive pneumococcal disease in adults aged 50+. Since its June 2024 launch, early commercial traction has been solid, with ~$244m in Q3 2025 sales, supported by ACIP’s decision to lower the recommended adult vaccination age from 65+ to 50+, expanding the addressable market. While longer-term uptake will depend on guideline durability and competitive dynamics, we see Capvaxive representing Merck’s clearest path to incremental growth in pneumococcal disease. • Vaxneuvance (V114) – Vaxneuvance serves as Merck’s primary pediatric pneumococcal offering and occupies a stable but secondary competitive position versus Pfizer’s Prevnar 20, with an estimated ~30% market share. The asset functions largely as a defensive product, ensuring Merck maintains relevance in pediatric vaccination and enabling bundling w

The remainder of the impact will be spread across other assets including Oral CGRPs, Linzess, Creon, Eye Care, etc. AbbVie expects assumed that part D redesign impact will spread evenly across quarters. AbbVie has delivered robust revenue growth throughout 2025, and we expect this momentum to be carried into 2026. Pfizer’s deal with the Administration partially removed the overhang for MFN & Tariffs for the sector Recall, Pfizer recently announced a voluntary agreement with the U.S. government to participate in the U.S. government’s DTC purchasing platform, TrumpRx, and sell drugs through Medicaid at lower/MFN prices. Most of the company’s primary care treatments and some select specialty brands will be offered at savings that will range as high as 85% and average 50%. records.text: Impact on topline expected to be manageable Large-cap pharmaceutical companies' 4Q25 earnings calls have largely confirmed that the MFN agreements imposed minimal margin compression, with IRA/MFN pricing headwinds offset by patient access expansion and volume growth. Commercial payers were noted to continue to negotiate independently of Medicaid, focusing on formulary positioning and rebate economics. Alignment between domestic manufacturing and regulatory incentive The domestic manufacturing commitments embedded in the agreements ($100B+ cumulative across 17 companies) aligned with broader administration priorities around supply chain reshoring and resilience. The FDA's PreCheck program (launched in August 2025) and Strategic API Reserve (SAPIR) executive order (announced in August 2025) provided tangible incentives. In addition, potential reshoring tax incentives underwent legislative process. MFN concerns abate The dissipation of the U.S. drug pricing overhang represented a meaningful de-risking event for the U.S. biopharmaceutical sector in a decade. The MFN voluntary agreements, culminating in the JNJ and ABBV accords in January 2026, have taken the U.S. price cut overhang off the table and shifted investor focus back to company-specific fundamentals. 19 February 2026 17 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

Given the breakneck pace of supply-side shocks hitting the UK economy, we are keeping an open mind. But we do also note that general purpose technologies ultimately always result in more productive capacity and more employment. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The effective tariff rate and high-frequency container traffic The tariff rate on US imports slipped to ~9½% in December The Trump administration imposed additional tariffs on trading partners as of August 7 that pushed the effective tariff rate higher to 16.0%. Since then, negotiations with three of the US's largest trading partners – Mexico, Canada, and China – continue to proceed on a separate track. In addition, Section 232 reviews on trade in semiconductors, lumber, and pharmaceuticals, among others, remain ongoing. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on the legality of IEEPA tariffs in early November and we await a potential ruling, which could come any day that the court is in session. Given the calendar for the court, the earliest date for a decision to be released will be February 20. If IEEPA tariffs are invalidated, the effective tariff rate may move lower temporarily as the administration uses other trade authority to reconstitute its tariff regime. See here for more detailed views. In December, the effective tariff rate fell to an estimated 9 ½% from ~11% in the prior three months as the China share of imports fell. There has been some shift in the composition of US imports and in the countries they're coming from. If these patterns remain in place, the tariffs will likely stabilize around the recent 11% rate. The growth deceleration also goes hand in hand with further labour market softness and we project a year-average unemployment rate of 5.3% this year, up from 4.7% in 2025. Inflation is on track to drop towards 2% in the second half of the year. We expect a large base effect, alongside a level shift in energy bills, to cause a sharp drop in April next year. From there, we expect that further slack in the labour market, alongside weaker consumption, will help bring inflation back to target. The risks around the probability of hitting 2% next year though are relatively two-sided, and we remain conscious of the growing cost of employment as business are forced to digest another above-inflation settlement for the national living wage and the upcoming employment rights bill. In a more dovish scenario, which we assume as base case, higher costs feeds into softer labour market while deteriorating real wages - above the national living wage – both see a fall in household consumption. However, there remains the possibility that business seek to pass on higher costs through prices and ultimately a stickier services inflation. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 19 February 2026 Citi Research 15 Figure 21. Canada - Economic Forecast, 2024-2026F © 2026 Citigroup Inc. No redistribution without Citigroup’s written permission. Source: Citi Research, Statistics Canada Euro Area We revise our 2026 GDP growth forecast slightly up again to 1.3%. We see an ongoing improvement in the Eurozone growth trajectory, from around 1% in 2025, to 1.2% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027. Growth should be increasingly driven by domestic demand, in particular investment, aimed at transitioning the existing capital stock towards a greener, more digitalized, more AI-intensive one, rather than at expanding the existing capacity. This will help support manufacturing despite export weakness, which we expect to continue this year due to the delayed impact of US tariffs. Chinese trade diversion will also continue to represent a headwind for European manufacturers. Private consumption is unlikely to be a growth-driver, as we see job growth staying soft, although growing wages and a high saving rate represent buffers for consumption in case of negative shocks. The policy mix is turning from a headwind to a tailwind. We see the biggest change in the fiscal stance in Germany, but fiscal policy should remain supportive also in the European periphery, as the Next GenEu programme is entering its final year. We forecast the euro area aggregate fiscal stance is moving from marginally restrictive in 2025 to marginally expansionary (+0.3pp of GDP)

Month 1 trimmed mean matters most for signal into quarterly TM An important read-through for the RBA is the translation of monthly CPI to the quarterly trimmed mean. Despite the inherently monthly volatility and seasonality, there is still a lot of signal from the monthly trimmed mean. We find a 2-month change in the monthly trimmed mean for the first month of each quarter, at the aggregate and component level, provided a good guide to the quarterly measure (see Figure 4). We think this works for two reasons: 1) So called 'triangle weighting' when monthly figures are aggregated to a quarterly frequency mean that the largest weighting is for the first month of the quarter, because it sets the base for the subsequent months of the quarter. Taking a 2- month change over a 3-month (or 3m/3m) change better captures this effect. 2) The quarterly trimmed mean continues to be compiled using the pre-October 2025 method. That means price updates in month 2 and 3 for some components are not included, and hence there is even more (relative) signal from the month 1 values. records.text: Thymic Stromal Lymphopoietin (TSLP) is an epithelial cytokine released at the very source of the "river"—the airway epithelium. It acts as an environmental sensor, triggered by a broad range of insults including allergens, viruses, pollutants, and mechanical stress. Once released, TSLP activates dendritic cells, which in turn drive the differentiation of naïve T-cells into Th2 cells. Crucially, TSLP also directly activates Innate Lymphoid Cells (ILC2s), mast cells, and basophils. By blocking TSLP at the top of the cascade, Tezspire prevents the initiation of the immune response. Consequently, it reduces the production of all downstream Type 2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) simultaneously.23 Furthermore, because TSLP also mediates non-Type 2 inflammation via mast cells and structural cells, Tezspire demonstrates efficacy in patients without classic allergic or eosinophilic biomarkers — a population where Dupixent and anti- IL-5s are less effective. Dupixent targets the IL-4 receptor alpha (IL-4Rα), blocking the signalling of IL-4 and IL-13. These are downstream effector cytokines. IL-4 drives IgE production, while IL-13 drives mucus hypersecretion and airway hyperresponsiveness.16 Dupixent is exceptionally potent in Type 2 High inflammation, where these cytokines are dominant. Unlike Dupixent, which is restricted to eosinophilic COPD under its current U.S. label, Tezspire targets upstream TSLP signaling and could potentially address both eosinophilic and non- eosinophilic pheno

Krystexxa: strong efficacy, but durability constrained by LOE Krystexxa is a highly effective therapy in refractory gout, with well-established efficacy when used in optimized treatment paradigms. From a Horizon value perspective, however, its contribution is time-limited, with loss of exclusivity expected around 2030. Krystexxa (pegloticase) is a uric acid specific enzyme that converts the urate, the source of uric acid crystals, to allantoin, which is water soluble and mainly eliminated by renal exertion, thereby lowering serum uric acid and dissolving uric acid crystal build-ups. Renal exertion of allantoin is 10X more efficient than exertion of uric acid. We see significant improvement in Krystexxa's response rate and duration of response when Co-Administered with immunomodulators. Horizon developed the immunomodulation strategy, which focuses on increasing physician awareness of immunomodulation as an option to improve rate of response, duration of therapy, and safety profile of Krystexxa. He is likely to argue that the Fed should be forward looking about the disinflationary impact of the impending AI productivity boom. But we aren’t convinced that the committee will buy into this worldview. As Claudio Irigoyen and Antonio Gabriel recently noted, any longer-run improvement in productivity due to AI adoption will likely be preceded by a boom in investment and consumption, which could be inflationary. Moreover, higher productivity growth would also raise the neutral real policy rate, reducing the need for cuts (see: Is AI disinflationary? Not so fast…). “When” is as uncertain as “if” We have also gotten pushback on the timing of the two cuts in our forecast. We’ve penciled in the cuts in June and July. In our view, it would be politically expedient for Warsh to deliver the cuts as soon as he takes the seat, well before the midterms. Perhaps he could win some support for the cuts by agreeing to open the door for hikes next year. But clients have argued that June might be a particularly difficult time to cut because the fiscal impulse and tariff-driven inflation will both likely peak around then. They have noted that Warsh could earn his colleagues’ trust by not cutting in his first meeting. He might then find it easier to push for cuts in September, if there is another seasonal soft patch in the labor data over the summer. We don’t have major quibbles with this line of reasoning. However, such shorts have reverted to prior levels, leaving the basis misaligned with CLP positioning and implying a likely downward correction bias, in our view. Shelter inflation has generally been on a slowing trend and forward- looking indicators point to continued slowing in shelter inflation. Non-shelter services inflation should also slow further in 2026 as wage growth has generally been slowing. Tariff-related inflation will most likely be a one-time price increase in goods rather than sustained inflationary pressure. We expect core inflation to slow to around 2.4% by the end of 2026. Monthly private payroll job growth has generally slowed on a 3m average basis with the improvement in January likely mostly reflecting some seasonal strength. The unemployment rate has increased gradually over the last couple of years but has declined in the last couple of months to 4.3% in January. Labor demand has slowed more than labor supply which could put further modest upward pressure on the unemployment rate this year. The labor market continues to be defined by a low hiring rate but also low layoff rate, but we see some risk that layoffs could pick up. Beyond that we automatically “fade” sales for individual products at a HSD annualized rate. We assumed R&D spend is maintained on trend. This approach attempts to introduce an air of conservatism when more often than not, the default approach results in DCFs far higher than P/E or other relative valuation methodologies would suggest. Given this, we do not use our DCFs to set 12-month price targets. We also acknowledge they are a long-term theoretical construct whose output can be extremely dependent on a handful of long-term assumptions (e.g. terminal growth). Thus we consider these detailed DCF models to be most useful as a sanity check on market vs fundamental value, and especially for particular product assets – where our DCF models can give a quick and helpful idea of the discrete value associated with a specific asset (in-line or pipeline). records.text: The Current Trade-off: Depth vs. Coverage As a minimum, the EU Inc framework is likely to enable “once-only” business registration across EU member states and facilitate access to information on corporate, tax, and employment regimes that would remain national in nature. Implementation via EU regulation – which is directly applicable to all member states – would avoid generating 27 different versions of EU Inc. This more minimal approach would lower fixed administrative costs and potentially reduce competitive barriers, but keep most corporate law (as well as all tax and labour law) in national hands and barriers due to unharmonized product regulation largely in place. IMF estimates suggest that a minimal 28th regime could add 0.3% to the level of GDP over 10 years. A more ambitious proposal for a deeper 28th regime could introduce harmonised corporate arrangements2, bankruptcy law, and potentially a specialised dispute-resolution body. As prior experience suggests, this approach is likely to face more political resistance given concerns around national corporate traditions (such as co-determination) and the need to set up a whole new EU-wide corporate framework rather than just a unified entry point to existing national frameworks (Exhibit 5, left). A compromise, along the lines suggested in the Draghi report, would be to narrow the coverage of the new, more ambitious regime to a subset of companies, such as innovative start-ups. records.text: Upgrading our USD and EUR IG supply forecasts. The USD and EUR IG primary markets have both started off the year on a record-setting pace, with issuance already reaching $346 billion and €156 billion, respectively, both up more than 10% over this point last year (Exhibit 1). In the USD IG market, on the back of a strong year-to-date pace, upgraded GDP growth forecasts, and an even more accommodative funding cost environment, we are raising our full-year gross supply forecast to $2.1 trillion, from $1.9 trillion previously. This implies a 14% increase over last year’s total and would surpass the annual high reached in 2020 (Exhibit 2, left panel). In the EUR IG market, we are raising our full-year gross issuance forecast to €850 billion from €725 billion previously, implying roughly a 4% increase vs. last year’s record total (Exhibit 2, right panel). This upgrade is primarily driven by stronger-than-expected reverse Yankee issuance, which remains robust at €25 billion year to date as US firms continue to prioritize investor-base diversification. In addition, spread levels have tightened further since our last forecast revision, which should keep funding windows open and allow for some incremental supply this year. We do expect the vast majority of these projected increases in gross supply will end up being net new issuance. However, we do not see a meaningful catalyst that could drive near-term topline growth and rewind the momentum from the LOEs, while the company's recent pipeline setback also serves as further evidence of the company's pipeline struggle. Rocatinlimab's setback in Atopic Dermatitis: Dupixent set a high bar for new entrants Amgen recently terminated rocatinlimab development and commercialization collaboration with Kyowa Kirin, reflecting the high barrier to entry for the Atopic Dermatitis landscape. Atopic dermatitis (AD), widely referred to as eczema, is the most common chronic inflammatory skin condition, with a global prevalence of 2% of the population. AD managements typically follows a stepwise approach. Mild disease is often managed with skin hydration (emollients) and topical therapies, such as topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus). Moderate or severe cases would require phototherapy, systemic immunosuppressants (e.g., methotrexate, cyclosporine, or mycophenolate mofetil). Dupilumab stands as the current gold standard in the atopic dermatitis market, largely due to its robust clinical efficacy and established safety profile

records.text: 6. A quieter start to DM rates still carries risks. Relative to sharp shifts in parts of the equity and commodity complex, US rates have been a quieter place. With the pre-election pressure in Japan fading, US yields are now modestly lower along the curve in 2026. Our base case remains that inflation outcomes will be better than expected this year, allowing the Fed to resume easing later in the year and anchoring longer-dated yields even with better growth. But the scope for bouts of volatility is still clear. The deeper risks still skew towards lower rates—and bonds have illustrated their hedging value in the recent AI-driven volatility. But with growth poised to remain strong in 2026H1 and 2- and 5-year US yields back near their lows, we still worry about scenarios where rates could move back up again in the next few months. The key risk on the policy side is a further fall in the US unemployment rate—a milder version of the backdrop that has already pushed the RBA to hike the cash rate and to flag the risk of more. At the long end of the curve, a falling unemployment rate and a benign response to Japan’s election have undermined attempts to steepen the yield curve. But any renewed concerns about Fed decision-making, an IEEPA ruling that threatens tariff revenues, or simply persistent strength in the economy could reawaken past sources of volatility after the recent relaxation. records.text: M Idea 18 Looking at 4Q25 data, the read-through is still soft as banks reduced exposure in HTM across the board: -$17bn in conventional pass-throughs, -$4bn in Ginnie pass-throughs, - $4bn in CMOs, and -$1bn in agency CMBS. The lone bright spot was in AFS, where banks modestly added +$6bn of conventional pass-throughs and +$4bn of Ginnie pass-throughs, driven primarily by mid-tier and smaller institutions, although that doesn't offset the overall reduction in HTM. Moreover, CMO holdings in AFS also declined (-$2bn). On notable individual bank flows, Bank of America added +$6bn of agency CMBS in AFS while Wells Fargo net reduced -$7bn agency assets across portfolio accounts. Banks reduced their trading accounts by -$6bn for agency MBS pass-throughs quarter over quarter, led by Bank of America cutting $5bn, perhaps reflecting balance sheet constraints heading into year-end. On the other hand, banks added $62bn of Treasuries to their trading accounts. However, since bank trading accounts are often considered more correlated with broker-dealer balance sheets, we turn to look to banks’ AFS and HTM books to gauge “real money” portfolio demand. Our focus is on disinflation, and how rapid this process has been in France – in fact perhaps, too rapid. In France, disinflation is “holistic”: consumer price inflation is well below 2% in both core and headline. Even services HICP is already back at 2% yoy (see Exhibit 1). We expect 1.3% inflation this year and 1.5% next. Our forecasts are well below the Euro area average at 1.7% each year. Holistic disinflation it is, too It’s not just consumer prices. Wage growth has slowed to c 1.5% across various indicators. Labour productivity growth has resumed from lower levels but at a faster pace than pre-Covid. The labour market has plateaued; prominent shortages during the post-Covid rebound have disappeared. Lastly, unit profits have come well off their highs, too, further and faster than the Euro area aggregate. That’s quite a unique combination of data, akin to properly holistic inflation. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Retail sales | What was that? On the face of it, this was an exceptionally strong retail sales print – a 2%M uptick in ex-fuels volumes sold. However, we think that the number ought to be treated with some scepticism. For one, the ONS reported that online jewellers stated that demand "hit unprecedented levels" last month, with demand booming in recent months as gold prices jumped. Purchasing jewelry for the resale value of gold doesn't strike us as a clear signal of robust consumer health. It is also hard to see how this surge doesn't eventually correct. In addition, recent months have brought a lot of volatility in the historical data – where ex-fuel volumes were estimated to be up by 3.1%Y in December a month ago, today's revisions brought this figure down to 2.5%Y. The quality of the ONS data is improving, but long-standing quality issues with the retail sales numbers make us wary of taking much signal from this print. The 3M/3M volumes are up by 0.1%, which seems an accurate depiction of the sector at the turn of the year. Summing it all up: Our growth tracking stands at 0.3%Q for 1Q26 after today's data. This is in line with the BoE, and totalling all the numbers this week, we still see a cut in March. We do think that for any cuts beyond then, with an economy that is looking perkier, convincing further evidence of disinflation will be needed. For now, we stick with further moves in July and November.

records.text: CHF/JPY are usually well explained by its cross-asset correlations, but over the long run and at the tails of the inflation distribution, relative price pressures are the main explanatory factor. Recently, a sustained shift higher in Japanese inflation has altered the backdrop for CHF/JPY. Underlying price pressures in Japan have risen moderately, and risks to the upside have grown under the Takaichi administration. While the BoJ has hiked rates in the context of higher inflation, its primary objective has been to normalize policy without disrupting progress towards its 2% target. The BoJ does not see the right tail in inflation as a material risk right now, and in fact still needs convincing that it has sufficiently entrenched inflation expectations at 2%. Governor Ueda recently explained that the Bank would only hike next when the BoJ had sufficient conviction on the realization of its price outlook. These dynamics stand in clear contrast to the SNB, which said in its most recent Monetary Policy Assessment that its forecast that inflation will rise to 0.6% by 2027 is “within the range of price stability.” Despite the caution in Governor Ueda’s comments, markets have significantly repriced the BoJ’s reaction function over the past two weeks. Landscape of Major PCSK9-targeting Therapies Source: Barclays Research and Company Reports Biological innovations discovered and validated novel targets which can be addressed with broad therapeutic approaches PCSK9 for LDL-C lowering: PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) binds to the LDL receptor (LDLR) on the surface of hepatocytes, leading to the degradation of the LDLR and higher LDL-C levels. Multiple therapies were developed to inhibit PCSK9, increase the number of LDLR, and in turn reduce LDL-C from circulation. Repatha (evolocumab) from AMGN and Praluent (alirocumab) from REGN showed around 60% and 50% pbo-adjusted LDL-C reductions, achieving $1663M and $857M revenue in 2025, respectively. Other drugs include long-lasting siRNA and oral small molecule inhibitor to provide improved patient convenience and access. Leqvio (Inclisiran, from NVS/ALNY), is a semi-annual dosing GalNAc-conjugated siRNA which prevents the formation of PCSK9 protein, showing around 50% pbo-adjusted LDL-C reduction and generating $1198M revenue in 2025. Merck's enlicitide was a QD oral macrocyclic peptide, which achieved around 60% pbo-adjusted LDL-C reduction in CORALreef Lipids and HeFH studies. And it is not just a fluke from seasonality, it spreads across price components: Consumer price inflation is well below the Euro area average. Private sector unit profits have corrected lower than the Euro area average, too. And, wage dynamics are below 2019 levels, as well. How come? Monetary policy is likely much too tight for the economy. If the ECB hiking cycle went too far and cuts not far enough for the Euro area (our long-held view), it’s even more extreme in France, where the inflation peak was lower. The policy mix is back. records.text: European Economics 20 February 2026 Citi Research 2 At a glance T oday’s monthly fiscal data release in Germany suggests that fiscal support remains broadly on track. Single month figures should by no means be overinterpreted, but both headline expenditure as well as the most watched categories these days, investment and defence, broadly maintain their upward trends. There appear also to be first manifestations of the fiscal impulse in other economic data, though one should expect these measures to remain volatile in coming months. For more details, see main story further below. Deficit – The trend of Federal deficit widening continued in January, with the shortfall about €9bn wider than in January last year. This is not reflected in the same way in net borrowing, which does not have to follow revenue and expenditure patterns on the beat, as the government can use other resources. Revenues – Federal revenues were €26bn in January, compared to €30bn last year this month, which was however inflated by one-off effects. Expenditure – Federal expenditure has grown by €6bn compared to the same period in 2025 and stands at €55bn. Investment figures in particular showed an uptick, though much of this is loans, including to the Federal Employment Agency. Special funds – The Special Fund for Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality, the SVIK, saw new issuance of €5bn in January. The total now stands at €29bn. This blend is particularly important in the CPI context because Truflation subindex changes are highly collinear (for example, several food-related components move together, and multiple shelter indicators share information). records.text: European Equity Strategy20 February 2026 ab 3 European Equity Strategy UBS Research The Price of Being Optional Global equity markets are shaped as much by capital architecture as by macroeconomics. Some markets remain unavoidable destinations for capital; others become discretionary. The UK has transitioned into the latter category. Today, it is not optimism or fear that sets UK equity valuations, but something more structural: optionality, the fact that global capital can leave without penalty and must be persuaded to stay. The UK’s discount is not a mispricing to be corrected; it is the rational equilibrium of a market that has become optional. But optional does not mean irrelevant. It means the UK must be owned deliberately, not by default. How the UK Became Optional For most of the twentieth century, UK equities had a stable domestic bid. Defined benefit pension schemes held large structural allocations. Retail investors exhibited strong home bias. Institutional portfolios considered the UK a core holding. Ownership was sticky, valuation inelastic. That architecture has been dismantled. The first break came with the rise of passive investing. From the mid-1990s to early 2000s, passive assets scaled rapidly and overtook active as the dominant implementation vehicle. Once that happened, the marginal question changed. Additionally, outside the covid years of 2020 and 2021, core PCE in 1Q each year has been stronger than the rest of the year – suggesting some residual seasonality risks. These residual seasonality risks have been further heightened in the post pandemic years, where the seasonal adjustments likely do not fully account for annual front-loading of price resets. We also see near-term fiscal policy tailwinds, stimulative monetary policy, stimulative financial conditions, and emerging evidence that AI is starting to scale into the economy and driving a productivity boom – all adding to upward pressure on yields. Overall, we see upside risks to all – labor markets data, growth, and also inflation – making for an attractive period to stay positioned for higher yields inn the coming few weeks. records.text: Kelun Biotech’s OptiTROP-Lung05 Hits Primary Endpoint in NSCLC and demonstrated OS benefit In November 2025, Kelun Biotech announced that the Phase III trial OptiTROP-Lung05 (China Only Study), evaluating sac-TMT in combination with Keytruda (K) as first-line treatment for PD-L1–positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), met its primary endpoint in the pre- specified interim analysis of progression-free survival (PFS). The study demonstrated a statistically and clinically significant improvement, with a trend toward overall survival (OS) benefit. Notably, OptiTROP-Lung05 is the world’s first Phase III study of a PD-(L)1 plus ADC combination to achieve its primary endpoint in first-line NSCLC treatment. For the past decade, the division’s identity was defined by the global dominance of Gardasil (HPV), which capitalized on a "prevention over cure" secular trend and massive greenfield opportunities in emerging markets, specifically China. Currently, the trade deal announcement only aided INR's recovery to early-Jan levels, it did not lead to a significant downward movement, partly due to muted capital flows and broader BoP deficit. FPI net inflow in Feb MTD, at USD 2.3bn, has barely offset the Jan net outflow. The Jan-MarFY26 QTD trend for overall BoP shows a significant deficit of USD 10-15bn. However, as discussed earlier, most of the positive BoP seasonality in Jan-MarFY26 occurs in the month of March, leaving scope of USDINR to temporarily fall below 90 in the near term. Additionally, we also have a USD 20bn BoP surplus forecast for FY27 which has been bolstered by the interim trade deal with the US. The result: oral bioavailability of just 0.4–1%, necessitating large doses (25–50mg oral vs. ~2.4mg SC weekly) and strict fasting conditions. • Non-peptide small molecule GLP-1RAs represent a paradigm shift. These synthetic compounds bind the GLP-1 receptor via the transmembrane domain (TM helices 1, 2, 3, and 7) rather than the extracellular domain used by native GLP-1 peptide. This orthosteric but non-canonical binding mode confers several key pharmacological properties: ° Gs-biased agonism with reduced beta-arrestin recruitment, which is associated with less receptor internalization and desensitization, and theoretically reduced GI adverse events, ° Resistance to DPP-4 degradation — unlike peptide GLP-1, these molecules are not substrates for dipeptidyl peptidase ° High oral bioavailability (20–40% for orforglipron in preclinical models) ° No food/water restrictions, eliminating the major compliance barrier of oral semaglutide • We believe the convenience advantage of no food/water restrictions is underappreciated. In real-world use, the requirement to fast 30 minutes and limit water intake is a meaningful compliance burden for a daily medication intended for chronic use. This is particularly relevant for the primary care setting where orforglipron will compete — PCPs are more likely to prescribe the simpler regimen. The flip side of this old-economy outperformance has been a more challenging backdrop for AI-related themes. Our view has been that the likely productivity gains from AI are real and the macro investment story has room to run. But we have worried that the market has already priced a lot of those gains, mostly into those directly involved in the AI boom, and that increased debt-financing of the capex boom was likely to come further into focus. Hyperscaler capex projections have risen sharply, supporting the investment story, and newer models and applications are showing evidence of enhanced capabilities. But this good “macro” news has led to negative market reactions and violent rotations under the hood, as markets have worried about the drain on hyperscaler cash flow and the potential for disruption to software providers and parts of the financial/real estate complex. These fears highlight the scope for big distributional shifts and significant winners and losers as the AI boom progresses. Intersecting with the focus on physical assets, (more AI-defensive) goods versus (more AI-disruptable) services may become another axis to watch. This improvement will be supported by a recovery in industrial activity reflecting firmer external demand and a more expansionary fiscal stance. Despite an increase in registered unemployment, the labor market remains tight, with persistent labor shortages translating into above-average wage growth. Inflation dynamics therefore exhibit a clear “two-speed” pattern: while headline inflation is expected to undershoot the 2% target this year due to a one- off administrative government intervention in energy prices and ongoing food price disinflation, still-elevated core inflationary pressures are likely to ease only gradually. In this environment, we expect the CNB to keep policy rates unchanged at 3.50%. Hungary Hungarian economy finished 2025 on a weak footing, with year-on-year GDP growth reaching only 0.5% in 4Q25 and thus underperforming versus regional peers. High frequency data has confirmed trends from previous months as industrial output continues to shrink, while retail sales increases at a moderate pace. Emerging Cardiology portfolio - maybe not enough to offset Eliquis but seeing blockbuster potential Milvexian – base case a major Eliquis LOE offset...blue sky case an even better atrial fibrilation treatment Oral anticoagulants (or "blood thinners") such as Eliquis (apixaban) are current standard of care for the prevention and treatment of venous and arterial thromboembolism. Oral anticoagulants as their name implies work by making the blood take longer to clot, lowering the risk of serious conditions like strokes, heart attacks, pulmonary embolisms and deep vein thrombosis. However, bleeding risk is a key concern (since these drugs interfere with the body's natural clotting process) and this contributes to significant underuse or underdosing of oral anticoagulants. Factor XI is a promising target since it plays a key role in blood clot formation but a lesser role in hemostasis (the process of stopping bleeding); as a result, Factor XI has potential to act on blood clot formation just like the oral anticoagulants, but with less risk of bleeding. This is supported by genetics; patients with Factor XI deficiency have lower risk for thromboembolism and ischemic stroke but also rarely have spontaneous bleeding compared to patients with normal Factor XI levels. We see the next key catalyst(s) for Bristol Myers' milvexian as Phase 3 data in stroke prevention (Librexia-STROKE) in 2026. FIGURE 156. records.text: M Idea 2 4Q GDP The GDP report mostly fit our expectations for slowing after a strong 4Q. The slowdown to an 1.3% pace was exaggerated by the government shutdown, but private final domestic purchases too slowed to 2.4% vs 2.9% in 3Q and 2.5%y/y. The slowdown was led by consumption, and tariffs will likely be a bigger drag on consumptoin in 1Q. Capex remained narrow outside of AI, but there were some signs of improvement in R&D spending. Residential investment fell -1.5% after a 7.1% decline in 3Q. For the year, the 4Q GDP report underlines the gradual slowing in domestic demand. At times last year, that slowdown was obscured in the GDP data by large swings in inventories and imports. But real consumer spending decelerated to 2.2%y/y in 4Q from 3.4% a year earlier. Business capex picked up slightly including non-AI spending ( Exhibit 8 ). Real residential investment was down 3.7% y/y in 4Q after a 1.3% rise a year earlier. Trade and inventory investment together added 0.3 pct pt to growth, in line with our estimate. We do not expect further drops in imports as they have likely retraced frontloading effects. The surge in imports last spring had appeared to be frontloading ahead of tariffs. There was some of that, but more of the surge appears to have been AI- related purchases of tech. Public finances | HMT versus Laffer – 1:0: This was a very strong public finances print. The monthly surplus rose to £30.4 billion, boosted by January self-assessment income tax receipts and £17 billion of capital gains tax receipts. This was ~£1 billion higher than the OBR had expected, and ~£7 billion more than normal, likely due to realised gains into the 2024 Budget, when the capital gains tax rate was hiked. Overall, the £6 billion beat came from £1.9 billion higher tax receipts, and £3.2 billion less spending than expected, with interest payments much lower than expected. We assume that this is to do with more benign RPI data than the OBR factored into its projections. Totalling it all: In FY2025/26, public sector borrowing is running at £8.3 billion lower than the OBR pencilled in back in the November EFO. One should take the ONS data with a pinch of salt – public finances numbers are prone to revisions – but this was a very good print. Rising Labour Costs and Cyclical Recovery Likely to Have Increased Productivity Growth We now explore what factors could be driving the difference between productivity outturns over the past two years and our trend productivity growth estimate. We begin by decomposing productivity growth into contributions from capital deepening and total factor productivity (TFP) growth. The latter refers to how much output the economy produces relative to its labour and capital inputs. We find that roughly half of the 0.3pp gap to our trend growth estimate is driven by capital deepening, with the difference concentrated in 2025. This reflects declining employment growth over the past year, while elevated business and government investment have likely pushed up the capital stock. Total factor productivity growth accounts for the remainder, with most of the gap in TFP growth relative to our trend estimate coming in 2024 (on a Q4/Q4 basis). One would expect the amount of capital that businesses choose to use in their production process relative to labour to depend on the relative cost of capital versus labour. Indeed, the strong contribution from capital deepening to productivity growth in 2025 coincided with high real wage levels (after strong growth in 2024) and a 1.5-2% increase in employment costs on the back of the employer National Insurance (NI) hike. This explanation for increased capital deepening chimes with reports from the BoE’s Agents that firms are using automation to partially offset labour cost pressures. To give a sense of the magnitudes, in standard economic models a 1.5-2% increase in employment costs would – all else equal – result in a similar increase in the capital-to-labour ratio, which would generate approximately a 0.6% increase in labour productivity. Adjustments in real wages would reduce the size of the response, but nonetheless this suggests that it is plausible that rising labour costs could account for much of the increase in capital deepening seen last year. Our NPV approach: We employ two principal methods to assess the sector: our fundamental valuation view is driven by a long-term cash flow NPV model. Given the largely explicit IP visibility on pharmaceutical assets and ability to make long-term forecasts with some (variable) degree of confidence, pharmaceutical companies are very well suited to valuation using a detailed long-term NPV forecast model. Our shorter-term valuation view and near-term order of preference is heavily informed by multiples, and in particular P/E and PEG ratios: the Pharma sector being one of the few where the ‘E’ in P/E arguably represents a reliable approximation of cash and a useful ‘real earnings’ metric. The summary of our NPV methodology is as follows: Beyond 2035E, a terminal capital value is calculated for all products incorporating an automatic terminal growth or fade assumption on residual sales: typically a fade at 7-10% pa. for pharmaceutical assets (which have defined short-term patent lifespans). This fade may vary for individual products by type of product and IP/market/competitive circumstances (e.g. those facing imminent expiry may be faded at 20-30% beyond the explicit forecast period). 19 February 2026 9 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

We think AI has held the economy afloat, and can drive a higher neutral rate: We recently noted the significant contributions of AI driven capex and the associated wealth effects (If you build it, AI will come, 17 October, 2025). We think that AI has kept the US economy out of recession. In How will immigration and AI impact the neutral rate?, November 20, 2017 - we noted the stronger productivity associated with a widespread use of AI can put sharp upward pressure on the neutral rate over time. Additionally, we noted that Fed policymakers will also be attentive to the labor market if labor slack increases due to worker replacement or augmentation from AI. And in this case, even when the neutral rate is perceived to be higher, the Fed could cut rates to support the employment side of its mandate. We see two scenarios that US rates market can price: Scenario 1: The AI continued boom scenario: a twist steepener? In this scenario, one can assume that AI investment continues unabated into 2026, propping growth and productivity, and raising the perceived neutral rate, while also negatively affects parts of labor market. In this scenario we could see the market price a higher long term neutral, and high issuance (to fund AI projects) in the long-end – alongside a dovish Fed accounting for the Fed’s recent imbalanced reaction function - adding a bear or twist steepening risk to the curve. records.text: Neurology: Kisnula commercial build continues ahead of early AD trial anticipation Scale advantage underappreciated here; large novel markets will require significant resources and we believe Eli Lilly is becoming increasingly well positioned. Eli Lilly's neuroscience franchise, anchored by Kisunla (donanemab-azbt) and reinforced by a deep clinical pipeline spanning Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, pain, and neuropsychiatry, represents what we view as an underappreciated contributor to the LLY investment thesis. Kisunla exited Q4 2025 at a $109M quarterly run rate — and has captured more than 50% of U.S. amyloid-targeting therapy total prescriptions, making it the U.S. market leader over Eisai/ Biogen's Leqembi in under 18 months post-launch. While neuroscience is currently a minimal contribution to Eli Lilly's total revenue, the franchise's optionality is enormous: consensus peak revenue estimates for Kisunla of ~$4-5bn 2033-2035 appear achievable in the base case but potentially conservative if TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3 succeeds. This is a prevention trial enrolling~3,000 cognitively unimpaired individuals with positive p-tau blood tests and we believe represents a binary catalyst with primary completion currently projected for November 2027 (but event-driven trial) that could expand Kisunla's total addressable market by 5-10x from ~1.3M symptomatic patients to the 10-15M Americans estimated to harbor preclinical amyloid pathology. A parallel benchmark model using only month fixed effects is estimated in the same recursive manner, serving as a seasonality-only baseline for comparison. Clark & West forecast comparison test To evaluate whether Truflation-based elastic net models improve upon the benchmark seasonal model, we apply the Clark & West (2007) test. The test adjusts for the fact that larger models (like an elastic net with many predictors) mechanically can reduce in-sample error even when the additional variables add no true predictive value. By correcting this bias, the Clark & West test answers the economically relevant question: Do Truflation variables provide statistically significant incremental information for forecasting CPI, beyond seasonal patterns alone? The test is conducted using out-of-sample forecast errors, not in-sample fits. Extracting variable importance As an additional step, using the elastic net fit on the full sample, we: • identify all nonzero model coefficients, • filter out seasonality dummies and lagged predictors, and • report the top three Truflation indicators for each CPI category. As many apparently seismic headlines as there have been so far this year, one constant from 2025 remains a mainstay of the first six weeks of 2026. Institutional investors were net sellers of US dollars on 73% of trading days last year; they are net sellers of US dollars on 74% of trading days this year. The USD was the second-worst-performing G10 currency last year after the JPY. It sits at the bottom of the rankings this year, with its (ever diminishing) rate advantage offering little cushion to a weaker spot trend. Higher volatility commodity currencies have taken over the top spots on investors’ wish lists, but positions on both sides of this view are getting crowded (Figures 1 and 2 below). Even so, we see few catalysts for change. Institutions have turned less aggressive buyers of commodity FX but are also selling the dollar as strongly as ever. Portfolio. The key drivers are easier fiscal and monetary policy, and our expectation of more growth-friendly trade policy. We now project that consumer stimulus from the OBBBA will be more front-loaded into tax season. This prompts us to tweak our forecasts: we modestly raise 1H 2026 growth and lower 2H. In the near term, supply-driven inflation due to tariffs should push inflation towards 3% y/y as businesses continue to slowly shift costs to consumers. records.text: Immunology: letting the data lead for best-in-class assets...whilst combinability could be upside in the years ahead Lebrikizumab (Ebglyss): Third to Market, Differentiated by Dosing Lebrikizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to IL-13 with high affinity and specificity, preventing the formation of the IL-13Rα1/IL-4Rα heterodimer signaling complex. Unlike dupilumab, which blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling through the shared IL-4Rα chain, lebrikizumab selectively neutralizes IL-13 — the dominant effector cytokine in atopic dermatitis skin pathology. This selectivity, combined with a monthly maintenance dosing schedule (versus biweekly for dupilumab), constitutes lebrikizumab's core commercial differentiation The ADvocate 1 and ADvocate 2 Phase 3 trials demonstrated IGA 0/1 response rates of approximately 43% versus 13% for placebo and EASI-75 response rates of approximately 59% versus 16% at Week 16 in adults and adolescents with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. Lebrikizumab's Q4 2025 global sales reached $134 million, with U.S. TRx growing 25% sequentially versus Q3 2025. In Europe, Almirall reported €75.5 million in lebrikizumab sales over the first nine months of 2025, representing a greater than 3x year-over-year increase, driven by the continued expansion of launch markets beyond Germany. However, consumer sentiment collapsed during 2025 on fears of rising living costs . US vehicle sales peaked in Q1 2025 on a combination of Trump optimism and later in the quarter as buyers sought to get ahead of potential tariff effects. However, full-year 2025 sales growth slowed to 2.4% from 3.6% in 2024, with Q4 sales contracting by 3.6% y/y. UK inflation forecast update The weight(s) of late winter We update our forecasts to reflect the January CPI print and released basket weights for 2026, making minimal changes to our forecast future path. Our headline CPI forecast is revised lower by an average 5bp over the next 12 months, while core is revised higher by 6bp on average. • January headline CPI was 7bp higher than our nowcast on Wednesday, printing at 3.0% y/y (3.01 at 2dp). For our detailed analysis of the print, please read One small step for Mann. Given our nowcast was tracking above the published forecast (see Up, but no balloons for housing) going into the print, the miss was 9bp above our forecast. However, applying the correct weights for 2026, the miss would have been 12bp (Figure 1). The front month miss was driven by stronger services, which printed 0.2pp above our expectation at 4.4% y/y. The strength in services came from less volatile components, but we do not change our sequential path on the back of the surprise. Core goods came in line with our expectation, but FAT was weaker than anticipated. This was offset by stronger energy, which was caused by an increase in electricity prices and its associated weight, in contrast to a reduction in the gas weight combined with a contraction in prices. • Overall, we still expect annual headline inflation to average 2.2% in 2026, but now expect headline CPI of 1.9% in 2027 (-0.1

It is also consistent with debt accumulation rais- ing the term premium. • This suggests that historically tight credit spreads may also reflect the deterioration in fiscal conditions alongside perceptions about the creditworthiness of issuers. • Looking forward, the CBO projects that US debt-to-GDP will continue growing quick- ly, rising from 98% currently to 126% by 2040. Our model suggests that is in theory worth up to ~50bp of downward pressure on high-grade corporate spreads. • For an investor with a ~10 year horizon, the starting yield on a bond index with duration of ~5-7 years is generally a good gauge of returns that can be expected over that period. Capital gains/losses are generally offset in time by income losses/gains. We thus previ- ously argued that long-term investors should not hold any DM government debt – the typical HG corporate spread has more than compensated for ~40bp of historical losses to downgrades. records.text: ing, IT, and research roles. International adoption growth is now accelerating rapidly. Australia, Brazil, the Netherlands, and France show the fastest growth in business customers currently. ChatGPT usage among business customers continues to scale globally, with the US, Germany, and Japan among the most active markets by message volume. McKinsey November 2025 88% of surveyed organizations are regularly using AI in at least one business function, up from 78% last year. However, most surveyed organizations are still in the experimentation / piloting phase of AI and nearly two-thirds have not begun scaling AI across the enterprise. 39% reported experimenting with AI agents specifically and the use of AI agents is most commonly reported among TMT and healthcare businesses. Respondents reported the greatest revenue benefits from AI in marketing and sales, strategy and corporate finance, and product development. A plurality of respondents had little to no change in employee headcount due to AI use over the past year. 32% of respondents expect an overall workforce reduction of 3% or more due to AI use and larger organizations are more likely to expect workforce reductions. Inaccuracy is the AI-related risk that was most commonly experienced and the top priority that organizations are working to mitigate going forward. records.text: Horizon Portfolio: portfolio keeps growing, but not too much additive from pipeline In 2022, Amgen acquired Horizon Therapeutics for $27.8bn, implying ~7.7x 2022A revenue. While Horizon’s portfolio clearly contains assets with continued growth potential, the valuation paid at the time of acquisition sets a relatively demanding economic hurdle. Under a more conservative multiple of approximately ~4x peak sales, Horizon assets would need to generate ~$6.5–7.0bn in peak revenue to fully support the transaction economics, from which ~$4bn would be supported by Tepezza. In our view, while growth remains visible across the portfolio, achieving this level of durable peak sales appears increasingly challenging as key assets mature and incremental growth drivers narrow. Tepezza: difficult to reaccelerate from an increasingly flat revenue base Tepezza remains a differentiated and clinically meaningful therapy in thyroid eye disease (TED). However, based on the revenue trajectory over the past several years, we believe the probability of Tepezza reaching a ~$4bn peak sales profile has diminished. Revenue growth has already flattened, with the strongest quarterly performance occurred in 2021, followed by a period of faded growth. This pattern is consistent with commercial dynamics typically observed for finite-duration regimens, which tend to peak quickly once the prevalent pool is addressed. FIGURE 115. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 7 The Decision Summary of Supreme Court decision on Learning Resources, Inc. v Trump The Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. Specifically, the Court invalidated tariffs imposed by President Trump under IEEPA authority to address drug trafficking and trade deficits. A key decision factor, in our reading of the decision, was the explicit vesting of the power to levy tariffs with Congress, not the Executive. Key takeaways from the ruling: IEEPA Does Not Authorize Tariffs. The Court ruled that IEEPA’s authorization to “regulate … importation” does not include the power to impose tariffs. Tariffs are taxes, and the Constitution assigns taxing authority – including duties on imports – exclusively to Congress. While IEEPA allows the President to block, prohibit, or otherwise regulate transactions involving foreign property, it does not authorize duties or tariffs. Major Questions Doctrine Applies. The Supreme Court applied the "major questions doctrine" in arriving at its decision. The doctrine refers to the notion that Congress must clearly authorize a delegation of extraordinary power. The Court said tariffs involve vast economic and political significance and constitute a core congressional power, and found no clear delegation of authority in IEEPA. records.text: US Money Markets Stigma no more? Modest mid-month firming in repo from Treasury settlements sparked the first material use of the SRP since year end, even as triparty cash rates remained low. This suggests the Fed's effort to reduce stigma is gaining traction, but without clearing, balance sheet constraints may still be a hurdle. This week's funding markets started to get a bit more interesting as front-end frictions returned over the past few days. We think this is largely a function of the mid-month Treasury coupon and regular T-bill settlements which combined totaled about $60bn on Tuesday. Treasury recently bumped up bill account sizes after having reduced net supply in December and into January. That means T-bill settlements have gone from a tailwind to more of headwind since then, with $50bn in net settlements this week and about $60bn/week over the past few weeks. Overall, the rise in these pressures suggests that reserve demand may not be far away from the steeper part the curve, and when frictions from settlements, for example, may more readily feed through to funding markets. This is all more reason for the Fed to keep the pedal to the floor on RMPs and maintain the elevated pace ($40bn/month) through the March purchase period and ahead of the April tax date, when the reserve drain from the TGA will be most acute ( Figure 1 and Figure 2). But we are unsettled by the combination of a declining input costs index – suggesting a slowing in the pace of cost pressures – paired with another big prices paid uptick in the services sector. The upbeat narrative around UK this year was one of growth without an acceleration in inflation. If UK corporates are using even a moderate upswing in demand to hike prices and improve their margins, this is clearly a hawkish concern. For now, we point to more benign manufacturing output prices, and do note that moves in the PMIs can be driven by non-consumer-facing sectors. Indeed, commentary by external MPC member Mann on the sectoral breakdown of the pricing intentions data in the DMP survey suggests that strength might be concentrated in the business-to-businesses sectors. Catalyst.Metric: Padcev FDA approvals and label expansion in bladder cancer

records.text: Seagen ADCs currently in development, for example SV - discussed below - could provide additional revenue growth in the coming years, if approved. Padcev is expected to generated ~$1.9bn in FY25 from sales predominantly in the locally advanced/metastatic 1L and 2L bladder cancer settings. In FY26 and beyond, we expect continued strong growth for the product driven by market share gains in 1L/2L metastatic settings as well as from label expansion into the muscle invasive bladder cancer setting (MIBC) following the successful EV-303 and EV-04 clinical trials. FDA approved Padcev in combination with Keytruda for MIBC in cisplatin-ineligible patients on 11/21/25, and FDA approval in cisplatin-eligible patients (EV-304) is anticipated in 2026. These new approvals in MIBC would double the addressable market for Padcev. Beyond MIBC, Pfizer is planning to start a pivotal trial in 2026 in non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), an even greater market opportunity with annual incidence of ~106,000 patients in the U.S. 19 February 2026 256 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

Catalyst.Metric: Spending Review; defence spending to 3% of GDP; unallocated capex ~GBP 5bn

records.text: l budget to defence (this would crowd out other investment but would be net neutral on the public finances). Deploying defence spending toward equipment procurement, infrastructure, cyber capability, AI systems would all count as capex and may not require new funding. The more the government can tap into the unallocated capital budgets over the coming years or simply redirect already planned capital expenditure into defence the easier and cleaner it would be on the public finances. How much cash could be deployed via existing capital budgets? While the Spending Review will have mostly allocated cash towards day-to-day and capital projects for the next few fiscal years, the Government could backload a sizeable amount of cash into 2029/30 - the final year of the current Parliament. How much unallocated capex does the Government have? Based on current underspend on central government net investment, we estimate that there may be roughly GBP 5bn in unallocated capex spend that could be diverted into defence spending. Redrawing capital budgets at the next Spending Review (due next year) could also allow Government to carve out additional funding from other departments to fund additional defence spending - potentially even accounting for nearly half the gap to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP. For many core macro assets—US rates, major DM equity indices and many major currencies— volatility has remained moderate. But that has coincided with extreme dispersion underneath the hood of the US equity market, and huge moves in non-US indices such as Korea and in commodities, especially gold and silver. These moves speak to the sharpness of the shifts in perceptions of the distribution of winners and losers, and the repositioning around those themes. As part of this, “spot up, vol up” dynamics have also been visible across a range of assets including Korean and Japanese equities, precious metals, and cyclical FX. Although record low levels of correlation have dampened US index volatility, longer-dated (1- and 2-year) SPX implied volatility has continued to drift to new YTD highs, even with US equities a bit higher so far. We continue to think that long volatility expressions like these, which are highly negatively correlated with equities and quite liquid, are good portfolio additions that could pay off even in a continued bull market. In solid tumors, PD-(L)1xVEGF bispecifics will be a key focus area in 2026 with both regulatory and clinical data catalysts. On the regulatory front, investors will watch for regulatory feedback and possibly FDA approval of Summit's ivonescimab in 2L+ EGFR NSCLC with a PDUFA date of November 14, 2026. Also in the 2H26, we should see topline data from Summit's pivotal (HARMONi-3) trial of ivonescimab in 1L squamous NSCLC, followed by topline data in non- squamous NSCLC in 1H27. Both studies will have important read-through to the space. HARMONi-3 is a global trial designed to answer the question of whether ivonescimab (PD1xVEGF) is superior to Keytruda (anti-PD-1) in patients with lung cancer. A positive result here would have significant positive read-through to all major PD-(L)1xVEGF programs in development. We also expect to see updated Phase 1/2 data sets from multiple assets in earlier stages of development, including for Bristol/BioNTech's pumitamig (PD-L1xVEGF) in lung cancer. 19 February 2026 42 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

Fiscal debt accumulation structurally compresses corporate spreads and may soften that argument in the future, though it clearly also raises the risk of fiscal stress. As the finances of the US government have deteriorated over the past two decades, the gov- ernments share of the aggregate US bond market has grown markedly. Figure 1 shows the Treasury share of US Aggregate Bond Index outstandings, and the investment-grade corpo- rate spread (right, inverted). As the US federal budget moved into a surplus in the late-1990s and early-2000s, the Treasury share of the bond market shrank rapidly. In the two decades since then, Treasury outstandings grew rapidly as budget deficits burgeoned, raising the Treasury share of outstandings to ~46% as of the end of 2025. At a low frequency, this shift in the relative supply of Treasuries appears inversely related to the evolution of corporate spreads. This suggests that the growing supply glut of government debt in the last two decades may have steadily diminished the so-called ‘convenience yield’ of US Treasuries – the premium investors are prepared to pay for their perceived unique safety and liquidity. Competing toxins from players like Revance (Daxxify) or Evolus (Jeuveau) have achieved only modest uptake, largely due to pricing challenges, limited brand recognition, and entrenched physician loyalty to Botox. The cash nature of the cosmetic market amplifies AbbVie’s pricing power and margin stability, as patients are less sensitive to small price adjustments and more influenced by brand trust and treatment familiarity. This dynamic allows Botox to sustain premium positioning and high gross margins despite emerging entrants. AbbVie’s integrated royalty and incentive structure between Botox and Juvéderm has strategically strengthened physician economics. By aligning discounts, rebates, and loyalty rewards across its aesthetic portfolio, the company has effectively lowered unit acquisition costs for practitioners while enhancing procedural profitability. This ecosystem—supported by shared salesforce, bundled promotions, and streamlined ordering—encourages cross-product adoption and long-term engagement with AbbVie’s platform. As a result, clinics perceive AbbVie’s suite not merely as individual products but as a synergistic business model that simplifies operations and improves cash flow, creating a formidable competitive moat against single-product rivals.
