We like the deal as it set Merck up for a leading position in the next-gen backbone therapy for IBD. In addition, Tulisokibart has the potential to be both first-in-class and best-in-class TL1a, and capture meaningful share in both IBD and other key immunology indications (RA, SSc-ILD, etc.). TL1A is a type II transmembrane protein in the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) family that functions as a chemical messenger and acts as a regulator of cellular immunity. TL1A interacts with its functional receptor, the death domain receptor 3 (DR3), and exhibits the highest homology to TNFR1 among the TNF-receptor superfamily (TNFRSF) members. There is compelling evidence indicating that interactions between TL1A and its functional receptor, DR3, deeply influence gut mucosal immunity, both in homeostatic conditions and various inflammatory states. In the case of elevated levels of TL1A in IBD, it enhances T-cell activity, promotes pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and contributes to intestinal fibrosis and barrier dysfunction—key drivers of IBD pathophysiology. 19 February 2026 224 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

Andy Burnham, while popular locally as Manchester mayor, is not currently an MP . records.text: European private credit: Slower fundraising and tempered returns. In July, we flagged that European private credit fundraising appeared more resilient than in the US, but updated Preqin figures paint a less upbeat picture. European private debt fundraising reached $66 billion last year, up from $41 billion in 2024 but still well below the $80 billion peak in 2023. Meanwhile the number of new funds fell to 58, the lowest since 2014 (Exhibit 5). Simply put, the market is maturing, with capital increasingly concentrated among fewer, larger managers. Total AUM has nevertheless resumed growth after stalling in 2024, reaching $560 billion by mid-2025 from $530 billion at end-2024 (Exhibit 6). Looking ahead, we think the durability of the growth story will hinge on relative returns and perceived downside risk. European private credit total returns were about 6% annualized in 2025 (through Q3), modestly ahead of EUR HY bonds at 5% and leveraged loans at 4% for the first time since 2022 (Exhibit 7). That said, 6% is below the 10-year median of 7%, which may be consistent with tighter public-market corporate credit spreads spilling over into private credit. The second pillar—the promise of more stable returns—faces a higher bar as investors scrutinize US portfolio marks amid last year’s loan defaults and renewed focus on software exposure. records.text: PUBLICATIONS ON OUR MOBILE APP What’s changed: We have seen a notable reversal in the direction of Treasury yields and the curve – from a bear/twist steepening trend to a bull/twist flattening trend. We think the market is dealing with a positioning clearing event as opposed to a fundamental re-evaluation of curve steepening trends. We have seen a lot of this adjustment in the past two weeks – and we favor swapping out of our 1s30s curve steepeners into a pay 10y swap trade. Four reasons we are here: (1) a re-evaluation of highly positioned trades in macro markets; sharp swings in precious metal prices and equity market rotation have threatened the market’s steepening bias; (2) a sharp rally in Japan has seeped into the US long end; (3) economic data have not been strong enough for investors to feel nervous about adding duration; and (4) real money investors have been looking to trade for lower yields, on what they see as a dovish Fed in 2026 (not our view). Five reasons paying 10y swaps could be good tactical risk-reward: (1) economic data are likely to stay healthy in the near term; (2) options market skew indicators show worried buying of US duration (see Figure 1); (3) term premiums are at the bottom of their recent mean-reverting range; (4) IEEPA ruling could re- ignite deficit concerns; and (5) we see scope for higher yields in Japan and steeper curves in Germany. We swap our 1s30s curve steepeners into paying 10y SOFR swaps, carrying an implicit spread-widening bias. B

records.text: 8. Japan—cyclical versus structural tensions. Sanae Takaichi’s landslide election victory earlier this month has raised expectations of a fresh fiscal boost to support the economy in the short term, and potentially a larger structural boost to defense spending as well, helping Japanese stocks to outperform. Since the election, the Yen has strengthened, and the curve has flattened with long-end rates declining. This cross-asset imprint is partly consistent with a more front-loaded tightening cycle, though the challenge to that interpretation is that there is little additional pricing for upcoming BoJ meetings. With wage growth and underlying CPI inflation still below levels consistent with the 2% target, our baseline remains that the BoJ will deliver the next 25bp hike in July, but the risks of an earlier/faster hiking cycle have risen. The threat of joint FX intervention has likely also played a role in supporting local markets, as have indications that the additional fiscal spend may not rely on bond issuance (and instead draw on profits from foreign assets). In any case, Japan’s strong external asset position, coupled with recently improving primary balances, means that some of the more extreme fiscal concerns are overdone. But with negative real rates at the front of the curve, it will be tough to sustain Yen strength if the BoJ reaction remains as subdued as we expect, and global and local cyclical impulses could push USD/JPY back into the 155-160 range. But 2026 is starting to look more like 2019-20, and the Fed’s efforts to improve the SRP appear to be paying off. This is because the Fed’s counterparties tapped the SRP for over $30bn this week even as triparty rates remained quite contained. “We should take another step to improve the SRP’s effectiveness. Of the remaining two, one came during the pandemic, when rates were already near the zero lower bound, when measures such as quantitative easing and aggressive fiscal support were enacted instead to counter the deflationary effects of the shock. The other came during the stagflationary period of the late 1970s, when a misery index constructed as the sum of the unemployment rate and retail price inflation rate breached 15 and then 20% before the 1979 general election. Yesterday’s confirmation of unemployment rising nearly to the level seen during COVID sparks thoughts of whether the Bank of England needs to do much more to combat a slowing economy. The Fed remains on hold through most of 2026, then raise the policy rate in 4Q26 as inflation moves up and the unemployment rate moves down. Hikes continue in 1H27 reaching a peak of 4.375%. In other news, a V A funding bill continues to make its rounds on the Hill that would poten- tially increase the upfront fees charged on IRRRLs from 50bp to 140bp. Note that the latest iteration has dropped a potential rise in the initial funding fee on purchase loans from 2.15% to 2.45% and from 3.3% to 4.3% on subsequent uses of the V A loan program. This could be the first positive change for mortgage investors in V A structure in many years, as a higher charge on IRRRLs would increase the balances and payments for borrowers as most capital- ize the funding fee. This 90bp fee increase is equivalent, in payment terms, to roughly an 8bp elbow shift. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS We like BRL. Brazil has attracted strong financial inflows this year, benefiting from broad USD weakness and renewed investor appetite for emerging markets. The country’s exceptionally high carry , 15% in nominal terms and roughly 10.6% on a 12-month ex-ante real basis (Figure 2), continues to be a powerful magnet for capital. Against this backdrop, we continue to favour the BRL among LATAM high yielders in the near to medium term, ahead of a period when political risks are likely to rise and the election cycle becomes the dominant market driver. Recent COPOM minutes reinforce this constructive view, revealing policymakers’ strong intention to begin the easing cycle as early as March. While inflation and expectations have not fully converged to the central target of 3%, h eadline inflation at 4.44% is already within the tolerance band, providing sufficient room to justify the start of monetary easing. Market pricing currently implies around 250bps of rate cuts before the October election, roughly 50bps at each of the next five meetings, with a terminal policy rate near 11.9% by around April next year. Even under this easing path, the risk premium embedded in Brazilian rates remains attractive relative to the central bank’s estimate of the neutral rate of around 5%. To make the model computationally efficient while maintaining statistical rigor, we tune these hyperparameters once per CPI category using cross-validation on the full historical sample. This determines whether a CPI component is best modeled by: • a sparse, LASSO-like structure, or • a smoother, Ridge-like structure that combines multiple correlated Truflation indicators. Once tuned, these hyperparameters remain fixed during the forecast evaluation stage. Expanding-window pseudo out-of-sample forecasting Rather than evaluating the model in-sample, we construct a full real-time pseudo out-of-sample forecasting sequence. The structure is not technically completely out-of-sample, as the hyperparameters are estimated up front across the entire sample, and then held constant in the expanding-window out-of-sample estimations. We also do not make adjustments for any historical revisions to the Truflation data, were they to have occurred. Beginning with an initial five years of data, the model is re-estimated each month using only information available up to that point. It then produces a one-step-ahead CPI forecast. This recursive process continues through the end of the sample, producing a sequence of pseudo out-of-sample forecasts for all CPI categories. When US mega cap growth dominates index performance, benchmark weights mechanically drift toward the US and away from regions like the UK. This is not a macro verdict, it is flow mathematics. These windfall revenues would help narrow the structural deficit and could reduce the urgency of implementing the full fiscal adjustment announced by Kast during the campaign. records.text: 8 Sources: IBGE, BNP Paribas Brazilian presidential and congressional elections scheduled for October stand to have key consequences for the economy and markets throughout the year. We anticipate a very close presidential contest, with polls swinging between the incumbent Lula and a right-wing challenger right up to the end of the second round of voting, potentially sparking volatility throughout the year. The “Car Wash” corruption scandal dominated the 2018 election and worries about high inflation were prominent in 2022. This year, voter priorities are centered around improving economic fundamentals on the one hand and public-safety concerns on the other. Over 2023-2025, Brazil’s real GDP growth averaged 2.8% (we forecast 2.4 % for last year), while inflation fell to 4.26% by December 2025 (from 5.8% three years earlier) and unemployment hit a historical low of 5.1%, driving the “misery index” down steadily in Lula’s third term (Figure 5). If our forecast proves right, H2 2026 – when election campaigning peaks – will play out against a still-healthy economic backdrop. Yet crime remains the top voter concern (Figure 6), with recent corruption scandals, falling inflation, new policing measures and expanded social benefits having only briefly affected government approval ratings. Meanwhile, the fiscal deficit – the key theme for markets — is almost a nonexistent concern for voters. Merck has an extensive patent estate that extends beyond Keytruda’s composition-of-matter patent. This could offer a potential path to longer market exclusivity in the U.S. that goes beyond 2028. Humira’s composition-of-matter patent expired in 2016; however, AbbVie constructed a patent thicket of more than 130 patents across formulation, device, manufacturing, and indication claims. Through serial litigation and staggered settlements with individual biosimilar manufacturers, AbbVie effectively postponed meaningful U.S. biosimilar entry until 2023— roughly seven years later—and even then preserved share by migrating the market to a citrate- free, high-concentration formulation that biosimilars struggled to match. Humira still maintains meaningful share of the adalimumab molecule. Enbrel, whose original COM patent expired in 2012, maintained its U.S. monopoly for more than a decade beyond that date. This was achieved not through a single patent but through acquisition and restructuring of key Immunex IP , plus two critical patents (’182 and ’522) that Amgen successfully defended in federal court and at the Supreme Court. 19 February 2026 214 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

But we don’t think Warsh will be too concerned about dissents, as long as he has the seven votes needed to cut rates. He has billed himself as a disruptor rather than a consensus builder, and as we argued recently, the era of consensus building at the Fed is probably ending (see Fed: Agree to Disagree ). Uncooperative data = uncompelling case for cuts The issue for Warsh is that the recent data flow substantially challenges the case for cuts. In the last two months, the u-rate has dropped by 25bp. This would increase the target policy rate by 25-50bp in the various Taylor Rule models the Fed looks at. And although CPI inflation is falling, PCE inflation is likely to move up meaningfully in the next two months. We think core PCE will probably come in at 3.0-3.1% y/y in January, compared to 2.8% as of November. This would raise the target policy rate by another 30bp-plus across the Fed’s various Taylor Rule models. Moreover, the u-rate is now only a tenth above the FOMC’s median natural rate estimate of 4.2%. Additional declines would make it very hard for the Fed to maintain a dovish bias, given that inflation is stuck above target even ex of tariffs. To be clear, Warsh has eschewed this sort of data dependence. He is likely to argue that the Fed should be forward looking about the disinflationary impact of the impending AI productivity boom. B

We update our view on the trading range for 10y OAT-Bunds in 2026, to 50- 95bp (lowering the low bound from 65bp to 50bp in light of the strong appetite for carry that supports all EGBs). In a risk‑on environment, OAT–Bunds can grind tighter in line with historical beta to BTP–Bunds. But we see limited scope for France to outperform within the rest of the EGB spectrum, especially as political “cheapness” has normalised and event risk (2027 budget/election) lingers. On the demand side, domestics will continue to support— banks have capacity but comparatively less than in 2025, instead we expect lifers to take the baton. Non- domestic inflows can deepen, especially from private investors, but levels may be more modest relative to peripheral peers, which limits potential for sectoral outperformance. Politics: temporary relief from structural difficulties In recent years, political uncertainties in France have had significant impact on the pricing of OATs vs EGB peers (Exhibit 10), and we assume it will continue to play an important role given the absence of a stable majority and ongoing fiscal strain. As such, licensing activity has become a key barometer of China biotech’s integration into the global innovation supply chain. This wave of outbound partnering is commonly referred to as “going global” within the domestic market. This dynamic accelerated meaningfully from 2023 onward, as global pharma demand for externally sourced innovation increased while internal R&D productivity remained under pressure. Against this backdrop, China’s combination of lower development cost, faster clinical readouts, and improving data quality has enabled licensing-out to scale rapidly from opportunistic transactions into a structurally embedded funding and commercialization pathway for the sector. This dynamic is structurally positive for large-cap pharma but increasingly challenging for U.S. SMID biotech. This operating environment has proven structurally beneficial for U.S. large- cap pharmaceutical companies, while creating growing headwinds for SMID-cap U.S. biotech developers. 19 February 2026 22 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

records.text: n by our equity strategists recently (see here), Europe stands out as the region expecting to shrink workforce most aggressively on the back of AI — a net 35% of companies plan to reduce their workforce. This compares to shares in their low teens in most other regions. So far, reductions in the European workforce are not visible, however: employment has slowed down but net job creation remains positive at +0.7%Y in 4Q25 and the unemployment rate has been remarkably stable since 2024. A recent ECB study reports that while firms aim to reduce R&D costs through AI, the workforce is not yet expected to fall. Firms interviewed in the survey reported flat employment, as "integration of AI into work processes had enabled businesses to grow without needing more staff". We also note arguments in favour of a progressive transition rather than abrupt changes to the labour market: 63.5% of the euro area labour force is employed in SMEs (see here), and recent research (here) suggests slower adoption rates for SMEs, as only larger firms "possess the resources, technical expertise, and economies of scale needed to absorb (AI) integration costs". records.text: 11 Brazil 18/02/2026 A polarized electorate Fig. 11: Candidates’ rejection by voters’ political position Lula versus Bolsonaro: The main feature of this year’s presidential election is the replay of 2022’s Lula-Bolsonaro clash, although with a younger member of the right- wing family as the likely second-round challenger to the incumbent. Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro both have high disapproval ratings (50-60% depending on the survey), but they also have the support of large and consolidated pools of voters who are highly unlikely to change sides. In a 20 January poll by AtlasIntel and Bloomberg, 92% and 90.5% of respondents who voted respectively for Lula and Jair Bolsonaro in 2022’s second round said they would do the same this year. According to the Genial Quaest survey published in January (Figure 10), Brazilian voters are split into three roughly equal blocs: independents, backers of ‘Lulism’ and the left wing, and supporters of Jair Bolsonaro and the right wing. Within these left and right blocs, around 90% would refuse to vote for the other side’s candidate in a Lula-Flávio Bolsonaro scenario (Figure 8). Independent voters look set to be the deciding factor in what will probably be a tight election. The Genial Quaest survey also suggested that an average of 33% of independents would be willing to support Lula, 35% have no plans to vote and 30 to- 60% would back a right-wing candidate (depending on whether that was Flávio Bolsonaro or Tarcísio de Freitas). Citi’s POLLS indicator has suggested some tactical caution, and as a result the SPX is in a messy sideways range, but the bigger story is the sector level rotation, which has become one of the key macro debates – see Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas - Debating the rotation. Our equity strategists believe that the broadening has more room to run, and we therefore reduce our risk in the technology sector, adding some cyclical risk instead. For a longer discussion of what plagues technology, see the US equity section. records.text: Foreign Exchange Forecasts 19 February 2026 Citi Research 3 A quick note on our forecasts We have lowered our 0-3m EURUSD forecast to 1.15 from 1.16, and raised our 6- 12m forecast from 1.10 to 1.11. However, this should not be read as a forecast change. We show our forecasts in two ways: (1) a rolling period forecast (i.e., 0-3m, 6-12m, Figure 1) and (2) a fixed date forecast (e.g., December 2026, Figure 36 in the Appendix). These are not independent forecasts, but rather show different parts of the same forecast curve. In today’s forecast, we did not make any changes to our EURUSD fixed date forecasts; in other words, there is no change to our forecast this month. However, the rolling windows are now moving to greater reflect the parts of the forecast curve where we expect an H1 ’26 USD rally (as seen in the 0-3m EURUSD forecast falling); as well as the subsequent reversal higher starting towards the end of the year (as the impacting fiscal impulse in EU starts to improve the growth outlook for the region). This “glide path” should continue in coming months. We have written extensively over the past year about whether to focus more on structural or cyclical impacts to FX and how this influences our forecasting. While the structural USD headwinds remain in place, the actual flows are fickle and episodic. And we continue to see cyclical factors as better for forecasting over a 3– 12-month horizon. records.text: European Rates Weekly 19 February 2026 Citi Research 15 Covered bond yields have rallied significantly since the start of the year. In the past 1.5 months, covered bond yields have rallied by 10-30bp in 2-15y (Figure 24; bonds issued after QE net asset purchases ended in July 2022). SSA yields followed suit, albeit to a slightly lesser extent allowing covered bonds to outperform SSAs so far this year (Figure 17). Given how SSA spreads to EGBs were already stretched (see SSA & Covered Bond Navigator: The conundrum of SSA relative ‘value’), the YTD outperformance of covered bonds has not only reduced their attractiveness to investors looking at their RV against EGBs, but also versus SSAs. This has left covered bonds spreads to EGBs in most core markets in the 15-35bp range (Figure 25) The YTD outperformance of covered bonds has reduced their attractiveness to their main buyers. The relative value proposition of covered bonds to bank treasuries, that are their largest buyers (see Figures 9 here), has certainly weakened owing to their continued swap spread tightening. Similarly, the value they offer versus EGBs and SSAs is starting to look increasingly stretched when considering their capital treatment and weaker liquidity. Finally, given their YTD yield rally outright buyers are likely to question how much further they can tighten, unless EGB yields rally further. records.text: Strategic M&A turns more credit friendly. Announced strategic M&A volumes have started the year out on a subdued pace with just $141 billion announced year to date. This would put 2026 squarely in the middle of the pack through this point in the year compared to the past 10 years (Exhibit 3). So far this year, announced strategic M&A volumes have tended to be more credit friendly in nature than last year. Only 16% of this year’s deal volume has come from mega deals ($20+ billion) compared to 36% of last year’s volumes and only 38% is expected to be funded with a debt component, down from 46% of 2025’s volumes. There has been a dramatic shift in the composition of announced strategic M&A volumes this year with nearly 50% coming from the Healthcare and Oil & Gas sectors while last year the top two sectors were Tech and Telecom. Looking ahead, what should credit investors expect from M&A for the rest of the year? First, we would note that activity in the first seven weeks of the year is not typically indicative of full-year volumes (Exhibit 4). For example, 2025 is a case in point with slow M&A volumes through February and then ending the year with record volumes. Second, we still expect roughly $200 billion in M&A-related supply in the USD IG primary market this year, as much of the large backlog of deals that have been announced but net yet completed (currently >$800 billion) will end up closing and getting funded. Treasury auctions point to rising trend in foreign participation. This shift began to emerge in the second half of 2025 and has carried into the start of the year, most notably in the January auction cycle. The resilience in overseas demand is notable, given concerns about USD weakness, as well as BoJ policy intervention. While domestic investors continue to absorb the bulk of issuance with allocations running near 70%, a rising trend over the past decade, foreign buying has picked up recently. Although foreign demand has generally remained low and stable in recent history, it has strengthened meaningfully with investors taking down more than 20% of the auction supply in recent auctions, the highest allocation in more than a decade ( Figure 1). A rough back of the envelope calculation suggests those added maybe 10bp to aggregate productivity in 2025 compared to past trends. The last piece of the AI puzzle is inflation. If it is too early to assess the impact of AI on growth, it is surely also too early to see any impact on inflation. As we detail in our inflation preview for February (here), the descent in services inflation remains steady but slow, while goods inflation has been stable over the past 18 months. Hard to see any impact yet in these data. With no sign of AI impacting inflation, we take recourse in a thought framework of some of the forces that would be at play. The most obvious macro argument is that AI adoption should boost productivity, with a potentially negative impact on labour demand. Upside risks to supply, combined with negative risks to demand, mean downside risks to inflation. Another disinflationary force could come from changes in the distribution of wages across the economy. For example, if AI adoption has the capacity to automate high paying white collar jobs, while having a much more limited effect on lower paid blue collar jobs then, all else equal, the composition of employment would shift toward lower wage occupations. records.text: Therapeutic Theme #2: Total eclipse of how we're treating the heart...a new wave of therapies in cardiovascular Relevant for MRK, LLY, PFE, BMY, CYTK The modern pharmaceutical industry was shaped by therapeutics for cardiovascular diseases, which produced some of original blockbusters including Capoten, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor for hypertension, Humulin, biosynthetic human insulin for diabetes, and Mevacor/Lipitor, statin for dyslipidemia in 1980s. Such multi-billion dollar revenue streams sustained double-digit growth for pharmaceutical industry over past decades and led to the emergence of global biopharmaceutical companies. This golden era of drug developments for cardiovascular disease came to an end when former blockbusters went generic and biopharma industry's focus shifted to specialty drugs (e.g. oncology and immunology) from the 2000s. It coincided with declining cardiovascular mortality rates in the developed countries due to the first wave of cardiovascular medical innovation and public health campaigns for lifestyle improvement, when novel cardiovascular drugs at the time often delivered diminishing incremental therapeutic benefits. Nevertheless, significant unmet needs continue to exist. In 2021, major CVDs (ischemic heart disease, stroke, etc.) were the leading causes of age-standardized deaths. Central Bank Buying (Temporarily) Slows on Volatility from Diversification Demand Over recent months, a rise in private sector diversification demand—partly expressed through gold call‑option structures—has driven elevated volatility in gold prices (Exhibit 1). This is because, as prices move higher, dealers who have sold these calls are forced to buy gold to maintain hedges, mechanically amplifying upside moves. Conversely, even modest pullbacks can prompt dealers to shift from buying into strength to selling into weakness, potentially triggering investor stop‑outs which in turn may lead to further losses, as we have observed in late January. This rise in volatility, in turn, has led to a slowdown in our central bank demand nowcast (22 tonnes in December 2025, with the 12-month average now at 52 tonnes), which we see as temporary (Exhibit 2). While we have characterized a sustained slowdown in our central bank demand nowcast as an important marker for the gold price outlook, we believe this slowdown will be temporary based on our conversations with central banks, the structural shift in how reserve managers perceive risks since the freezing of Russia’s reserves in 2022, and our view that large EM central bank gold allocations remain well below their likely targets. Our conversations suggest that reserve managers remain willing buyers of gold to hedge geopolitical and financial risks but prefer to delay purchases until prices stabilize. records.text: 6 Global Economic Weekly | 20 February 2026 The quality of growth has certainly improved over the last few quarters, with capex playing a more prominent role, helped by the implementation of NGEU (Next Generation EU) and a reduction in overall uncertainty, as well as government consumption contributing much less than in previous years (Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 6). This should remain the case going forward. However, a strong Euro, together with weakness among key trading partners, poses a significant downside risk, particularly for the tourism sector. Dealing with the NGEU cliff With the deadline to submit final payment requests for NGEU disbursements looming (Sept 26), we keep being asked how recipients of large support will deal with the “fiscal cliff”. We are not worried, at least for now. Cohesion funds have barely been used and will likely serve as a bridge for now until the new EU budget is in place. In Spain’s particular case, that will be coupled with the creation of an investment fund, called “Spain grows”, that will provide continuity. Details are still scarce, but the idea is to create a fund managed by the public institution ICO (Instituto de Credito Oficial), with equity of EUR13.3bn (EUR10.5bn coming from NGEU loans and the rest from transfers), which would allow ICO to invest up to EUR60bn. Ideally, by promoting co-investment, that number could reach up to EUR120bn. Those may be optimistic figures, but the important takeaway is that the new fund provides continuity

Data centers can be broadly classified by tenancy, namely hyperscale, enterprise and retail co-location (Figure 5S & P d a t a c e n t e r A B S p o o l c h a r a c t e r i s t i c s ) . Each of these categories differ in terms of size, number of users, power requirements and typical lease duration. For example, hyperscale data centers typi- cally have one or very low number of tenants and require at least 40MW of power capacity. Hyperscale data centers usually have long term leases (~10 yrs), and offer relatively stable cashflows since tenants in this segment are limited to some of the largest corporates (AAA and/or investment grade). records.text: 9 Presidential election front-runners: Our latest “poll of polls” still points to three names dominating the presidential election’s first round: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro and Tarcísio de Freitas. The official slate currently lists Lula, the incumbent president, as the PT (Partido dos Trabalhadores) party’s candidate, while Flávio Bolsonaro was hand-picked by his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, to carry the PL (Partido Liberal) party’s banner and extend the Bolsonarist legacy into the next ballot. Freitas, the incumbent governor of São Paulo province, recently announced that he will seek re-election and will support Flavio Bolsonaro. As a result, we anticipate a shift in support toward Bolsonaro, a trend that is already visible in the most recent polling data. Even so, Lula is maintaining a comfortable lead, securing a place in the second round of voting under virtually every scenario. Other contenders: In addition to Freitas, two other provincial governors appear in the polls as candidates: Ratinho Júnior of Paraná and Romeu Zema of Minas Gerais. Both have lingered in the single-digit range since the first rounds of polling, occasionally approaching the 10% mark but never quite breaking through. Their performances have been modest, yet steady enough to keep them in the picture as potential swing-vote aggregators for a broader centrist coalition in the second round. Uplizna is an Anti-CD19 humanized igG1 monoclonal antibody engineered for B-cell depletion. It binds to CD19, a transmembrane protein that broadly expressed in all B cells. CD19 plays two different major roles in human B cells: on one hand, it acts as an adaptor protein to recruit cytoplasmic signalling proteins to the membrane, on the other, it works within the CD19/CD21 complex to decrease the threshold for B cell receptor signalling Pathways. As a CD-19 + B cell depleter, Uplizna is uniquely placed in the MG landscape, as it offers more efficient B-cell depletion as CD 19 proteins have broader presentation than CD20 protein, and a convenient dosing internal. In myasthenia gravis (MG), while Uplizna is approved across antibody subtypes, its strongest mechanistic and clinical fit is in MuSK-positive MG, a relatively small subset of the overall MG population. In the larger AChR-positive MG segment, Uplizna is more likely to displace CD20- based therapies such as Rituximab, rather than meaningfully expand the treated population. 19 February 2026 110 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

In Ginnies, this phenomenon has been accelerated in recent years by strong CMO demand feeding back into the creation of more marginal custom stories. For example, 100% FHA is a popular story these days, and that’s caused the V A% to grow as a share of the multi-issuer pools. That in turn has led to a deterioration in the convexity of the TBA and higher peak prints (and, in a vicious cycle, stronger demand for specs). However, as we have previously noted, we expect a plan B given the effort and importance of the tariffs put in place as a component of the administration's policy agenda, including the recent investment deals linked to trade policy. In this blog we discuss the possibility of an early departure by Lagarde from the ECB: why, and what it means. We also discuss what new leadership would mean for ECB policy going forward. In our view the structure of the current monetary policy framework is robust. It should mean that policy decisions will continue to be data dependent, not personality dependent under a new President. As such, our outlook for ECB policy remains unchanged. Our baseline has the ECB on hold for the time being. The risks are skewed to further cuts in 2026, but our baseline has the next move as a hike in mid-2027. Why Lagarde could be considering an early resignation The next French Presidential election will be held in April 2027. US economy: In a good place: We’ve been optimistic on the US outlook, and have argued that the labor market is more resilient than the Federal Reserve and others have given it credit. Recently we, and many other forecasters, have been dialing up that optimism. Starting with the January payroll report - o ur view has been that less intense holiday - season hiring will entail fewer - than - usual job cuts after the period. This should be reflected in stronger seasonally adjusted hiring in January. Our estimate for January nonfarm payrolls is a gain of 105k, and we expect a steady unemployment rate at 4.4%. January payroll growth would be nearly double the numbers required to maintain the unemployment rate (see US January jobs preview: Better days ). Recent data also pose some upside risk to our already above-consensus growth estimate for Q4 (see Figure 3), and we see momentum continuing in Q1 as households see record tax refunds in the wake of last year’s OBBBA. records.text: However, respondents appear to expect the Fed to provide more support to the housing market. Two-thirds of respondents expect the Fed under a new chair to take action aimed at lowering long-term mortgage rates (beyond simply reducing the fed funds rate), with most expecting this to occur in coordination with the Treasury. A similar share expects the Fed to target lower mortgage rates specifically, through measures such as ending the runoff of MBS on the Fed’s balance sheet. We see these moves as less likely because they would be at odds with established principles including a preference for using the funds rate as the primary tool for setting monetary policy, a reluctance to allocate credit to specific sectors, and a preference for holding primarily Treasury securities. Unsurprisingly in light of these results, the majority does not expect the Fed to reduce the size of its balance sheet. Kevin Warsh, whom President Trump has announced he intends to nominate to take over as Chair from May 15, has spoken extensively in favor of shrinking the Fed’s balance sheet. However, changes in balance sheet policy would require support from a majority of FOMC voters and a substantial reduction would require moving away from the ample reserves framework that has broad support among Fed officials. More plausibly, changes in regulatory and supervisory policies could reduce the demand for bank reserves, and some moves in this direction seem likely over the medium term. Exhibit 5: No Consensus

On financial system vulnerabilities, the staff maintained that vulnerabilities were “notable” on balance, with “elevated” asset valuation pressures a key pillar of that assessment. The staff noted that equity price-to-earnings ratios were at the upper end of the historical distribution, reflecting expectations of strong earnings growth for technology firms and elevated investor risk appetite, and the staff also highlighted that credit spreads were low by historical standards. In the staff’s taxonomy, vulnerabilities tied to nonfinancial business and household debt were characterized as moderate, though the staff noted that financing of AI investment would likely require higher debt issuance over time. They assessed that low debt loads at most technology firms and muted aggregate debt growth in recent years suggested capacity to accommodate that issuance. This is a view our analysts share. By contrast, vulnerabilities associated with financial-sector leverage were characterized as notable, with high leverage at hedge funds and life insurers standing out, while funding risks were characterized as moderate, including an assessment that stablecoins remained small relative to other short-run funding instruments. In our view, this discussion reinforced our belief that the Committee is attentive to “excess” even if it avoided labeling them as bubbles.

The UK is overweight financials, energy, materials, staples and healthcare, and structurally underweight platform technology. Markets tilted toward banks and commodities do not command the same multiples as those driven by high duration growth. But the more revealing lens is growth adjusted valuation. On a PEG basis, the FTSE 100 trades largely in line with the S&P 500 and MSCI ACWI. Once lower earnings growth is accounted for, UK large caps are not anomalously cheap, they are priced coherently with their trajectory. Global allocators are not mispricing UK large caps; they are discounting them rationally. The true divergence sits in SMIDs. FTSE 250 companies trade on materially lower PEG ratios than global peers, reflecting a structural risk premium on earnings tied to domestic sentiment, policy and liquidity. This is where optionality becomes most punitive. The Microstructure Shift: Buybacks as the New Domestic Bid In the absence of domestic institutional flows, buybacks have emerged as the most consistent source of demand. records.text: full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 60k in 2026. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate remaining at 4.5% in 1H26 before dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at the January meeting, as expected. In the characterization of current conditions, the Fed leaned into the Dec u-rate decline. Powell’s comments on the labor market mirrored the optimism in the statement. But he also highlighted some pockets of concern. We remain comfortable with our view that the Fed won’t cut again under Powell. We have penciled in two 25bp cuts under the next Chair, with low conviction, in June and July for a terminal rate of 3.0- 3.25%. Policy under the next Chair will depend a lot on the composition of the FOMC.

records.text: We update our AI adoption tracker through February 2026. n AI-related investment growth remains strong, particularly for semiconductors, n where equity analysts expect global revenue growth of 43% from current levels by the end of 2026. AI-related investment in the US national accounts also continues to rise and now stands $271bn above its 2022 level. AI-related hardware shipments from Taiwan to the world increased further to $56bn in January. AI adoption by firms now stands at 18.9% among US establishments (with n adoption expected to rise to 22.1% in the next 6 months) according to the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey. Information services, professional services, education services, and finance/insurance firms continue to lead adoption. At a detailed industry level, web search and publishing firms report the highest use of AI today, with broadcasting firms reporting the largest expected increase in adoption over the next 6 months. Establishments with over 250 employees continue to lead in adoption (34.8%), while establishments with 50-99 employees have shown the largest increase in adoption since the start of the year (+7.6pp to 25.1%). There are still potential political flashpoints ahead (26 February by-election, 7 May local and Scottish/Welsh elections) but our base case is that any leadership challenge would likely occur later in the year, perhaps ahead of the 27-30 September Labour Conference. While political noise could create a persistent headwind to gilt performance, there are offsetting tailwinds from BoE dovishness and relatively supportive issuance trends. Indeed, if wasn’t for the headlines around the PM, we suspect there would have been greater bullish follow through for gilts following the dovish 5 February BoE meeting. That meeting set up for the next cut by April and then left all options open thereafter. The guidance has switched from path- dependency to data-dependency, and we expect the BoE will be patient in determining a resting rate for the easing cycle. Our house view has moved to 3% in November (from 2.75%) for the trough rate, but this remains lower than market pricing. records.text: up to 0.4%. Most details were known from previously released CPI and PPI. Portfolio management fees were up 1.8%MoM, airfares and healthcare prices were close to flat. Citi’s take – Q4 real GDP along with December income, spending and inflation do not significantly change the outlook. Most readings were close to our expectations and will leave in place our and Fed officials understanding that activity is holding up even as underlying inflation is slowing and hiring has been weak. Core PCE inflation is above target at 3.0%YoY and above 3% on a monthly annualized basis as well. But most of the elevation in inflation is due to stronger readings for goods inflation in prior months that should fade as firms complete the pass-through of tariff costs to consumers. Shelter inflation is slowing and with the labor market looser there should be less concern about upside risk in other services inflation. January core inflation readings have been boosted by residual seasonality in recent years, so a more “normal” reading in the next PCE release – even if still elevated – is also reassuring. The most interesting development in the GDP report was strength in AI-related investment that was offset by weakness in other categories of investment. Information processing investment added 0.65pp to real GDP and investment. Software intellectual property investment added another 0.17pp. Summing these two, AI-related investment accounted for 0.82pp, or about 1/3 of private final demand growth in Q4.

The current structure of QT operations does not allow for sales of sub 3yr maturity gilts and with the DMO constrained by redemptions, the APF lending facility becomes an important safety valve in preventing specialness and a disorderly richening in ultra-short gilt spreads. Ultra-short issues are attractive for delivery in BoE repo operations since they command lower haircuts – 1.5% for 1-3y bonds vs 3.5% for 5-10y bonds. The deals typically pay only interest until the principal is repaid at the ARD (anticipated repayment date). ARDs on data center transactions range often between 3-7 years, with the legal final maturity at 30 years. The structure also includes provisions for a DSCR-linked cash trap and sweep early amortization triggers to protect noteholders from credit deterioration. Falling below a cash trap threshold, typically set at 1.3-1.35x, locks out the issuer from receiving any excess cash flow and diverts it into a cash trap reserve account. The cash sweep feature, typically triggered if DSCR falls below 1.2x, uses all excess cash flow to pay down the outstanding principal amount on the notes. records.text: ll else equal, the composition of employment would shift toward lower wage occupations. On the other hand, the need for large scale investment in AI infrastructure can exert significant price pressure along supply chains and in some sectors. Some deeper analysis and constant monitoring is warranted here. The price of investment (and ultimately the GDP deflator) might go up, but whether or not this would affect consumers is less clear. Lets wrap up. Markets are trying hard to understand the impact of AI on our economies, and we think there will be a lot to be learned in coming months. So far, either the macro impacts are still too small to be picked up, or data in Europe is simply not granular and timely enough to show it. For now, macro-economists are still very much walking in the dark on AI in Europe. That said, an AI-related investment boom, European style, is clearly the biggest upside risk to our short- term growth profile. A materialisation of that risk would very likely see the ECB on hold for the foreseeable future. The even more interesting question lies further ahead. Can AI rescue Europe from the adverse growth implications of its falling labour force? Either way, we think Europe stands to gain a lot from AI.

records.text: Ulacamten Phase 2 AMBER study in HFpEF Ulacamten is an oral, small molecule cardiac myosin inhibitor designed to reduce the hypercontractility associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Distinct from aficamten, CK-586 was designed to selectively inhibit the ATPase of intact cardiac myosin but not the ATPase of myosin subfragment-1, which translated to a shallower dose- response relationship. CK-586 molecule was also optimized for shorter half-life, given HFpEF patients are generally older and more vulnerable to potential AEs than HCM patients. Ph1 study PK/PD data showed a half-life of ~15 hrs and a plasma concentration to LVEF relationship of -0.004% per ng/mL, which potentially supported a fixed dosing without routine ECHO monitoring. Phase 2 AMBER study was initiated to enroll ~60 patients in three 12-wk cohorts with doses ranging from 150 to 600 mg QD. Mgmt expected to complete first two cohort studies by YE26. CK-089 in Muscular Dystrophy CK-089 is a fast skeletal muscle troponin activator, which was designed to amplify skeletal muscle response to nerve input, extend time to fatigue, and increase muscle force with potential applications in muscular dystrophy. The asset was disclosed in Nov 2024 and evaluated in Phase 1 study. 19 February 2026 272 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

GDP growth slows, underlying pace stable 4Q real GDP growth slowed to 1.4%q/q, saar from just over 4% in the prior couple of quar- ters, with the BEA saying the government shutdown took off at least 1.0%. The shutdown drag was larger than we expected but should be reversed this quarter, leading us to raise our 1Q forecast from 2.25% to 2.75%. Despite a large deceleration in headline GDP growth, underlying demand looks much more stable. Final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 2.4%. These have remained steadily within roughly a 2-3% range for each of the last five quarters (Figure 2). For the year overall, this metric rose 2.5%, compared to 2.9% in 2024 and 3.6% in 2023, so it has gradually slowed over time. That deceleration likely stems in part from the slowdown in labor supply over this period.

records.text: 18 February 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 In a surprise move , François Villeroy de Galhau announced last week that he would be stepping down from the Banque de France (and hence also the ECB’s Governing Council) in May, rather than seeing his full term out to October 2027. His resignation will mean Macron appoints a new central bank governor for a six- year term, rather than the appointment being made by the next French President (which would have been the case if Villeroy served his full term). A lawmaker from the RN party said Villeroy’s early resignation was aimed at putting in place an anti- RN ally. But in recent interviews, Villeroy has stated that his resignation (to head up a charity) was purely for personal reasons. Tensions about Villeroy’s early resignation could influence Lagarde’s decision. Could there be a ‘block deal’ for all the executive board seats? The discussion of Lagarde’s early departure could also tie into another story from Monday. Bloomberg reported that EU leaders were starting to consider a deal to select all the upcoming ECB executive board seats in one go. As we detailed in a recent note, it is not only Lagarde’s tenure that will be ending by the end of next year, but also Chief Economist Philip Lane (May 2027) and Isabel Schnabel (December 2027). records.text: t disease death, MI, or urgent revascularization, and the trial is expected to complete in 2027with roughly four years of follow- up, making it the second major readout in the Lp(a) outcomes sequence. LLY's ACCLAIM-Lp(a) is the largest and most ambitious outcomes study in the Lp(a) field, enrolling approximately 16,700 patients and uniquely incorporating both secondary prevention (ASCVD) and primary prevention cohorts, broadening the potential addressable population. Entry criteria require Lp(a) ≥175 nmol/L, representing a middle ground between inclusivity and enrichment. Lepodisiran is administered 400 mg subcutaneously every six months, reflecting its best-in-class durability profile observed in Phase 2. The primary endpoint is MACE, including cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, and urgent revascularization. With an expected readout in 2027–2028, ACCLAIM-Lp(a) trails earlier programs but could meaningfully expand the long-term commercial scope of Lp(a) lowering if successful. Muvalaplin’s Phase 3 strategy remains earlier and less defined, with pivotal trial parameters still evolving. The program is expected to target high-risk ASCVD patients with elevated Lp(a) levels, though final thresholds and endpoints have not yet been disclosed. As an oral, daily therapy, muvalaplin offers a differentiated convenience profile but lacks the durability advantages of RNA-based approaches, potentially necessitating longer exposure to achieve cumulative risk reduction. The clinical edge mattered—it set the floor for Zepbound's credibility—but the share trajectory we observe in the IQVIA data required commercial execution of an entirely different order. Novo Nordisk's position in June 2021 was enviable. Wegovy was the first FDA-approved GLP-1 for chronic weight management, launched to enormous patient and media interest. The addressable market was vast, the clinical data were strong (reinforced by the SELECT cardiovascular outcomes trial, which in August 2023 demonstrated a 20% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events), and Novo had the manufacturing infrastructure of a company that had been making injectable peptides for a century. But almost immediately, Novo was unable to capitalize on its head start. By March 31, 2022—just nine months after launch— Wegovy was added to the FDA drug shortage list. The semaglutide shortage would persist for nearly three years, not being formally resolved until February 21, 2025. During this critical period, Wegovy prescriptions fell significantly: TRx went from ~297K in Q4 2021 to ~188K in Q2 2022 and ~186K in Q3 2022, per IQVIA data. Novo was turning away patients at the exact moment the obesity market was inflecting. Underlying services inflation rose. At the same time, the labour market data showed a pickup in 3m unemployment rate from 5.1% to 5.2%, above consensus and BoE’s expectation of 5.1%. While annual wage growth slowed, monthly increases in wages firmed up. The big decline in January inflation, rise in unemployment and easing in annual wage growth keeps us comfortable with our base case of the next cut in March. However, the upward payroll revisions, stabilization in vacancies, pick up in underlying services inflation and firming up of monthly private wage increases should keep the BoE gradual. In our view data isn’t weakening enough to significantly increase risks of a back- to- back cut in March/April. We continue to expect cuts in March and June to 3.25%. As covered bonds are starting to look rich on an outright basis and versus swaps/EGBs after the YTD outperformance, we expect them to trade soft in the near term. Are we seeing the first signs of weakness? Covered bond primary supply has continued at a brisk pace with €45.2bn issued YTD, almost a fifth more than during the same period last year (+20.3%). As of 19 February, 27% of our €170bn supply forecast has been achieved, up from 24% in 2025 (Figure 13). Our short-term EM FX risk appetite index – which we rely on particularly for EM currencies – gave overbought signals in January, hitting all-time high levels and we reduced our EM FX position to MW as a result (see here and here). For EM sovereign and corporate credit, the song largely remains the same. Fundamen- tals are on aggregate unconcerning after the 2022-2024 stresses, but EM credit spreads are historically very low and expensive after an ongoing grind tighter, which is common across global credit markets. EMBIGD ex-CCC and CEMBI spreads are just 28bp and 39bp from their all-time spread lows in 2007, a time when enormous leverage drove credit spreads to unsustainable levels and when EM debt levels were lower. We have not been fighting this grind tighter, but have been positioning for it more by overweighting higher spread countries or segments we find attractive, while staying MW at the index level in both EM sovereigns and corporates. And in our view, there are enough dovish voters this year for Warsh to push through a couple of cuts (Exhibit 1). Waller (who dissented in favor of a cut in Jan) and Bowman (even though she didn’t dissent) would probably be supportive. Meanwhile, Powell, Williams and Paulson have indicated that they see a relatively low neutral rate (though Williams’ own model estimates of the neutral rate are moving up, see Exhibit 2). While they seem content to stay on hold for now, their bar for getting rates closer to 3% is likely low. We haven’t heard a lot from Jefferson and Cook, but our assessment is that they are close to Powell in their policy views. The remaining four voters – Barr, Hammack, Kashkari and Logan – are hawks who would not support cuts unless the economy is significantly weaker than we are forecasting. Solbinsiran (from LLY), another GalNAc-conjugated siRNA, in Phase 2b study showed up to 53/12% pbo-adjusted reductions in TG/LDL-C on day 180 with doses on days 0 and 90. CTX310 (from CRSP , not covered) is an in vivo CRISPR/Cas9 KO of ANGPTL3, which showed up to 82/65% reductions in TG/LDL-C followed one infusion, despite small patient size and short follow-up (LINK). records.text: BoJ core CPI inflation eases further Core CPI inflation down sharply Goods contribution down sharply on effect of gasoline tax reductions, while services contribution also falls, but only slightly In the nationwide CPI data for January, inflation excluding perishables and energy (aka “BoJ core”) eased to +2.6% (December: +2.9%; Figure 1), as the contribution from food ex-perishables continued to decline due to y/y base effects; household durables and hotel charges also contributed to the deceleration. The result undershot market consensus by 0.1pp and our forecast by 0.2pp. Seasonally adjusted, the inflation measure stayed at +0.1% m/m (+0.1%). Meanwhile, the CPI excluding perishables (core) eased to +2.0% y/y (+2.4%), with a large negative contribution from energy on top of a smaller positive contributions from food (Figure 1). As a result, the index matched the BoJ's 2% inflation target after exceeding it for 45 consecutive months. Month on month, the index continued to fall at a pace of -0.1% (-0.1%). Meanwhile, overall CPI inflation eased even more sharply to +1.5% y/y (+2.1%), with the addition of a larger negative contribution from perishables. FIGURE 1. More limited hypertrophy (13-14 mm) can be diagnostic when present in family members of a patient with HCM or in conjunction with a positive genetic test. Myosin inhibitors are only approved disease modifying drugs in oHCM Historically, treatment of oHCM relied on nonspecific medications to slow heart rate and diminish LV contractility (beta blocker, calcium channel blocker, and disopyramide). These therapies would not address the underlying cause or improve functions. Disease modifying therapeutic approaches have been in various stage of development with mechanisms of actions (MOA) including small molecule myosin/sarcomere inhibitor, gene therapy, and RNA therapy. Small molecule cardiac myosin inhibitor (CMI), Camzyos (mavacamten) and Myqorzo (aficamten), are two only approved drugs in oHCM. CMIs selectively and reversibly diminish cardiac myosin ATPase activity, preventing the strong actin-myosin binding and reducing the hypercontractility, showing improvements in cardiac structure and functional outcomes. Since CMIs directly reduce the contractility of heart muscle, modest and reversible reductions in LVEF were observed and could lead to heart failure as noted in Camzyos and Myqorzo box warnings. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy Chopping around EUR rates remain at the mercy of spillovers from the US, with this dynamic set to continue until a shift in the domestic macro narrative materialises. In EGBs, we take stock of country-by-country YTD spread dynamics, before discussing upcoming supply and Q1 syndication allocations. Bullish momentum for EUR rates continued in the early part of this week, after which modest bearish pressures emerged. With dataflow relatively light (ahead of Friday's PMIs), focal points for investors have included geopolitics (with oil pushing higher on growing US-Iran tensions), FOMC minutes and the succession of Lagarde as ECB President (with the FT reporting that Lagarde will leave the ECB before the scheduled end of her term in October 2027). Taking a step back from the headlines, recent price action has underlined that EUR rates remain at the mercy of spillovers from the US, as illustrated by Figure 1 and Figure 2. Going forwards, EUR rates are likely to remain in the passenger seat, until a shift in the domestic macro narrative materialises. From a bullish standpoint, this could entail growing doubts on the sustainability of Europe's growth rebound, against a backdrop of scepticism around the growth impact of German fiscal stimulus. For domestic bearish impulses to materialise for Bunds, on the other hand, evidence for growth acceleration would likely need to accumulate, in turn driving renewed focus on longer-term prospects for ECB rate hikes. Despite JPY’s n recent appreciation following the lower house election, we think JPY weakness is likely to resume, especially against CHF given their relative correlations and domestic inflation dynamics. Generally, CHF/JPY tends to be positively correlated with rising equity prices, n higher yields, and commodities, and negatively correlated with the VIX. This reflects JPY’s tendency to outperform when growth expectations are falling, pushing equities and yields lower together, while CHF tends to strengthen when inflation expectations are rising and driving yields higher. This makes Yen a better safe haven for negative growth environments and CHF a better hedge against rising inflation risks. Over the longer run though, relative inflation stands out as the primary driver of n CHF/JPY. And the shift higher in inflation expectations for Japan has altered the backdrop for the cross. These dynamics have some parallels to those in 2013, when JPY depreciated on the introduction of Abenomics and CHF saw significant appreciation pressure in the aftermath of the GFC. Labor reform – structural objectives with near-term fiscal costs: The labor reform bill sent to Congress in December and approved in the Senate last week has fiscal implications, with static estimates pointing to a total cost of 0.4-0.5% of GDP once fully implemented. This implies that meeting the 2026 primary surplus target of 1.5% of GDP, as embedded in the budget, would require additional revenue measures and/or tighter expenditure control, while also increasing the likelihood that any future tax reform (nothing has been formally presented yet) will be moderate in scope. The labor reform aims to reduce hiring and dismissal costs, reduce litigation and increase predictability of outcomes for firms, with the objective of fostering formal employment. These objectives come with identifiable short-term fiscal costs. The main driver is the creation of the Labor Assistance Fund, financed through a reallocation of employer social security contributions. This mechanism implies lower inflows to the social security system and a fiscal cost of around 0.4-0.5% of GDP, borne primarily by the federal government. records.text: 7. Old and new flavours extend Dollar weakness. Dollar depreciation has extended into 2026, but the impulses have broadened from the Euro-centric moves in H1 2025 and the focus on carry in H2. The older flavours are still visible, with Dollar weakness versus the Euro on reruns of tariff and Fed independence concerns in January. Alongside the underperformance of US equities relative to Europe and Japan YTD (repeating the pattern in 2025), this has provided fresh impetus to the diversification and hedging discussions. Beyond that, two new dynamics are playing a more prominent role in Dollar weakness. First, in line with our global cyclical views, currencies at the intersection of cyclical beta, commodity exposure, and cheapness—AUD (Australian Dollar), ZAR (South African Rand), CLP (Chilean Peso) and BRL (Brazilian Real)—have been among the biggest gainers versus the Dollar. Second, there is more focus on FX policy, particularly among Asian currencies that have become very cheap relative to long-run valuations— the Yen and the Yuan in particular. The joint US-Japan ‘rate-check’ has successfully arrested the JPY depreciation trend for now (see Bullet 8 below), and the combination of successively stronger ‘fixes’ and comments from policymakers appear to be sanctioning consistent CNY strength (which should allow further strengthening of related low-yielders, such as KRW and MYR, that are also undervalued). However, we think it's more likely than not that risk weights move towards the lower side given the desire to incentivize mortgage origination and servicing retention by banks. With those caveats, if we simplistically assume right now banks have to hold about $165bn against their residential loans currently carrying a 50% risk weight - it's roughly 2.2tn of loans * 50% risk weight * ~15% risk-based capital ratio. If the blended risk weight on these loans they hold were to come down to 45% (and we think it could come down more), that could result in $17bn of capital freed up. If all that capital went into retaining additional residential mortgage loans, that could be almost another $250bn of loans they could hold. If that went into conventional MBS with a 20% risk weight today, ignoring every single other regulatory requirement, it would be an incremental $550bn of MBS. Now realistically, it's highly unlikely that the excess capital first goes to MBS; our financials team think it goes towards loan growth, share buybacks, and capital markets (particularly FICC financing), but this math shows how much a small change could result in material demand if things change from the investment perspective. The framework classifies the investment backdrop into distinct regimes using four high-frequency indicators - global economic surprises, inflation surprises, VIX and MOVE index - capturing each variable’s level, change (12-week), and the speed (4-week) of that change. Conditional on the identified regime, we then estimate each factor’s expected 4-week risk-adjusted return, providing a forward-looking assessment of relative factor performance. Clesrovimab (MK-1654) — RSV Prevention Clesrovimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody being developed for passive immunization against RSV in infants. From a differentiation standpoint, Clesrovimab’s primary advantage is logistical rather than mechanistic. Unlike Sanofi/AstraZeneca’s Beyfortus, which requires weight-based dosing (<5 kg vs >5 kg), Clesrovimab is administered as a single fixed dose across all infants, materially simplifying inventory management and administration for pediatric practices. While both agents target RSV prophylaxis, we believe this dosing simplicity could lower friction in real- world uptake, particularly in high-volume seasonal settings. Clinically, Phase 3 data demonstrated an 84% reduction in RSV-associated hospitalizations, supporting a competitive efficacy profile. Management expects a potential approval aligned with the 2025/2026 RSV season, positioning Clesrovimab as a meaningful entrant into a market that is still in the early stages of normalization following recent launches. B. V181 — Dengue Fever V181 is a live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine currently in Phase 3 development (MOBILIZE-1). The global dengue vaccine market has historically been constrained by safety concerns and dosing complexity. Sanofi’s Dengvaxia carries well-documented risks related to antibody- dependent enhancement in seronegative individuals, while Takeda’s Qdenga requires a two- dose regimen, which may limit compliance

House prices are rising, but, given recent population dynamics, house price inflation is more symptomatic of a housing shortage than a leverage-driven bubble like in the early 2000s. The guiding principle is to allow companies across the EU to incorporate as an “EU Inc” in a quick, digital way and to gain the right to operate under a single set of rules across member states, at least along some dimensions. Commission President von der Leyen has committed to presenting a proposal ahead of the next EU Council on March 19-20. Proposals floated so far differ in (a) ambition around what barriers to n cross-border activity will be reduced under the new regime, and (b) scope of the coverage of the new regime, and, in particular, whether it will be open to all or a subset of companies. Any ambitious proposal would face resistance related to its implications for existing corporate governance traditions, such as worker representation on company boards. A compromise could involve an ambitious regime limited to a small set of companies, as suggested in the Draghi report. records.text: Valuation Methodology Our 12-month price targets are P/E-driven, established in the context of our views on EPS growth and revision potential, near-term catalysts, and thematic outlook, overlaid with our long-term bottom-up NPV/DCF framework. For each company under coverage, we assign a target forward core P/E multiple relative to the US large cap biopharma peer group average, which we view as justified based on our detailed perspectives on the investment case, including the growth trajectory of in-line and newly launched assets, the risk-adjusted value of the clinical pipeline, LOE exposure and timing, and competitive positioning within core therapeutic franchises. Target multiples are set versus the peer average, with PEG ratios informing our order of preference across the coverage universe. Companies exhibiting above-average EPS growth visibility, limited near-term LOE headwinds, or de-risked pipeline optionality command premium multiples, while those facing material generic or biosimilar erosion trade at a discount. Our NPV/DCF analysis serves as a sanity check on each price target, not as the primary PT-setter. Where product-level granularity is available, we explicitly forecast in-line revenues and risk-adjusted pipeline assets over a horizon capturing the full IP lifespan. Terminal assumptions distinguish pharma segments, where cash flows are faded post-LOE, from non- pharma streams capitalized at WACC with modest terminal growth. records.text: UK labour productivity growth is showing signs of a pickup. Although official data n remain weak, this is likely the result of the Labour Force Survey (LFS) figures significantly overstating employment growth over the past two years. Administrative data point to weaker employment and so suggest that output per hour has risen at a faster 1.1% annualised pace over the past two years, 0.5pp above the 2010-19 average of 0.6%. Output per worker has grown even more strongly. Productivity growth has been volatile historically, which cautions against n assuming that the entire recent pickup represents a change in the trend. That said, our previous analysis does suggest that the underlying trend in output per hour could have seen a more moderate improvement to around 0.8%, which would explain 0.2pp of the increase relative to the 2010-19 average. A more rapid fading of Brexit growth headwinds or an earlier impact from AI could pose modest upside risks to this estimate, but we think it is unlikely that either of these factors would fully account for the strength in the recent data. Of the remaining 0.3pp gap between recent productivity growth and our trend n estimate, around half results from capital deepening and half from total factor productivity (TFP). Much of the increase in capital deepening likely reflects rising labour costs on the back of last year’s employer National Insurance (NI) hike. We continue to expect both GDP deflator and PPI to turn positive mid this year. We now expect China’s 2026 GDP growth target to be lowered to 4.5-5.0%, the first such downgrade in three years. Our earlier expectation was an “around 5%” target with more tolerance for weakness (see: 2026 Outlook: Mind the Gap). We maintain our growth forecast at 4.7%, which fits into both cases. 21 provinces out of 31 guided down their growth targets, including major provinces like Guangdong and Zhejiang. Beijing and Shanghai, which used to set the same growth target as the whole country, held it unchanged at “around 5%” , yet it may not be as indicative this time given the capital overshot its 2025 target at 5.4%. The potential cut would be the first after three years of GDP growth meeting the “around 5%” target. For each of these 4 variables, we use the z-score of each country's value. This allows us to form an aggregate score. Our data set is an average of the IMF WEO forecasts & the European Commission economic forecasts. Hence, these macro scores are updated twice every year. records.text: FIGURE 12. Annual Total Return - S5HL TH vs. SPX Source: Barclays Research, Bloomberg This recent wave of pharmaceutical pricing scrutiny began with a tweet. In September 2015, then-presidential candidate Hillary Clinton responded to news that Turing Pharmaceuticals, led by Martin Shkreli, had raised the price of Daraprim (pyrimethamine), a 62-year-old antiparasitic drug, from $13.5 to $750 per pill overnight, a 5,000% increase (LINK). Clinton's tweet "Price gouging like this in the specialty drug market is outrageous" (LINK) was followed by a 4.7% intraday decline in the NBI and a decade-long political debate about drug pricing. The Daraprim episode contributed to a growing perception that U.S. pharmaceutical companies may have been exercising pricing power in ways that raised concerns about patient impact. This narrative proved remarkably durable, developing across three presidential administrations, multiple Congresses, and shifting partisan coalitions. Rhetorical intensity transcended partisan line and continued after the 2016 presidential election. As reported publicly, Trump stated in February 2017 that pharmaceutical companies were "getting away with murder" and promised to "start bidding. " The Trump administration's July 2018 "American Patients First" (LINK) blueprint further proposed bold reforms, including international reference pricing (IRP) and rebate restructuring, but implementation stalled amid industry opposition. records.text: M Update 2 US Public Policy Ariana Salvatore, Michael Zezas, and Bradley Tian Our key takeaways from the ruling: 1) Refund picture still murky: The Court did not dictate whether the Trump administration has to repay the tariffs or do so over any specific timeframe. In his dissent, Justice Kavanaugh reiterated that the refund process "is likely to be a mess." That said, tariff collection likely stops immediately; given that the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariff authority broadly, continued collections would lack legal basis. As we anticipated, this will likely result in prolonged uncertainty as the question of refunds will be left to the deliberations of the lower courts. In the past, refunds were initially limited only to companies that proactively filed complaints or litigation through a process established by CBP or the Treasury, which may ultimately limit the scope of refunds. 2) Other paths are available, but potential sector-specific tailwinds are under the surface: President Trump has said he has a backup plan, and members of the administration have suggested that he will leverage other authorities to reimpose the tariffs. While we expected an announcement to be met with this response from the administration, we still expect the President to pursue a lighter-touch tariff policy under the surface. records.text: ,300 patients, showed no hepatotoxicity signal. Lilly explicitly stated that liver safety was "meticulously assessed" with no alarming trends. While seven patients showed elevated liver enzymes, investigators identified alternative explanations in each case. This clean hepatic safety profile across a large Phase 3 program meaningfully de- risks the molecule Importance of biased agonism. The concept of biased agonism is central to understanding why non-peptide GLP-1RAs may have differentiated tolerability profiles. Traditional peptide GLP-1RAs activate both the Gs/cAMP pathway (mediating insulin secretion, appetite suppression) and the beta-arrestin pathway (mediating receptor internalization, desensitization, and some GI adverse effects) while non-peptide agonists like orforglipron preferentially activate the Gs pathway while minimizing beta-arrestin recruitment. This Gs- biased signaling profile has several theoretical and observed implications: • Sustained receptor signaling due to reduced internalization • Potentially improved GI tolerability — though Phase 3 data showed GI AEs remain the dominant side effect class (33.7% nausea at highest dose), the discontinuation rate of ~10% is within the range observed for injectable GLP-1RAs • Lower occupancy requirement — Sloop et al. demonstrated that low receptor occupancy by orforglipron is sufficient for full biological response, suggesting a favorable therapeutic index 19 February 2026 161 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

If Lagarde were to step down early, it would potentially make doing a block deal more feasible, rather than doing sequential deals for each of the board seats as they become available. In today’s environment, that intermediary role is increasingly disinter mediated. With Chinese biotech companies now capable of vertically integrating discovery, preclinical development, and early clinical execution in-house — and doing so faster and more cost- effectively — large pharma buyers can access de-risked clinical assets directly at the source. This compresses the value proposition of U.S. SMID biotechs that lack proprietary platforms, differentiated biology, or clear execution advantages, effectively pushing many of these companies out of the BD value chain rather than merely intensifying competition. In our view, this dynamic represents not a cyclical funding issue, but a structural reordering of global biotech innovation flows: China has transitioned from being a service provider and outsourcing destination to a primary originator of clinically validated assets, reshaping incentives and bargaining power across the industry. Partially, external price competitiveness may have helped to buffer the potential effects on the economy via domestic demand, although the EUR appreciation of 2025 and the EURUSD appreciation at the beginning of this year tone down the effect. But to a larger extent, fiscal policy may have come to the rescue, albeit accidentally. Don’t get us wrong: the 2023 fiscal slippage and its lasting deterioration on the forward looking deficit trajectory meaningfully weighs on our otherwise still benign structural view on France. But swift disinflation means higher short- and long-term real interest rates in France than elsewhere in the Euro area, relatively speaking. Fiscal policy may have accidentally helped to avoid worse growth outcomes for the wrong reasons. Looking forward, that creates all kinds of fragility, and generally a risk balance to both growth and inflation that is firmly tilted to the downside, perhaps even more so than in the Euro area as a whole. Another round of Economic Policy Uncertainty into or after the 2027 presidential election cannot be ruled out, and is not in our growth forecasts at this stage.
