He has billed himself as a disruptor rather than a consensus builder, and as we argued recently, the era of consensus building at the Fed is probably ending (see our report Fed: Agree to Disagree ). Uncooperative data = uncompelling case for cuts The issue for Warsh is that the recent data flow substantially challenges the case for cuts. In the last two months, the u-rate has dropped by 25bp. This would increase the target policy rate by 25-50bp in the various Taylor Rule models the Fed looks at. And although CPI inflation is falling, PCE inflation is likely to move up meaningfully in the next two months. We think core PCE will probably come in at 3.0-3.1% y/y in January, compared to 2.8% as of November. This would raise the target policy rate by another 30bp-plus across the Fed’s various Taylor Rule models. Moreover, the u-rate is now only a tenth above the FOMC’s median natural rate estimate of 4.2%. Additional declines would make it very hard for the Fed to maintain a dovish bias, given that inflation is stuck above target even ex of tariffs. records.text: 20 February 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review ECB and Lagarde Early this morning (European time), Lagarde commented in an interview that her baseline is to finish her term as ECB president. Her comments were pushing back at an earlier FT story citing a person “familiar with [Lagarde’s] thinking” saying that ECB President Lagarde is considering ending her tenure early. That story followed an early Bloomberg story on Monday that EU leaders were starting to think about a block deal for the three board seats that would become vacant by the end of next year (Lane, Lagarde, and Schnabel). In a report we published following the FT story, we discussed the possibility of an early departure by Lagarde from the ECB: why, and what it means. We also discuss what new leadership would mean for ECB policy going forward. In our view, the structure of the current monetary policy framework is robust. It should mean that policy decisions will continue to be data dependent, not personality dependent under a new President. As such, our outlook for ECB policy remains unchanged. Our baseline has the ECB on hold for the time being. The risks are skewed to further cuts in 2026, but our baseline has the next move as a hike in mid-2027. Our KOL highlighted that Inclisiran is a very expensive drug and is often rejected by commercial payers. He further highlighted that an oral option will make payer reimbursement an easier process. We see over $4.5B risk adjusted peak sales opportunity for Elincitide: The market for non- statin LDL-lowering therapy is relatively under penetrated, with statin monotherapy representing 88% of the global market share. Merck estimates there will be over 80M treated, not-at-goal ASCVD and at-risk patients in the U.S., Europe, and Japan, and that the cardio metabolic market will be over ~$15bn by the mid-2030s. We have seen strong momentum for injectable PCSK9s, and consensus has modeled Amgen's Repatha to reach $4B peak sales by 2029. With injectable-level efficacy and an oral formulation, we see a clear value proposition for Elincitide within this market and believe it can capture near ~30% of the market. In cases of ambiguity or debate around safety/efficacy profile, larger resourced companies may benefit. The September 2025 decision by then-CDER Director George Tidmarsh to formally phase out AdCom meetings coupled with zero meetings scheduled for 2026 to discuss novel drug approvals (as of our early February analysis) suggest this is not a temporary fluctuation but likely a deliberate institutional choice. The main impact of this will likely be the reduced publicity around drug approvals that may have required an AdCom in the past, leaving more of the decision-making behind closed doors. In our view, while hard to determine the impact on drug approvals, which are always dependent on interpretation of clinical data in the context of unmet medical need, we see potential for such development to favor companies with more resources. For example, a larger company could be in better position to appeal a negative regulatory decision by the FDA, or to run another costly confirmatory trial, etc. All together, we believe this development is not negative, and potentially positive, for Large Cap Biopharma. records.text: happened, the marginal question changed. It was no longer how to own UK equities (active or passive), but whether to own UK equities at all, versus global or US alternatives. In parallel, the domestic anchor eroded. UK DB pension schemes cut UK equity holdings from roughly one-third of assets in the mid-2000s to under 2% by 2023. Maturity, tighter funding rules (Pensions Act 2004), mark-to-market accounting (IAS 19), and the rise of LDI strategies made equity volatility harder to tolerate. Equities shifted from strategic holding to residual risk budget. DC schemes did not replace this bid as their globally diversified defaults ensured the marginal pound flowed into global benchmarks rather than domestic equity. The UK lost its captive buyer. International investors now dominate ownership. Why Valuations Became Elastic When a market is domestically owned, capital is less price sensitive; valuation can remain high despite cyclicality, and shocks often cause temporary volatility with limited structural de-rating. However, when ownership is global and benchmarked, valuation must compete, and the impact becomes more structural without a natural stabiliser. Optional markets clear at lower prices. This is the foundation of the UK discount, which was then exposed and accelerated by Brexit which raised the perceived risk premium. Part of the discount is mechanical. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 20 February 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS The US trade deficit is alive and kicking You thought the US trade deficit was going to sustainably fall? Think again. The current account deficit, which is primarily the trade deficit, equals the difference between domestic investment and domestic savings. With a strong outlook for both investment and for consumption, coupled with a sizable fiscal deficit, this shortfall is nowhere near closing. As we have been arguing all along, tariffs are unlikely to solve the US current account deficit, as finally hinted by the widening trade deficit in December. The current account deficit is a story of imbalances The current account balance of an economy is equal to the difference between national savings (including the public sector) and investment. In a nutshell, when a country invests more than it saves, it needs to borrow from the rest of the world to finance that investment. This implies that the trade balance (which is the main component of the current account balance) is determined by the trajectory of macro variables. As a result, it cannot be thought of in a vacuum driven by tariffs or bilateral exchange rates, which of course are endogenous. Ultimately, the outlook for investment, consumption, and the public sector will determine the evolution of external accounts. If tariffs are going to affect the current account, they must affect saving and/or investment. Tariffs induced

records.text: European Rates Weekly 19 February 2026 Citi Research 2 If ECB President Lagarde does exit early, the choice of a replacement could either encourage twist-steepening or, perhaps more likely, add to hike premium for the coming years. Timing the exit: In what is otherwise a quiet holiday-impacted week, the ECB succession story stands out – for background, see European Rates – The Morning Call: Succession planning. While not officially confirmed, the FT reported on Wednesday morning that ECB President Lagarde, due to serve until October 2027, may step down early. Timing wise, a later FT report suggested nothing has been decided but it could be as early as this summer (see FT, 18Feb26). In our minds, an early departure only makes much sense if it is at least a year premature, not least given the European political calendar in 2027. Moreover, the complex process to decide a successor may take some time. Overall, our working assumption is that an exit by no later than October of this year seems most likely if at all. Why it matters longer-term: The choice of who will be the next president could have a longer-term influence on the policy setting of the ECB, and the style in which decisions are made. records.text: Foreign Exchange Forecasts 19 February 2026 Citi Research 13 CAD USDCAD Forecasts: 0-3m 1.41, 6-12m 1.38 n0-3m: We leave our forecast for USDCAD upside unchanged at 1.41, driven by US re-acceleration vs softer Canadian domestic demand, dovish BoC repricing potential, and USMCA headline risks as negotiations continue. On the latter, Citi Economics believes Canada does not appear to be as well-positioned as Mexico into renegotiations based on relative comparative advantages, which could lead the US to maximize leverage as talks continue. In the tail risk scenario that the trade agreement is scrapped, while a knee-jerk reaction could be likely CAD outflows, this outcome could also motivate Canadian holders of US assets to reassess their holdings and/or further adjust their hedge ratios. CAD real money buying jumped significantly after the April 2025 tariff announcements, and these flows have closely tracked USDCAD mis-valuation since then. In our base case, we assume the USMCA is successfully renegotiated, and the pace and magnitude of FX hedge ratio adjustments from last year are unlikely to repeat in 2026. But we monitor these dynamics closely for USDCAD in coming months. n6-12m: We turn less bearish CAD over the medium-term horizon, as the (eventual) abatement of trade uncertainty should support business confidence and investment, a dovish BoC is better priced, and as positive spillovers emerge from a rebound in US growth. We marginally revise down our 6-12m forecast to 1.38

records.text: US Economics 20 February 2026 Citi Research 2 Data – Real GDP advanced just 1.4% QoQ in Q4, below consensus for 2.8% and our projection for 3.1%. The Q4 government shutdown weighed on Q4 GDP by 1.0pp according to the BEA, and government spending subtracted 0.9pp from real growth. (Nominal GDP is not affected meaning the GDP deflator was stronger than is typical). Removing the effects of the shutdown and volatile trade balance, final private domestic demand advanced a solid 2.4% supported by a 2.4% increase in consumer spending. Most surprising relative to our projection was an only 0.2pp contribution from business equipment investment. Investment in computers and other equipment related to AI contributed a strong 0.65pp, but other categories of investment spending were weak. Residential fixed investment was slightly negative, reflecting the ongoing weak housing market. In monthly data, personal spending advanced a solid 0.4%MoM in December with a strong 0.7% increase in services and 0.11% pull-back in goods reflecting a decline in auto sales as well as broader weakness across other goods. Incomes were up 0.3%MoM meaning the savings rate fell from a low 3.7% to an even lower 3.6%. Core PCE inflation registered 0.36%MoM, close to our expectations for 0.33% but technically rounding up to 0.4%. Most details were known from previously released CPI and PPI. Initial excitement for this class of agents was driven by randomized clinical data for ivonescimab (Summit/Akeso) against pembrolizumab in a China trial in 1L PD-L1 (positive) lung cancer patients (HARMONi-2) trial in May 2024. Data showed clear separation of PFS curves (HR 0.51) favoring ivonescimab, supporting the notion that ivonescimab could potentially beat Keytruda. The clinical data from Summit/Akeso led to a number of large partnerships between U.S. and Ex-U.S. companies, notably Bristol Myers and BioNTech's partnership as well as Pfizer and 3SBio's partnership to develop PD(L)1xVEGF assets across a range of solid tumors. records.text: The evidence on the productivity impact to date is mixed. Government research finds significant effects amongst AI adopters. But the BoE’s Decision Maker Panel (DMP) points to a more limited impact to date, and we think that this is probably the more reliable guide given that it is employment weighted and so less likely to be skewed by the responses of very small firms. That said, the DMP still suggests that AI could have raised productivity (measured as sales per employee) growth by around 0.1pp each year over the last three years – whereas our own global baseline assumes no material impact until 2028 – though it is less clear that this impact is additive to the existing productivity trend. Overall, while a more rapid fading of Brexit headwinds or an earlier impact from AI could pose modest upside risks to our central estimate of the recent productivity growth trend, we think it is unlikely that either of these factors would fully account for the strength seen over the last two years. The YoY increase in service prices excluding rent registered a modest slowdown to +1.9% (from +2.0% in December), maintaining the stable trend of around 2% seen since the second half of 2024. This suggests that cost pass-throughs are continuing in the service sector, indicating persistent underlying inflationary pressures. Our estimate of the weighted median inflation rate also showed only a slight decline, from +0.8% in December to +0.7%. I&I a strong category, ABBV dominant in this field One-two punch of Skyrizi and Rinvoq - now bigger than peak Humira As an industry leader in Inflammation & Immunology, AbbVie has the best I&I portfolio within our coverage universe, driven by three key brands—Skyrizi, Rinvoq and Humira. AbbVie has achieved significant synergies within the portfolio. Humira generated over $20B in annual sales for multiple years, establishing itself as one of the largest payer and prescriber networks in the biopharma industry. This dominance created a powerful “paywall, ” combining entrenched formulary access, long-standing payer contracts, and deep physician familiarity. As a result, AbbVie built an unparalleled commercial infrastructure in immunology, making it easier to drive uptake for its next generation of therapies, Skyrizi and Rinvoq. Skyrizi, an anti-IL23 for autoimmune conditions, has an anticipated LOE around 2033, leaving significant room for growth. With portfolio synergies and a differentiated efficacy profile, we believe Skyrizi could reach Humira-level peak sales. Rinvoq is the leader among JAK inhibitors and has achieved solid growth since launch—over 50% Y/Y growth over the last three years. AbbVie’s recent settlement with generic manufacturers extended Rinvoq’s market exclusivity until 2037, adding long-term visibility to AbbVie’s immunology franchise and easing midterm BD pressure. Prescribers who could not get Wegovy for their patients turned to Mounjaro off-label for weight loss (it was approved for diabetes in May 2022), conditioning a large prescriber base toward tirzepatide before Zepbound ever existed. 2) It created a compounding ecosystem. The shortage enabled compounding pharmacies to legally produce semaglutide copies under the FDA's Section 503A/503B exemptions—a channel that would grow into a $1B+ market and continues to pressure Novo's pricing to this day. 3) It gave Lilly a manufacturing head start. By the time Zepbound launched in late November 2023, Lilly had been ramping tirzepatide manufacturing for Mounjaro since mid-2022 and had already invested heavily in capacity. Although tirzepatide was also added to the shortage list in December 2022, Lilly resolved its shortage faster—by December 19, 2024, the FDA formally confirmed the tirzepatide shortage as resolved. Novo's semaglutide shortage would not be resolved for another two months. If the clinical profile set the floor and the shortage gap provided a window, the vial strategy is what drove the bus. On August 27, 2024, Lilly did something unprecedented in branded biopharma: it launched single-dose vials of Zepbound at $399 (2.5mg) and $549 (5mg) per month exclusively through LillyDirect, its direct-to-consumer

To quickly walk through the logic of how the seasonal factors work, we multiply a factor to the non seasonally-adjusted (NSA) index to arrive at a seasonally-adjusted (SA) version, ie: NSA = SA × SF, implying that, as a close approximation, NSAm/m ≈ SAm/m + SFm/m, and NSAm/m − SFm/m ≈ SAm/m. As a result, for a given NSA change, any change in the SF m/m feeds through to a commensurate shift in SA m/m. Moreover, they are directionally opposite; any tweak where more/less growth is explained by seasonality (SF m/m increases/ decreases) means that the other component of the NSA growth would be lower/higher, respectively. We see exactly this play out in the 2026 vintage in March, for example, where the March SF was revised lower, leading to March SF m/m decreasing, and thus March SA m/m increasing from -0.05% m/m SA to 0.03% m/m SA ( Figures 3 and 4). 19 February 2026 15 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Curb your enthusiasm

This subgroup may contribute to secondary/ exploratory analyses and could potentially serve as an enriched population for regulatory filing if the overall CDR-GS 0 result is ambiguous. Why TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3 Is Not the A4 Study The most common bear case against TB-ALZ 3 is the A4 study failure: solanezumab, administered for ~4.5 years in preclinical AD, failed to slow cognitive decline (PACC: -1.69 vs. -1.4 for placebo; P=.26). We see this comparison as fundamentally flawed for four reasons: • Mechanism of action: Solanezumab targets soluble monomeric amyloid-β and does not clear deposited amyloid plaques. In A4, amyloid continued to accumulate over time in both treatment and placebo groups. Donanemab targets insoluble N3pG amyloid plaques and achieves 80-84% clearance. The prevention hypothesis has never been tested with a potent plaque-clearing agent. • Biological proof: TB-ALZ 2 demonstrated that amyloid clearance directly translates to clinical benefit in symptomatic disease, with greater benefit in earlier-stage (low/medium tau) patients. We forecast the euro area aggregate fiscal stance is moving from marginally restrictive in 2025 to marginally expansionary (+0.3pp of GDP) in 2026 and more so in 2027. At the same time, monetary policy is becoming less restrictive, as past rate cuts support growth of the most interest rate sensitive sectors sectors/regions (eg housing, construction). Slightly higher GDP growth does not mean near-term reflation. We still see slowing wage growth and imported disinflation driving core inflation lower from here in 2026 and 2027 (to 1.6-1.7% YY by 4Q-26, from 2.4% in 4Q25). We forecast inflation undershooting the ECB target both in 2026 and in 2017 (at 1.8%), but to rebound above 2% in 2028 (assuming ETS2 goes through). We see the ECB policy rate on hold at 2.0% for the foreseeable future, and at least until end-2027. Growth is unlikely to weaken enough to force the ECB into cutting rates below 2% (generally believed around neutral); but equally we see limited risks of inflation overshooting in the next couple of years and leading to rate hikes. However, large fiscal spending is likely to justify a tighter monetary policy eventually and we pencil in 50bp hikes in 2028. records.text: Euro Area Viewpoint | 19 February 2026 7 Demand profile: domestic investors Banks: more demand to be squeezed out Two factors argue for sustained French bank demand for OATs in 2026. First, French banks’ EGB exposure sits below the euro‑area average, comparable to German banks, implying capacity to add if price levels remain attractive (Exhibit 11). Second, relative to peers, they have been less inclined to diversify into non‑domestic EGBs recently — reflecting already diversified sovereign books and the relative attractiveness of OAT spreads in 2025 and earlier this year. That said, we expect a smaller euro‑area demand impulse in 2026 than in 2025. Reserves as a share of HQLA are already low versus the pre‑COVID period, limiting scope to continue replacing declining reserves with EGBs, as was largely the case last year. Finally, while French government bonds may still receive some residual diversification flows from EA banks, the recent richening reduces their relative appeal, and non‑French EA banks may increasingly rotate toward alternatives such as BTPs. records.text: In addition, Merck will receive a permanent J Code for SubQ Keytruda in the next 6 months. Passage of OBBBA pushed IRA implementation back by one year. The new provisions under the “Big Beautiful Bill” extend the orphan drug exemption and reset the negotiation clock for drugs that start with orphan indications. For Keytruda, whose first indication was orphan-designated melanoma, this means IRA selection could be delayed until 2029. If biosimilars are available or expected by then, the likelihood of Keytruda being chosen for negotiation drops significantly. We view Keytruda QLEX as a key defense for the Keytruda franchise, as biosimilars launching in 2028 are IV-only, while QLEX is a patented SC combination product. Biosimilar manufacturers can only launch IV pembrolizumab in 2028 because QLEX is protected by separate patents (pembrolizumab + hyaluronidase) that extend well beyond 2028. As a result, biosimilars cannot offer an SC formulation at launch, creating immediate and meaningful product differentiation in Merck’s favor. Merck can proactively switch patients from IV Keytruda to QLEX SC before biosimilars arrive, creating a “lock-in” effect. records.text: Leqembi – Modest topline growth so far, but we see potential for accelerated uptake Leqembi is the first approved disease modifying therapy for AD in two decades:The AD therapeutic landscape underwent a fundamental transformation beginning in 2023, following what is appropriately characterized as a "lost decade" of failed amyloid-targeting programs. Between 2002 and 2021, the clinical trial failure rate in AD exceeded 99%, with over 400 compounds abandoned — a record of futility driven by flawed trial designs (enrolling moderate- to-severe patients), imprecise amyloid targeting, and underpowered studies that failed to demonstrate the amyloid cascade hypothesis in vivo 24. The approval of Leqembi (January 2023, accelerated; July 2023, full) and Kisunla (July 2024) established the first validated class of disease-modifying therapies, demonstrating that selective amyloid clearance in early symptomatic populations could produce statistically significant and clinically meaningful reductions in the rate of cognitive decline as measured by CDR-SB 24. Collectively these drove a sharp rally in EURGBP and GBP underperformance more broadly. With only a small structural deterioration, the improvement will mainly come from the cycle and expiration of one-offs (eg the impact of flood-related spending). The fiscal situation is still fragile – although the economy has been growing north of 3% for two years, the budget deficit has narrowed by only about 1pp of GDP. And as we have highlighted many times – and as the OECD reiterated recently in its "Pensions at a Glance" publication – the main reason for that fiscal imbalance is still the pension system. However, there is no solution to the still-rising municipal debt, which could require government financial support. In September 2025, outstanding municipal debt to Eskom stood at over R100 billion. Transnet is key for the logistics sector reforms, a core element of the SONA speech. The company is too big to fail and get financial support from government. That is, the state- owned company used up a guarantee of ZAR47bn granted in December 2023, received ZAR51bn of new guarantees in May 2025 and requested a ZAR30bn cash injection in the 2025/26 fiscal year. The Treasury says there will be no new fiscal transfers to Transnet in the current year. Guarantee conditions for Transnet include turning around operational performance and debt liability management.

Inflation market implications The consequences of the BLS' seasonal updates are always somewhat circular logically, and depend on whether the market factors in the new seasonal factors to inform future seasonal patterns, and whether it forecasts CPI out on a seasonally-adjusted basis (in which case shifts in assumed seasonal factors would mechanically change projected NSA levels, and thus projected cash flows), or on a non-seasonally adjusted basis (in which case the BLS' seasonals likely have little direct consequence). Given the concerns with regards to distortions from the missing October 2025 data, we would be surprised if the market fully took the new BLS seasonals at face value. An example of how the seasonal factors could distort inflation markets can be seen in our tracking of market-implied "core" fixings in our Inflation-Linked Daily. records.text: Executive Summary 2 Key views: AI disruption related concerns have reignited volatility in Leveraged Loans, Private Credit and CLO markets given their high exposure to the Software industry. Higher leverage and lower revenues could lead to more credit stress for the Software sector, in our view. As AI disruption is an evolving process, we expect markets to discount more the fundamental risks and differentiate between Software issuer names and sub-sectors, potentially leading to more price dispersion in loans. While risks to CLOs could be material (including potential downgrades), we think these should be manageable overall. In CLOs, we expect (1) more decompression, potentially leading to wider spreads for junior debt tranches and (2) more dispersion depending on portfolio tail risks and Software exposures. We prefer Euro to US for IG tranches, given (1) their stronger technical backdrop, (2) their lower exposure to Software and (3) cheaper valuations (especially AAAs in Primary). We like Mezzanine bonds from ‘Mid-life’ deals, as they are due to exit the Reinvestment Period this year. We also like Quality US CLO Equity from H2 2024 vintage given their potential upside from reset this year. records.text: 19 February 2026 Global Economics Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 2 Overview Early 2026 has brought a dynamic and differentiated macroeconomic landscape. While geopolitical volatility remains a major topic, notably with US-Iran tensions, the market focus has widened to broader macro and thematic stories. Potential disruption from AI has been a top market theme though so far it has manifested more in accelerating market dispersion than in an aggregate market impact. And while questions over the economic disruption from AI have mounted, especially on the labour market, this discussion comes as much of the global economy is seeing a period of solid economic momentum. This backdrop comes with considerable differentiation across countries, notably on fiscal and monetary policy . This is perhaps best exemplified by the US, with markets pricing in more easing from the Fed than any other G10 central bank in 2026, even as US inflation remains broadly stable at above target (Figure 1). By contrast, other above-target G10 central banks are seeing a material slowing in inflation, except the RBA (which has now actually hiked). The dovish expectations for the Fed may be explained by a combination of AI concerns over the labour market, downside inflation drivers and the potentially more dovish bias from new Fed leadership, following Trump’s nomination of former Fed Governor Kevin Warsh for Fed Cha ir. The FDA then set enforcement deadlines for compounding pharmacies to cease production of injectable semaglutide by April 2025 (503A) and May 2025 (503B). Under Sections 503A and 503B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, compounding pharmacies are prohibited from producing drugs that are "essentially a copy" of commercially available FDA-approved drugs unless those drugs are in shortage. The FDA's guidance specifies that an "essentially a copy" determination rests on three factors: (1) same active pharmaceutical ingredient, (2) same or similar dosage strength, and (3) same route of administration. Hims' product checks all three boxes Novo Nordisk has stated the Wegovy pill is "available in all doses, in full supply, nationwide" , eliminating even the rhetorical justification for compounding. France reported negotiated wage growth at 1.6% yoy, private sector wage growth at 1.4% yoy and compensation per employee growth at 1.4% in 3Q25, with no apparent wage drift Exhibit 3. Of course, wage growth without a glimpse at productivity growth would be misleading. The focus on the drop in French labour productivity measures after Covid has vanished and perhaps for obvious reasons: the gap to Euro area productivity levels, at least vs 2019 reference points, has closed. There was a case to be made during that period that the significant rise in labour force participation and employment ratios in France pushed people into the labour market that previously weren’t. While labour productivity in conventional terms has suffered that, productivity of the total working age population (or, indeed, labour market potential) has significantly improved, a point forcefully made by Banque de France a couple of years ago. 2 And perhaps, as that process is slowing, “on-the-job productivity” improvements dominate again. In fact, since mid-24, France reports labour productivity growth close to two times its 2000-19 average, albeit from very low starting points (Exhibit 4). The economy-wide disinflation effect therefore works simultaneously through two channels: lower nominal wage growth and higher productivity growth. 2 Olivier Garnier, Thomas Zuber A Measure of efficiency in the use of labour resources: beyond productivity, Banque de France

ASI and AGT targeting for uncontrolled hypertension: Aldosterone synthase inhibitors (ASI) address hypertension treatment resistance by suppressing hormone synthesis rather than blocking the mineralocorticoid receptor. AZN's ASI drug baxdrostat Phase 3 study showed systolic blood pressure reductions of 14.5/15.7 mm Hg with 1/2 mg dosing vs. 5.8 mm Hg with placebo on top of background therapy for patients with uncontrolled hypertension. Angiotensinogen (AGT) is the primary substrate and sole precursor of all angiotensin peptides, representing another emerging target for uncontrolled hypertension. Zilebesiran (from ALNY/ ROG), a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA, targets AGT at the upstream of renin-angiotensin cascade to address RAAS escape and have lowering effect of blood pressure. The Phase 2 KARDIA-3 study showed a single dose of zilebesiran resulted in pbo-adjusted office systolic blood pressure reduction of 5.0 mmHg (p=0.043) at the month 3. Zilebesiran has been advanced in Phase 3 CVOT trial to evaluate combo use with 2+ antihypertensive drugs in patients with uncontrolled hypertension with high CV risk. This dual-IBD positioning is a genuine competitive advantage in a market where physician preference and treatment sequencing decisions increasingly favor agents with evidence across both conditions. The long-term extension (LUCENT-3, 152 weeks) demonstrated durable responses: using non-responder imputation, 71.6% of Week 52 responders maintained response at Week 152, and 49.5% maintained remission. Urgency scores remained stable, and safety was favorable throughout — a critical consideration for what is typically a young patient population on long-term immunosuppression. Amgen’s Amjevita was the first adalimumab biosimilar to launch, followed by a second wave in June 2023 (Pfizer, Boehringer Ingelheim, Sandoz, Samsung Bioepis, etc.). Many initially assumed a larger portion of Humira’s revenue would shift to biosimilars, yet AbbVie successfully retained most of that revenue within its immunology franchise. Instead of protecting Humira's market share by increasing rebates, AbbVie let the net price of Humira fall, resulting in a shrinking rebate pool for the PBMs. This decision successfully protected AbbVie's pricing power on Skyrizi and Rinvoq, which further allows AbbVie to compete for market share based on clinical outcomes rather than rebate dynamics. Both are from the IMF's WEO. Our twin deficit score TDS(t) is a weighted average of recent years' TD, i.e., TD(t), TD(t-1), …, TD(t-5), assigning a larger weight to the most recent print. We also incorporate the cumulative sum of TD of previous years. That allows to capture both the flow and stock characteristics of this variable. We then run daily regressions of each year's TDS vs 10y EGB spreads to Bund. The regression excludes Italy, Portugal and Ireland. These daily regressions generate time series of the slope (proxy for market price of risk), the constant, and the residuals of each country's spread. Olpasiran has demonstrated meaningful LP(a) reduction in the Ph.2 OCEAN (a) Dose study, where over 95% of LP(a) was observed across multiple dosages. Olpasiran was safe and well tolerated as well. However, the clinical connection between lowering LP(a) and reducing CVD has not been validated clinically. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] represents one of the most important genetically determined cardiovascular risk factors, affecting approximately 1.4-2 billion individuals globally. After decades of unmet medical need, the field has entered a transformative period with four distinct therapeutic modalities in advanced clinical development. Approximately 20-25% of the global adult population (1.4-2 billion individuals) have Lp(a) levels exceeding 50 mg/dL (125 nmol/L), the threshold associated with increased cardiovascular risk. In the relapsed/refractory population, ORR was 84.0% for Jaypirca versus 74.8% for ibrutinib. Tariffs induced stockpiling and intertemporal substitution 2025 saw a five-fold increase in US effective tariffs, from slightly above 2% to close to 11%. This shock put upward pressure on goods inflation, which climbed to keep overall inflation uncomfortably close to 3%. But what happened to the US external accounts? Did higher prices and a weaker dollar drive a collapse in imports? Not really. The prospect for higher tariffs led to an unprecedented import frontloading boom since Trump was elected until March of 2025, with the trade deficit widening by 50%. After this stockpiling and intertemporal substitution, the US trade deficit then shrunk to somewhat smaller levels than usual. However, the latest data for December 2025 shows the trade deficit widening again towards its recent trajectory of close to 2.5% of GDP. But investment is strong, savings are low, and the fiscal deficit sticky high Then, what should we expect going forward? We are more bullish on US growth than consensus, driven by strong investment and consumption, which means the current account deficit is here to stay. The AI- and tech-related investment boom in 2025 is expected to extend into 2026, even if its contribution to growth diminishes. Clinical studies for secondary and primary prevention of CVD would further drive uptake Landmark CVOT trials for GLP-1 included (1) Phase 3 SELECT trial evaluating Wegovy in patients with established CVD and obesity with data reported in 2023 and (2) Phase 3 SURMOUNT-MMO trial evaluating Zepbound in patients with either established CVD or CV risk factor with data expected in 2027 per clinicaltrials.gov. SELECT trial showed that patients had 9.4% weight loss with Wegovy vs. 0.9% with placebo with mean duration of drug exposure and follow-up of 34.2 and 39.8 months, respectively. A primary CV endpoint occurred in 6.5% patients in Wegovy vs. in 8.0% patients in placebo arm, indicating 0.80 HR with p<0.001. This study suggested that weight loss not only resulted in improvements in glucose levels, CV intermediate risk factors, and adipose tissue depots that may contribute to atherosclerosis and myocardial dysfunction, but also supported Wegovy's broader uptake for secondary prevention of CVD in patients with overweight and obesity. 19 February 2026 40 Barclays | U.S. Biopharmaceuticals

According to a survey conducted during Oct-Nov 2025 (LINK), 12% U.S. adults were taking GLP-1 drug and 43% obese/overweight patients who were not taking GLP-1 drugs were interested, showing a strong penetration trend. Given the expanding epidemic, obesity is estimated to overtake oncology as large-cap pharmaceutical companies' largest revenue segment with extraordinary growth headroom. Strong consumer demand Among those who reported ever taking the GLP-1 drugs in a recent survey, 61% said that they took the drugs to treat a chronic condition such as diabetes or heart disease, and 38% said that they took the drugs solely to lose weight (LINK). Notably, 15% of GLP-1 users reported no diagnosis of diabetes, heart disease, or obesity, suggesting prevalent off-label use - which is unprecedented in the pharmaceutical industry. Analysis of social media revealed behavioral patterns of consumer markets, including insurance-to-cash-pay switching, price-driven brand switching, consumers teaching consumers, and episodic/seasonal use patterns. Oral products unlock new patients Oral once daily 25mg Wegovy and 36mg orforglipron achieved 16.6% and 12.4% weight loss in clinical studies, respectively, both representing substantial improvement over the pre-GLP-1 oral therapies. records.text: 10 Europe Economic Weekly | 20 February 2026 Services inflation fell to 4.4% but the decline was less than expected. Within services, there was a decline in housing services, transport services and miscellaneous services/ education. Airfares fell by 26.5%m/m in Jan. vs a 19% fall last January causing a fall in airfare inflation. At the same time, there were favourable base effects as the rise in VAT on private schools last Jan dropped out. The main categories within services that strengthened were recreational and personal services (which rose from 4.1% to 4.6%) and communication. Within recreation, there was a pickup in non-catering recreation and personal services and accommodation. Overall underlying services rose- services ex accommodation, airfares, education and packaged holidays rose from 4.5% to 4.6% and BoE’s measure of underlying services inflation (services excluding indexed and volatile components, rents and foreign holidays' measure) rose from 4.0% to 4.3%. We expect inflation to fall more decisively from April, partly due to Budget measures, to reach 2% by H2 2026. Our forecasts for inflation remain at 2.2%/2.0% in 2026/27 while our forecasts for core move a bit higher to 2.4/2.0% (from 2.3%/1.9%) partly due to weight changes. records.text: core CPI rose just 0.17% and 0.30%, respectively, in January, somewhat lower than our and consensus forecasts. Core CPI ticked down to 2.5% on a year-ago basis, the lowest in nearly five years. records.text: Foreign Exchange Forecasts 19 February 2026 Citi Research 19 CZK Martin Motl EURCZK Forecasts: 0-3m 24.3, 6-12m 24.4 Over a three-month horizon, we expect the EUR/CZK exchange rate to trade at a slightly weaker level, around 24.31. This projection primarily reflects the CNB’s communication, which has pointed to a preference for waiting for appropriate conditions to implement a modest rate cut in an environment where headline inflation has fallen below 2%. Such guidance may reduce the relative attractiveness of koruna-denominated assets. This tendency could gradually intensify as elevated core inflation pressures continue to ease. At the same time, the economy is entering a phase of mild overheating, driven by strong domestic demand and a more expansionary fiscal stance. In the short term, this may increase the import intensity of growth and dampen appreciation pressures on the currency. In the medium term, we therefore anticipate a further moderate weakening toward 24.44 EUR/CZK. Over the longer horizon, we expect the koruna to strengthen again toward 24.2 EUR/CZK. This outlook is underpinned by the combination of a still relatively restrictive monetary policy stance—reflected in a positive interest rate differential vis-à-vis euro area rates—and the continued robust performance of the Czech economy, which should benefit more visibly from a recovery in external demand, translating into stronger net exports. With this and the India-EU FTA having become a reality now, downside risks to growth have reduced. The median estimate of professional forecasters for FY27 growth is at 6.8%yoy (FY26 at 7.5%), as per the RBI’s latest survey but note that this survey was done before the announcement of the India-USA trade deal; so, it is likely that the FY27 growth forecasts will be revised higher, incorporating the positive news. Inflation and monetary policy: For FY27, our headline CPI inflation forecast is unchanged at 4.3% (median estimate of professional forecasters is at 4.0%). Landscape of Major FXI-targeting Therapies Source: Barclays Research and Company Reports FXIa (Factor XIa) targeting for thrombosis: FXIa plays a key role in the activation and amplification of the coagulation cascade via the intrinsic pathway. The coagulation cascade generates thrombin, activates platelets, and produces fibrin, which are structural backbone of a thrombus or blood clot. Initial Phase 3 studies for this class faced major setbacks. BAYN's Phase 3 OCEANIC-AF trial, evaluating asundexian for stroke or systemic embolism prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), was terminated in Nov 2023 due to inferior efficacy vs. apixaban. BMY/JNJ's Phase 3 LIBREXIA-ACS, evaluating milvexian in patients with recent acute coronary syndrom (ACS), was discontinued in Nov 2025 due to unlikeliness meeting its primary endpoint. In Feb 2026, BAYN reported positive Phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE data, showing that asundexian reduced recurrent ischaemic stroke by 26% vs. placebo without increasing major bleeding risk. The absolute risk reduction of stroke was 2.2% (6.6% vs. 8.8%; csHR 0.74, p<.0001) and the absolute risk increase of major bleeds was 0.2% (1.9% vs. 1.7%; HR 1.10). This study represents the first successful Phase 3 validation of FXIa inhibition for the prevention of recurrent stroke. This composite improvement was driven by gains in both the services and manufacturing sectors, though manufacturing saw the more significant upturn. The Manufacturing PMI surged 1.3 points to its highest level since June 2022, spurred by strengthening demand that prompted firms to increase production and build inventories. This improved demand outlook appears to be offsetting any potential headwinds from a stronger currency. While price pressures in the services sector eased slightly, they remain at a high level. Conversely, price pressures are mounting in manufacturing, with firms passing on rising raw material costs, a sign of confidence in future demand. Overall, the latest PMI data paint a constructive picture of the euro-area economy gaining momentum after a softer start to the year. The data point towards an impending acceleration led by the core countries, with the manufacturing sector poised to become the primary driver of growth. While strong domestic demand may be moderating as the effects of monetary policy normalisation fade, the strengthening manufacturing sector signals that the economy is on track to expand above its potential this spring. There are, of course, some pockets of weakness: China’s PMIs have had a soft start to the year, and US consumer data have undershot, although there may be some weather impact there. But the broader picture is still consistent with our above-consensus growth outlook for 2026, with tailwinds from easier financial conditions and fiscal support. Alongside the US fiscal impulse this year, there are more signs that German fiscal spending is leading to a pick-up in German industrial dynamics, and after the landslide election victory for the LDP in Japan, fiscal support there is also likely to be bolstered. Market pricing of growth has been choppier relative to the signal from the data, but our estimates are that the market is still pricing growth below the 2.5% we see for the US through the year, so there is room for the market to upgrade its cyclical view further. records.text: In this Analyst, we examine why productivity growth has improved and assess the implications for the outlook. Underlying Trend Probably Improving but Unlikely to Fully Explain Recent Uptick Our forecasts have for some time assumed that trend productivity growth would increase. Our baseline expectation has been that the underlying growth trend should improve to 0.8%, with further improvement from 2028 onwards as the impact of AI kicks in. On our estimates, then, an improvement in trend productivity could account for around 0.2pp of the improvement in productivity growth relative to 2010-19 average. The recent data raise the question of whether we should assume a larger increase in the underlying trend, as opposed to assuming that the increase relates to more temporary factors. However, productivity growth has been volatile historically, which cautions against assuming a more significant trend change based on a few quarters of data. This low signal-to-noise ratio means that a simple statistical model designed to extract the trend from temporary fluctuations only finds a modest uptick in the underlying pace recently. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 12 February 2026 J P M O R G A N AI-ppetite for Disruption (Take Two) “AI-ppetitite for Disruption” in our 11/25/2025 CLO Outlook seemed to presage the trend in the early part of this year. AI Disruption may not immediately erode credit quality, but the impact on software loan pricing has been rapid and widespread, posing risks to CLOs. To recap, US CLOs have an average of ~12.4% software (see here) and Euro CLOs ~9.0% (see here), which, while not systemic, is high enough to have started affecting market sentiment. Wages in the public sector are set to rise 5.8% cumulatively over 27 months (2.8% in Apr-26, 2% in Mar-27 and 1% in Jan-28). This is a clear step down compared to the last settlement at ca. 11% rise over 25 months (a €200 base rise followed by 5.5%) and well below the unions' initial ask for 7% over 12 months. In our update, we also reflect that the agreement is applied to other workers close to the public sector and covers in total ca 2.2mil employees (4.8% of total employment). This raises the total coverage of the tracker coverage to 17.8mil employees (39% of total employment), and puts it on par with the German sample in the ECB tracker (see here). The tracker projects a notable step down in negotiated wage growth (2.9%Y from 5.3% in 2025): We continue to see a notable decline in negotiated wage growth, excluding one-offs (Exhibit 17 ). On average, negotiated wage growth could fall to 2.9% in 2026, after 5.3%Y in 2025 in our tracker (vs 5.5%Y for Bundesbank's indicator in 2025). The CPI is designed to track how the average cost of a fixed basket of goods and services has changed over time, while the Truflation metric tracks more near-term price changes for a constantly evolving basket of goods and services. As a result, it seems intuitive that the top-line CPI and Truflation measures are not perfectly correlated. records.text: Foreign Exchange Forecasts 19 February 2026 Citi Research 10 JPY USDJPY Forecasts: 0-3m 152, 6-12m 145 n0-3m: Despite the landslide victory by the LDP led by PM Sanae Takaichi at the February 8th general election, USDJPY has declined. Another gain by Japanese stocks should be producing JPY weakening pressure via hedge activities by domestic and overseas investors. Under the recent risk-on market environment, it will not be easy for the pair to decline below the support at around 152 in our view, the level registered when USDJPY dropped late January with the rate checks by the Japanese and US currency authorities. Even so, the narrowing US- Japan interest rate differential is thought to be putting downward pressure on USDJPY. Thus, the pair has been range-bound despite the re`cent substantial rally in Japanese equities. In the case USDJPY tops 160, we suspect the Japanese government and the MoF will resort to JPY-buying interventions. n6-12m: Our outlook doesn’t depend on the intervention story, but it will be a factor to cap the upside of the pair. Thus, we continuously believe around ¥155/$ will be the long-term ceiling for the USDJPY and the pair will correct lower toward ¥145/$ over the next several months. In our view, JGB yields have already reached the level where Japanese long-term investors invest in domestic bonds more aggressively, and we believe the elevated bond yield will start contributing to JPY’s medium-term recovery. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 20 February 2026 Weekly view Still hoping for the best This time last week, EU leaders held their informal retreat. The result was a promise to look into progress on the Draghi and Letta reports: the savings and investment union; deepening the single market; and simplifying EU rules for business. In essence, getting closer to a proper EU single market, rather than today’s goods-sector-centric version thereof. A follow-up on the discussion is now planned for the formal 19-20 March EU summit, with a roadmap from the European Commission on “one Europe, one market”. We are still hoping for progress, of course, but would need more evidence thereof to get excited. The track record of “hope” as a base case so far has not been great. Letta’s report on the future of the single market was released in April 2024, Draghi’s report on EU competitiveness was released in September that year. Promises have been recurring, follow-up action not so much. Perhaps we are too dismissive, and something really is different in the EU modus operandi in 2026. Typically, Europe needs big shocks and an acute sense of urgency to move and arguably the geopolitical situation and deteriorated US relations qualify as such. Last year’s Munich Security Conference was one of these events, and probably helped the German move to deliver very big fiscal reform unexpectedly and swiftly, despite adverse election outcomes. Japan fiscal year end approaches The April 1 st fiscal new year in Japan brings with it perceived tendencies for spot and volatility. The thinking is that repatriation flow prior to the date strengthens the JPY and pushes volatility higher, and then these reverse in April when outflows recommence, with volatility reversing course. In spot terms, this was more a feature of price action in the 1980s and 90s and hasn’t really held up – March has tended to bring more yen weakness than April over the last 30 years. But volatility markets still seem to price for it, with a pronounced hump in curves, especially for puts, centered on the 2-3 month point. AUD hedgers in focus Eight years ago, we highlighted the importance of Australian investors in their contribution to flows and movements in the AUD. The selling of the AUD in Figure 1 on page 1 is in stark contrast to strength in the currency and the domestic hedging community might explain the difference. records.text: Second part of report title 2 Aluminium: Deteriorating supply outlook, growing price support KEY MESSAGES We upgrade our 2026 and 2027 aluminium price forecasts: We lift our end-2026 price expectations by USD200/t due to deteriorating supply growth and a tighter market. We also upgrade our H1 2027 forecast but leave our already bullish end- 2027 target unchanged . Limited supply growth: The market should tighten in 2026-27, even allowing for slower demand, due to China reaching its self-imposed production cap, slow Indonesian capacity build-out and ramp-up, as well as smelter closures or outages (Mozal, Grundartangi ). We expect a global deficit of at least 431kt this year, rising to more than 600kt in 2027, with tightening fundamentals and time spreads supporting prices. Heavy fund flows since November have added to the price-positive narrative: Speculative net long positions in LME aluminium reached record highs in January 2026, as part of a wider rotation into metals from the energy complex. We see growing speculative interest in hard-asset exposure as a result of heightened geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty. Deeper backwardation beckons in LME forward curve: Near-term (cash-to- 3month) and longer-dated (3-15month) LME aluminium spreads have narrowed since the ‘Liberation Day’ tariff shock on 2 April 2025. While spreads have eased into February, we expect growing physical tightness to push the market into deeper backwardation in 2026. Risks: We see the main risks

records.text: European Economics 20 February 2026 Citi Research 4 Is the fiscal impulse seen in activity data yet? There has been, until recently, no clear statistical manifestation in activity data of Germany’s fiscal push, though there might have been indirect effects. The budgets for 2025 and 2026 were only passed in autumn last year, which is also when the SVIK started borrowing operations (though its theoretical coverage was backdated to January 2025). It’s thus not surprising that tangible impact is limited, though that does not mean it was non-existent: sentiment indicators had been picking up on the back of spending promises for a while (and even dipped again due to disappointment at pace, magnitude and nature of deployment), and consumption, investment and employment behaviour might well have been impacted accordingly. These indirect effects are however hard to gauge and separate from other drivers, e.g. the generalised pick-up in investment which, we think, looks at least partly to have been caused by AI-related expenditure. Similarly, for 2026, central banks are generally projected to either ease further (including the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England) or remain on hold (such as the ECB). Notably, the global economy has not endured a downturn driven by economic, financial, or even geopolitical factors since the GFC nearly two decades ago—The only full-blown recession during this two-decade period was triggered by a global pandemic, which was an entirely exogenous shock. A breakdown of sticky inflation reveals that goods fell to 3.4% from 3.8%, while general services held at 2.2%. • Looking ahead, we expect goods inflation to continue easing, led by food, due to y/y base effects. However, we look for services to underpin overall inflation as the synergy between wages and inflation strengthens with the irreversible structural changes in the labor market. As a result, we expect inflation to trend slightly above the 2% inflation target until the start of 2027. Reflecting the January data, we project BoJ core CPI inflation of +3.0% in FY25 and +2.2% in FY26, along with core inflation of +2.7% and +2.0%, respectively. • Today’s nationwide CPI data for January reaffirmed that BoJ core inflation, which is not directly affected by energy policies, remains on a gentle downward trend led mainly by food. This is likely in line with the inflation path envisioned by the BoJ, suggesting any impact on the the rate hike trajectory should be limited. Even as BoJ core inflation remains on a downward trend, the “composite index of inflation expectations, ” one of the underlying inflation indicators that the BoJ relies on as a basis for rate hikes, continues to show an upward trend. records.text: CMI market expansion in HCM, expecting strong launch for Myqorzo with best-in-class potential HCM - a chronic genetic heart disease Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a chronic and genetic heart disease characterized by a thickened left ventricle (LV), which reduces the amount of blood pumped by heart and impairs longevity and quality of life. About 2/3 of HCM patients develop obstructive form (oHCM), which is characterized by dynamic LV outﬂow tract obstruction (LVOT), and 1/3 patients are considered to have non-obstructive form (nHCM). HCM is caused by mutations in genes encoding cardiac sarcomeric proteins that destabilize the super-relaxed state of myosin and promote excessive actin-myosin cross-bridges. HCM prevalence is estimated at 1 in 500 people carrying genetic mutations and 1 in 3,000 developing symptomatic HCM. Both forms of HCM are highly symptomatic and can cause shortness of breadth, pounding heartbeats, chest pain, and decreased exercise capacity. Historically, oHCM patients with refractory or severe symptoms were referred to a surgeon for myectomy/ablation and transplant for nHCM patients, due to lack of disease modifying therapies. The clinical diagnosis of HCM in adult patients can be established by imaging with echocardiography (Echo) or cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showing a maximal end- diastolic wall thickness of ≥15 mm in the left ventricle (LV). Obstacles to internal trade include (a) regulatory barriers, (b) administrative barriers, (c) enforcement barriers, (d) competition-related barriers, and (e) other barriers (Exhibit 1). For a business from one EU member state to establish a permanent presence in another EU member state, generally requires the incorporation of a local subsidiary. This involves navigating differences in the corporate law system (e.g. governance, board structure, securities, and bankruptcy) and business regulation, and dealing with national tax agencies and judicial systems. This stands in contrast to the prevailing approach in the US, where most firms incorporate in Delaware – the national incorporation hub, allowing for same-day incorporation – and remain subject to its law for all internal affairs (e.g. corporate governance). While conducting business in other US states generally requires setting up local branches and dealing with state law on employment and taxation matters, the Delaware system and a harmonised bankruptcy and securities law across all states provide clarity and predictability to corporates. Approval must happen by 31 May: Morena plans to start discussing the reform as early as February and to aim for approval before the regular legislative session ends in April. If this does not happen, the party will seek to convene an extraordinary session to approve the reform. The timing is crucial as the 2027 electoral cycle formally begins on 1 September 2026, and Article 105 of the constitution states that any federal or local electoral law must be published at least 90 days before the start of the cycle in which it is to be applied. Passage may be difficult: Constitutional changes require two-thirds majorities in the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, plus at least 17 of 32 local congresses. That equates to 334 deputies and 86 senators. However, Morena’s coalition partners – the Green Party (PVEM) and the Labor Party (PT) – have rejected the proposal in its current form, as it implies their extinction. The "easy growth" era of Gardasil volume expansion has been disrupted by geopolitical and competitive headwinds, forcing a strategic pivot toward new high-barrier assets in the adult pneumococcal, RSV, and Dengue markets. records.text: erg Company Overview and Context Company Overview AbbVie is a global biopharmaceutical company headquartered in North Chicago, Illinois, that discovers, develops, manufactures, and commercializes medicines across immunology, oncology, neuroscience, aesthetics, and eye care. The immunology portfolio is anchored by Skyrizi (risankizumab), an IL-23 inhibitor approved across psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis, and Rinvoq (upadacitinib), a JAK inhibitor approved across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, atopic dermatitis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, ankylosing spondylitis, and giant cell arteritis, with additional indications in development. Humira (adalimumab), formerly the world's best-selling drug, faces ongoing biosimilar erosion following U.S. loss of exclusivity in 2023. In neuroscience, AbbVie markets Vraylar (cariprazine) in psychiatry, Ubrelvy (ubrogepant) and Qulipta (atogepant) in migraine, Botox Therapeutic, and Vyalev (foscarbidopa/foslevodopa), a continuous subcutaneous infusion for motor fluctuations in advanced Parkinson's disease. Within the year, Bank of America showed some appetite for agency CMBS ($11bn in AFS) and reduced substantially in conventional pass-throughs (-$31bn in HTM). Meanwhile, Wells Fargo ($11bn) and State Street ($7bn) were notable buyers of CMOs. Citi and US Bank also showed selective interest in Ginnie exposure in AFS. records.text: 4 Europe Economic Weekly | 20 February 2026 Euro area Spain: momentum now, headwinds later Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com • We continue to expect Spanish outperformance of the Euro area in 2026/27 with growth at 2.3% and 1.6%, respectively. • Recent tailwinds should still help for a while. Concerns over an NGEU fiscal cliff or a housing market bubble seem overdone. • But we reiterate our long-held view: the challenge of upcoming population ageing for growth and public finances is very big. Still outperforming, though risks loom Spain continues to grow faster than the Euro area, helped by strong immigration, solid consumption, and steady support from EU recovery funds. The quality of growth has also improved (less government support), fiscal policy remains supportive, and we see no housing bubble (lack of supply, rather than a credit boom). However, the longer-term picture is more uncertain as EU funds come to an end. We are optimistic Spain can bridge the gap and there will be no fiscal cliff. For gilts with residual maturity of greater than 3yrs, the maximum lending term remains one week. The change in lending capacity availability would add approximately £22bn to the APF's collateral pool taking to it around £45bn from £23bn currently. The Bank describes the increase as " a precautionary measure to ensure a sufficient supply of remaining APF gilts is available for on-lending to the market, if required, as the size of the APF continues to fall" . In our view, this is the Bank indirectly conveying an important operational message to the market. It is a tacit admission that the medium-term pace of collateral replacement is never likely to be fast enough to prevent ongoing and increasing repo market frictions. This is because as its repo operations grow, collateral that is tied up in the APF cannot be permanently returned to the market due to practical constraints on the size of future QT cycles. This leaves the on-lending facility likely to be a main conduit for APF collateral recycling. A sharp drop in inflation at the beginning of the year and moderation in service price momentum create some space for gradual monetary policy easing. We expect the National Bank of Hungary to embark on a rate cutting cycle already in February and we expect at least three rate cuts in full 2026, with risks skewed in the direction of even more easing. The key factor to watch over next two months is the general election scheduled for April 12th. Poland The Polish economy remains resilient and we expect GDP growth to reach at least 4% in 2026. The inflow of EU funds this year will likely help boost investment activity and the growth will be supported by accommodative fiscal policy. In January inflation fell less than we had expected, but we assess the upward surprise was largely due to changes in calculation methodology, rather than an actual increase in underlying price pressures. Our forecasts suggest the CPI will fluctuate around 2% in the coming months. After cutting its policy rate by 175bps in 2025, the central bank is likely to shift toward a more gradualist approach. Given that the real rate is already close to its long-term average and fiscal policy remains loose, we believe the scope for further rate cuts is limited. Our base case assumes two more rate cuts this year, with the policy rate finally reaching 3.5%. Pipeline therapies could address unmet needs with improved convenience or muscle preservation Obesity drugs in pipeline for weight loss mostly focused on decreasing energy intake. Key programs focused on (1) targeting novel gut hormones (glucagon, amylin, calcitonin, Peptide YY agonists, etc) with/without GLP-1/GIP agonism and (2) reduced treatment burden with GLP-1 oral formulations (semaglutide, ECC5004, GSBR-1290, LY3549492, orforglipron, TERN-601, PF-07976016) or less frequent Q4W injection (MET-097i, etc.). records.text: EDG-7500 Phase 2 efficacy appeared better, but safety worth a closer look EWTX's (not covered) EDG-7500 is the 3rd gen small molecule cardiac sarcomere modulator EDG-7500 aimed to slow actin-myosin engagement in HCM without LVEF reduction. Although the target was not disclosed, preclinical data showed that EDG-7500 preserved the enzymatic activity of myosin ATPase, suggesting a distinct MOA compared to Camzyos and Myqorzo. EWTX reported Phase 2 CIRRUS part B data from 12 oHCM patients and part C data from 7 nHCM patients with 4-wk follow-up in April 2025. oHCM data showed dose dependent activity, including 43/58% (50/100 mg) reduction in valsalva LVOT-G, 38/71% reduction in resting LVOT-G, 47/62% reduction in NT-proBNP , 43/78% patients with ≥1 NYHA improvement, and 4/20 increase in KCCQ-CSS. nHCM data showed 16/22 increase in KCCQ-CSS and 32/42% reduction in NT- proBNP with 50/100 mg doses. Additionally, a shallow plasma concentration to LVEF relationship with narrow dispersion suggested no meaningful LVEF reduction in current dose regimen. EDG-7500 safety worth a closer look. Adverse events reported from Phase 2 CIRRUS part B/C from 29 patients with 4-wk follow-up, included 4 (13.8%) atrial fibrillation (afib), 5 (17.2%) upper respiratory tract infection, and 8 (27.6%) dizziness in which 1 patient discontinued. Bloomberg reported (here) that in anticipation of a potential ruling nearly 1,000 firms had filed cases with the Court of International Trade (CIT), likely to ensure eligibility for a refund. The CIT confirmed in December that even if importers have had their final duties assessed, it has the authority to order refunds though reliquidation (see here for details). The court also stayed all IEEPA refund cases awaiting a ruling from the SCOTUS. But, the next steps on eligibility and the process for refunds still needs to be decided by the CIT. records.text: iopharma. Will Staffing Shortages Materialize or Have Meaningful Impact in 2026? We believe the near- to-mid term impact may be more limited than feared. In FY25, the FDA approved 46 new drugs, which is right in line with historical average in the 2015-2025 period (average of 46). Of the 46 new drugs, 39% (18/46) were granted fast track status, increasing the level of communication between FDA and sponsor, 33% (15/46) were granted breakthrough therapy designation, which offers intensive FDA guidance and involvement from senior managers, and 46% (21/46) of all drug approvals in 2025 received priority review, reducing the review time from ~10 months to ~6 months. In addition, 24% (11/46) of new drugs were approved under the accelerated approval pathway. This pathway enables approval using either surrogate endpoint(s) or an intermediate clinical endpoint, both of which are deemed reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. Another key metric - meeting PDUFA goal date – was also high in FY25 with 96% of drug reviews (44/46) meeting their PDUFA goals. In FY26, we anticipate the pace of new drug approvals is likely to keep pace with historical levels, which is another positive tailwind for the space. records.text: President Claudia Sheinbaum remains very popular in Mexico well into her second year in office (Figure 24) despite a weak economy. Electoral reform’s goal – boost the ruling party: The proposed electoral reform would reduce the number of plurinominal seats by half. records.text: Bristol Myers has shown encouraging Phase 2 data for admilparant (LPA1 antagonist) as well as for a prior first-gen asset. For admilparant, at 60mg BID, there was a 44% benefit in mean FVC decline over a 26 week period, although another dose level tested (30mg BID) performed worse compared to placebo. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 45 Weekly Summary for Overseas Investors Market Recap While the recent lows in the mortgage rate were notable, we think the most important thing this week was the Fedspeak, as Governor Bowman seemed to view this week as one in which she wanted to consistently share her views on possible regulatory easing that could be coming. On Tuesday, she spoke about Revitalizing Bank Mortgage Lending, One Step with Basel where she suggested two changes were coming - one that would no longer remove the requirement to deduct mortgage servicing assets from bank regulatory capital, and another to potentially ease risk weights on mortgage loans that banks hold via a granular L TV approach instead of giving every loan the same 50% risk weight. We discussed this in a note out earlier this week with our consumer finance and banking analysts, but this very much aligns with our expectations of reduced regulatory actions being positive for bank demand for risk assets in general. We still have a few questions, including the actual details of the plan to determine how much relief there may be for banks, but on Wednesday, Governor Bowman then said that the proposal is on track for 1Q26, which is likely the earliest that we think this could be realistically done. If we simplistically assume right now banks have to hold about $165bn against their residential loans currently carrying a 50% risk weight - it's roughly 2.2tn of loans * 50% risk weight * ~15% risk-based capital

Lp(a) lowering: Lp(a) [lipoprotein(a)] is codified by the LPA gene and synthesized in the liver, containing apoB-100 (apolipoprotein B-100) covalently linked to apoA (apolipoprotein A). GalNAc-conjugated RNA therapies were developed to knockdown LPA messenger RNA and inhibit apoA protein synthesis. Significant and durable Lp(a) reduction were achieved in early clinical trials, and the impact on secondary cardiovascular disease prevention is the key focus with data expected in 2026 and onwards. Pelacarsen (from IONS/NVS) was an ASO, which achieved up to 80% Lp(a) reduction with monthly injection. Olpasiran (from ARWR/AMGN) was an siRNA, which reduced Lp(a) by 98% with quarterly injection. Similarly, lepodisiran (from LLY) reduced Lp(a) by 98% with semi-annual dosing. records.text: Previous Attempts The 28th regime/EU Inc initiative is not the first attempt at an optional EU-wide corporate form. In 2001, the EU introduced the Societas Europaea (SE), an optional and partly harmonised company form available across the EU that aimed to facilitate cross-border mobility and enjoyed modest take-up. The statute was implemented in a hybrid form with an EU regulation defining how an SE can be formed, its minimum capital requirement, and procedures for cross-border transfers, while other elements – including governance, insolvency, reporting, and labour and tax law – remained subject to national law. The SE statute attracted criticism as it could facilitate the circumvention of corporate governance laws in jurisdictions with strict rules on co-determination1 and because of elevated barriers for SMEs. Today, cross-border transactions remain the preferred option for company mobility (Exhibit 4, left). Given the limited take-up of the SE statute by start-ups and SMEs, the EU attempted to introduce similar regimes targeted at smaller-sized firms, through the Societas Privata Europaea (SPE) in 2008 and through the Societas Unius Personae (SUP) in 2014. Both envisioned digital registration and facilitated cross-border mobility but failed to receive support due to concerns around tax avoidance and corporate governance circumvention (Exhibit 4, right). 1 Participation of workers in the management of the company, for example via seats on the management or supervisory boar

records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 19 February 2026 Citi Research 5 The Outlook for Inflation & Central Banks Global growth has been supported by the quiescent performance of inflation. In recent years, headline inflation has retreated to 2%, and “core” inflation—while tracking slightly higher—has also been subdued (Figure 4). With growth projected to remain near trend, which suggests limited additional pressures on labor markets and other resources, we see inflation staying contained going forward. A year ago, we were worried about inflation pressures from a global “trade war” in which US tariffs would elicit significant retaliation from trading partners. But once US tariffs were actually in place, most countries chose to negotiate rather than retaliate. Moreover, even in the United States, the tariffs’ inflation effects have been surprisingly contained as, by our calculations, US firms have absorbed roughly half the toll. The upshot is that the inflationary imprint of the tariffs has been more muted than we had feared in both the United States and the rest of the world. In this context, we also are watching the evolution of commodity markets (Figure 5). Recent geopolitical developments, particularly in Venezuela, have pushed up the price of Brent oil to around $70 per barrel. However, this upward move is likely to be short lived. Favorable underlying supply conditions look poised to bring oil prices back down to near $60 per barrel in coming months. Figure 4. Global Inflati

records.text: (Figure 9). With the bulk of Q1 syndicated supply out of the way and idiosyncratic risks contained, we think peripheral spreads are likely to continue trading with a high correlation. Regarding high-quality core EGBs, Irish spreads had previously been lagging somewhat, but have tightened over the past trading session. We see potential for Irish spreads to remain supported, with the DMO having already placed its 10y deal (raising €5bn versus the planned €10-14bn funding range), while rating upgrades are a possibility (Moody's and S&P have had positive outlooks in place since August and November 2024, and will review Ireland on 20 February and 20 March, respectively). Elsewhere, 10y Dutch spreads have been trading with a resilient tone lately; the question will be whether they can maintain this resilience into the 10y DDA on 3 March. As for the long end, Figure 10 illustrates 60d z-scores for 10s30s boxes versus Germany. In general, these boxes have remained resilient, following on from bull-flattening dynamics seen last year (as discussed in the EGBs chapter of our 2026 outlook). We think recent moves may have been exacerbated by stop-outs of Buxl ASW longs, putting cheapening pressure on 30y Bunds (and thereby driving 10s30s Germany steeper versus other EGB curves). For example, should Lagarde step down this year, there may not be any French representation until May 2027 at the earlier (when Philip Lane’s term ends). Further, Spain will have no representation on the Executive Board after May. Is there a trade? Given the above, it is difficult to get too excited about an obvious trade. As a heuristic exercise to assess how consequential these estimated effects of fiscal debt changes are in the short- through long-term, we can assess the changes in high-grade corpo- rate spreads that would be implied by the trajectory of US government debt in recent decades based on these estimates. This exercise is shown in Figure 3, where the blue line shows realized spreads, while the orange line shows how spreads might change over time if driven by debt alone, after setting the initial level at year-end 1989 so that the debt-implied level roughly aligns with the prevailing spread levels in the past two decades. Quite clearly, the accumulation of government debt cannot account for cyclical movements in spreads. However, it does appear to be a quantitatively significant driver of longer-term movements, particularly since the GFC. During the 1990s, spreads generally tightened while debt-to-GDP was increasing and widened while it was decreasing, though debt does not appear to explain much of the observed change. Debt-to-GDP was reasonably stable in the pre-GFC 2000s, and thus cannot explain the period of tighter spreads in 2003-2007. However, we see a switch to better demand in Europe, but slower demand growth in the US. European auto sector outlook still challenging but some signs of improvement: Auto registrations showed modest growth through 2025, up 1.5% y/y. Consensus expectations are for this to jump to about 2.9% in 2026. More importantly for metals demand, order intake for European auto manufacturers improved through H2 2025, thanks to auto inventories being drawn down, we think – a trend we expect to continue . Europe construction activity has been beset by problems: European construction has been contracting since April 2025, but we see clear signs of the down-trend bottoming out. Indeed, we note some signs of improving optimism on pan-European pledges to increase infrastructure and defence spending. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 20/02/2026 04:07:12 GMT Distributed on: 20/02/2026 04:07:12 GMT 20 February 2026 Deutsche Bank Group Research Japan Japan Economics Data Flash Date Largely in line with expectations The nationwide Consumer Price Index (CPI) for January, released today, showed a deceleration in growth across all major indices. The headline CPI rose by +1.5% YoY (vs. +2.1% in December), the core CPI (excluding fresh food) rose by +2.0% (vs. +2.4%), and the core-core CPI (excluding fresh food and energy) increased by +2.6% (vs. +2.9%). While the core CPI matched the market consensus, the core- core CPI came in slightly below the consensus of +2.7%. However, given that the exact figure is +2.64%, the result can be considered broadly within the range of expectations. Slowing inflation driven by energy and food prices The primary drivers behind the deceleration in inflation were falling energy prices and a slower rate of increase in food prices. For energy, the effect of gasoline tax cuts contributed to the decline, and the resumption of government subsidies for electricity and gas from February is expected to be a further downward factor. In addition, a drop in fresh food prices (Jan: -6.9% YoY vs. Dec: -2.7%) pushed down both the headline and core CPI, while growth in food prices excluding fresh food also slowed (Jan: +6.2% vs. Dec: +6.7%), which in turn curbed the rise in the core- core index. records.text: TRADE IDEA T R A D E I D E A 19/02/2026 1 EM rates: Entering a CLP basis receiver *October-January AFP FX hedging uses total FX derivatives as proxy Sources: Bloomberg, BCCh, Superintendencia de Pensiones, BNP Paribas Fig. 1: The gap between foreign holdings and FX hedging remains (USDbn) We are entering a CLP basis receiver trade (1m1y). This is supported by a likely increase in FX hedging by Chilean pension funds (AFPs), which is putting downward pressure on the CLP basis. At the same time, the recent spike in the basis, driven by offshore investors’ short-CLP exposure that has now receded, leaves the basis vulnerable to a likely downward correction, we think. More AFP hedging puts downward pressure on CLP basis: The CLP basis is likely to drop as AFPs increase their FX-hedging in the coming quarters. Historically, AFPs’ hedging activity has tracked the size of their foreign-asset holdings, but that relationship broke down at the end of 2023: foreign assets surged while the corresponding hedge volumes lagged behind (see Figure 1). Given the mismatch between AFPs’ foreign-asset holdings and their hedges – and the persistent weakness of the USD, which encourages AFPs to shore up currency-risk protection – we anticipate the funds will step up their USDCLP NDF sales, narrowing the gap between foreign holdings and AFP FX hedging. Citi Commodities still sees medium- term headwinds for gold as trade uncertainty abates, global growth remains supported, and Fed independence concerns diminish (our base case). In moments of panic selling, it makes sense to refer to our AI risk framework (see here) and be better buyers of software companies that are enterprise-focused, maintain strong balance sheets and proprietary datasets, and are mis- sion-critical. We’d be better sellers of names that have sizeable near-term maturities that could face refinancing pressures amid a more skeptical market or operate in a competitive, fragmented market. For many names, it will take time for a refinancing crunch to materialize (see here). One wrinkle is that many CLO credits are private or loan-only, and hence difficult and time consuming to individually underwrite for AI risk. At some point, it’s likely that most or every sector will see an impact from AI. Which domino will start falling next? After AI-driven fears of disruption in the software sector, this seems to have extended to insurance and financial companies as markets consider business model risk. While still a developing theme, we observe US BSL CLO exposure to financials aver- ages 9.2%, ranges as high as 17%, and includes an average 3.1% insurance. While not all CLO exposures are at risk, the market has already started pricing-in a some- what steeper liability credit curve. records.text: Second part of report title Slow Indonesia smelter build-out drives Chinese investment elsewhere: While three new smelters in Indonesia are either built or in-build, progress has been dramatically slower than the typical build and ramp-up time scales in China. This appears to be prompting a pickup in investment elsewhere by Chinese companies, including in Angola and Saudi Arabia. While Angola’s small (120kt/y) Huatong smelter project should start in H2 2026, the Shandong Innovation Group 500kt project in Yanbu, Saudi Arabia will not, in our view, be in production until well after 2028. We remain sceptical about US smelter capacity growth: The main objective of the 50% section 232 tariffs on US primary aluminium imports was to incentivise the development of US smelting capacity. US aluminium production dropped from about 6Mt/y in the early 2000s to about 670kt last year, with only four operating smelters, down from 22 plants at the start of this century. The main issue is high power prices and a lack of base load power availability, which we see deteriorating with the scrapping of renewable energy projects, combined with the rapid growth of AI data centre-related power demand. In addition, tariff uncertainty is still a significant barrier to long-term smelter investment. Media reports on 16 February 2026 hinted that the Trump administration was planning to roll back aluminium tariffs that are, in our view, negatively impacting US aluminium demand.
